#9566. What Narcissists, Psychopaths And Sadists Have In Common

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Narcissists, psychopaths, sadists and manipulative people share a dark personality core that predicts selfish and antisocial choices.

This common tendency helps explain whether people exploit others, retaliate against them or refuse to trust them.

The crucial feature is a willingness to pursue personal interests at other people’s expense, accompanied by beliefs that justify doing so.

Known as the dark factor of personality, or D, this tendency brings together traits that can look quite different on the surface.

Narcissism involves an inflated sense of self-importance, Machiavellianism centres on manipulation, psychopathy includes callousness, and sadism involves enjoying others’ suffering.

The idea that these traits share an underlying disposition was established in earlier research examining their overlap and links to harmful behaviour (Moshagen et al., 2018).

The latest findings suggest that this shared core is more consistently associated with antisocial decisions than any of the four traits considered separately.

In other words, knowing what these personalities have in common may reveal more about their choices than knowing which particular label fits them.

The research involved over 10,000 people across ten studies using eight types of decision-making game.

Participants completed personality questionnaires before making hypothetical choices involving another person they did not know.

Depending on the game, they could decide how much money to share, whether to return someone’s trust, whether to retaliate or whether to cooperate.

Some situations allowed people to benefit themselves at someone else’s expense, while others explored whether they would trust another person when cooperation could benefit both.

People scoring higher on the dark factor consistently made fewer prosocial choices across all eight games.

The individual dark traits also generally predicted less prosocial behaviour, but their associations were weaker.

Once their shared dark core was taken into account, the separate traits usually added little to the explanation.

There were a few exceptions, particularly involving Machiavellianism in situations where distrust could influence decisions.

One possible explanation is that dark personality traits combine harmful tendencies with other characteristics that are not inherently antisocial.

For example, boldness does not necessarily involve harming anyone, while wanting admiration does not automatically mean exploiting others.

Earlier research proposed that these additional characteristics help distinguish dark traits from one another, while their shared core captures what makes them socially harmful (Bader et al., 2023).

Measuring a broad trait such as psychopathy may therefore mix callous self-interest with features that have little relevance to a particular moral decision.

Focusing on the common core could provide a clearer picture of someone’s willingness to disregard other people’s welfare.

Importantly, the dark factor extends beyond wanting a larger share of the rewards.

It also encompasses a readiness to hurt others and beliefs that can make selfish conduct seem acceptable.

Distrust may fit this pattern because expecting other people to behave selfishly can provide a convenient justification for doing the same.

That is a proposed psychological explanation, rather than evidence that distrust caused the choices observed here.

The findings do not mean that everyone with dark traits will behave selfishly in every situation.

Nor do they establish that personality caused the decisions participants made.

All the games were hypothetical, so participants were describing what they would choose rather than making decisions with real financial consequences.

This matters because associations between dark traits and antisocial choices can be stronger in hypothetical situations than when money is genuinely at stake.

Participants also volunteered through a website offering dark-personality assessments, so they were not a representative sample of the wider population.

Even with these qualifications, the results support a simpler account of apparently different dark personalities: much of their connection to harmful choices lies in the same underlying disregard for others.

The study was published in the journal Judgment and Decision Making (Hilbig & Thielmann, 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9565. How to dream more: 6 tips to increase how often you dream

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA

We all know that one person who says, “You’ll never believe what I dreamt last night!” Many people who dream can become obsessed with the stories their minds show them at night. Some people believe their dreams provide insights into their subconscious, while others say they inspire creativity. And those who aren’t into the deep dream interpretation simply like the fantasy world that their minds create when they’re asleep.

If you’re fascinated by your dreams for any of these reasons, you might want to learn how to dream more and make your dreams more vivid. And while you can’t control everything—like the inevitable falling nightmare everyone has had at least once—you can do things to dream more frequently and to make those dreams easier to recall. Here are a few simple techniques and lifestyle changes you might want to try to make the most of the time you spend asleep.

When you sleep better, you’re more likely to enter the rapid eye movement (REM) part of your sleep cycle, when most dreaming occurs. This sleep cycle may increase the chances of having more frequent and vivid dreams, so here are a few tips to encourage deeper sleep.

Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day to help regulate your sleep cycle and increase the likelihood of dreaming. To get enough REM sleep, aim for 7–9 hours of sleep each night.

💙 Try relaxing an hour before bed with Soften Into Sleep, a meditation that can help you release tension at night.

Read, take a warm bath, or practice mindfulness to ease into rest and create an environment for dreaming. Avoid screens for at least an hour before bed, as the blue light can disrupt your body’s natural sleep-wake cycle. If you must use devices, try a blue light filter or dim your screen.

💙 Explore these nine tips to help you build a better bedtime routine.

To improve sleep quality and increase your chances of dreaming, keep your bedroom dark, quiet, and cool. The ideal temperature is about 60–67 degrees Fahrenheit (or 15–19 degrees Celsius). Use blackout curtains to block light, earplugs or a white noise machine to drown out noise, and invest in a comfortable mattress and pillows to support your posture.

Lastly, keep your bedroom tidy and use it only for sleep and relaxation if you can. This can help you create a mental association between your bedroom and restful sleep.

💙 Press play on one of our relaxing Soundscapes, like White Noise Ocean Surf, to help you drift off to sleep.

Practice meditation, yoga, or deep breathing exercises to help decrease anxiety so you can get a good night’s sleep, which may promote more vivid dreaming. Regular exercise can help too, but remember to avoid vigorous activity too close to bedtime.

💙 Keep stress at bay by tuning into 7 Days of Managing Stress, a stress reduction series hosted by Tamara Levitt.

Heavy meals, caffeine, or alcohol before bed can disrupt sleep and decrease dream frequency. Opt for light snacks if you're hungry, and avoid caffeine or alcohol close to bedtime.

💙 Add mindfulness to mealtime with our session on the Benefits of Mindful Eating.

Drink water throughout the day to support sleep quality, but try to limit water intake about an hour before bed to prevent trips to the bathroom in the middle of the night.

During your wind down routine, you can sip teas like chamomile or valerian root. These are thought to have calming effects that may promote relaxation and improve sleep quality, which may lead to more vivid dreams.

💙 Listen to a relaxing Sleep Story before bed, like Why Do We Sleep, while sipping tea as part of a new nighttime ritual.

Sleep is divided into several stages that cycle throughout the night, typically lasting about 90 minutes per cycle.

Stage 1 (light sleep): This is a transitional phase where you drift in and out of sleep.

Stage 2 (deeper light sleep): Your body temperature drops and your heart rate begins to slow.

Stage 3 (deep sleep): Known as slow-wave sleep, this stage promotes physical recovery and health.

REM sleep: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, where your brain activity increases and your eyes move rapidly under your eyelids, is when the most vivid dreams occur.

Melatonin is a hormone your body naturally produces that helps to regulate your sleep-wake cycles. Levels rise in the evening to help you feel sleepy and decrease in the morning to help you wake up. Some people take melatonin supplements to help with sleep issues like insomnia, jet lag, or other sleep disorders, but it may also affect your dreams.

Some studies suggest that melatonin may enhance REM sleep. This might lead to more frequent and vivid dreams, and some people who take melatonin report more intense and memorable dreams.

Melatonin may also help with dream recall by enhancing overall sleep quality.

The effect of melatonin on dreams can vary from person to person. Remember to always consult a medical professional before you take any supplement, as they can interact with other medications or simply not be right for you.

People like remembering their dreams for a number of reasons. Perhaps it sparks their curiosity about what they could be feeling on a subconscious level or could provide them with an escape from reality. Whatever your reason for wanting to remember your dreams may be, dream recall can become easier and more natural with time and practice.

Keep a dream journal: Write down your dreams as soon as you wake up, even if you can only remember bits and pieces of them. Over time, this can train your brain to pay more attention to your dreams. Review your dream journal during the day to help reinforce your memory and increase your chances of remembering future dreams.

Set an intention: Before you go to sleep, reinforce your desire to remember your dreams. Repeating a phrase like "I will remember my dreams" may increase your chances of recalling them when you wake up.

Stay still upon waking: Moving too quickly when you wake up can cause you to forget your dreams, so before you get out of bed, lie still for a few moments and try to focus on your dream. Sometimes a single image or emotion can trigger the memory of the entire dream.

Reflect on your day: Before bed, think about your day and journal about it. This can help create a connection between your waking and dreaming life and associate both with memories and self-reflection. Thus, this practice may make it easier to remember your dreams.

Practice mindfulness: Regular mindfulness and meditation practice can improve your overall awareness and attention, including your ability to remember dreams. Meditate before bed to clear your mind and prepare for a restful night’s sleep. These six tips for meditating in bed can help you get started.

Wake up naturally: Waking up suddenly can startle you into thinking intensely about the here and now, making it harder to remember dreams, so try to avoid using an alarm clock if you can. Pay attention to your body's natural sleep cycles and try to go to bed early enough to wake up naturally. If you need an alarm, set one that wakes you gently, perhaps with soft sounds or a sunrise effect.

Vivid dreams can be more engaging and memorable than other forms of dreaming that are less detailed.

Before falling asleep, visualize a recent dream or imagine a scenario you’d like to dream about in as much detail as possible. This can help stimulate your mind and lead to more vivid dreams.

Experiment with different sleeping positions to see if they influence the vividness of your dreams.

Get natural light during the day and reduce light exposure before bed to help regulate your sleep cycle and improve the quality of your REM sleep. Improving your sleep cycles and natural circadian rhythm may lead to more vivid dreams.

Creative activities like drawing, writing, or playing music can stimulate your imagination and enhance your dreams.

Meditate before bed to help calm your mind and prepare for a restful night’s sleep. This may increase the chances of having vivid dreams. As you’re releasing stresses from the day, you may create space for your subconscious mind to flourish as you rest. These 10 mindful activities can help you release stress quickly at the end of the day.

Some people use supplements like galantamine, choline, or vitamin B6 to try to enhance dream vividness. Consult a healthcare provider before using any supplements, as they can have side effects and interactions with other medications you’re already taking.

Once you’re remembering your dreams most mornings, you might get curious about steering them. That’s lucid dreaming: knowing you’re dreaming while it’s happening, which can let you look around, change the scene, or just enjoy the ride.

It takes practice, and it doesn’t happen for everyone. The good news is that things you may already be doing, like keeping a dream journal and setting an intention before bed, are also how many people start learning it.

If you’re curious, our step-by-step guide can help you learn how to lucid dream, with techniques like reality checks, MILD, and wake back to bed.

Certain foods and nutrients may influence your dreaming patterns. For example, foods containing tryptophan, like turkey and dairy products, can promote sleepiness and may impact the quality of your dreams. Foods rich in vitamin B6, like bananas, chickpeas, fish, and fortified cereals, may help with recall.

Eat a balanced diet with a variety of nutrients to support your overall sleep health, and avoid heavy meals and caffeine close to bedtime, as they can disrupt sleep and reduce dream frequency.

Several factors can affect your ability to remember dreams.

Poor sleep quality, such as disruptions in your sleep cycle, can hinder dream recall.

Stress or anxiety can interfere with sleep and make it harder to remember your dreams.

Sleep disorders like insomnia, sleep apnea, and restless leg syndrome disrupt sleep and impact dream recall.

Some medications, particularly those that affect the central nervous system, can interfere with dreaming.

Alcohol and drugs can alter sleep patterns and reduce the likelihood of remembering dreams.

A lack of interest in dreams can mean the brain doesn’t focus on retaining them.

Sleep disorders can significantly impact dreaming. Insomnia, which makes it difficult to fall or stay asleep, can reduce the amount of REM sleep you get, leading to fewer dreams and poorer dream recall.

Sleep apnea causes repeated interruptions in breathing during sleep, disrupting REM sleep cycles and reducing the frequency and vividness of dreams. Treatments like CPAP therapy for sleep apnea may improve sleep quality and dreaming.

Restless leg syndrome can also interfere with falling and staying asleep, which can impact dream frequency and recall.

Narcolepsy is marked by excessive daytime sleepiness and fragmented nighttime sleep. It may lead to vivid (and sometimes bizarre) dreams or dream-like hallucinations.

Generally, there are few risks to trying to dream more. Supplements like melatonin or galantamine may cause side effects or interact with other medications, so talk to your doctor before taking them.

Paying more attention to your dreams can sometimes lead to more vivid nightmares, especially if you have underlying anxiety or stress.

Understanding your dreams may reveal hidden thoughts, fears, and desires, and can help process emotions, particularly those you may not fully address during waking life. This may help in emotional healing.

Dreams can also offer creative solutions to problems or provide new perspectives for challenges you face in waking life.

#9564. Behind a Van Gogh picture: the stories revealed on the reverse

The reverse of Van Gogh’s Daubigny’s Garden (June 1890)Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)

Adventures with Van Gogh is a weekly blog by Martin Bailey, The Art Newspaper's long-standing correspondent and expert on the Dutch painter. Published on Fridays, stories range from newsy items about this most intriguing artist, to scholarly pieces based on meticulous investigations and discoveries.

Explore all of Martin’s adventures with Van Gogh here.

The backs of Van Gogh paintings can reveal hidden stories. Daubigny’s Garden, at Amsterdam’s Van Gogh Museum, is a picture with a tale to tell. Painted in Auvers-sur-Oise, a village just northwest of Paris, it depicts the garden of the artist Charles-François Daubigny, whom Van Gogh greatly admired.

Van Gogh’s Daubigny’s Garden (June 1890)Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)

A photograph of the reverse reveals two horizontal red stripes woven into the material of Daubigny’s Garden (June 1890), running close to the top and bottom of the picture. For this work, Van Gogh did not paint on conventional canvas, but on a striped kitchen towel (this household linen is known in French as torchon).

A detail of the reverse of Van Gogh’s Daubigny’s Garden, with the red stripe of a kitchen towelVan Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)

As the Van Gogh Museum’s web entry on the picture explains, the artist "had probably run out of canvas temporarily and reached for whatever was available”. Most likely he simply obtained the square of towelling from the kitchen of the inn where he was staying, the Auberge Ravoux.

Daubigny’s Garden was to prove the start of a more ambitious project. On 17 June 1890, Vincent wrote to his brother Theo to say that he had just completed “a small study” of Daubigny’s house and garden—the work on a kitchen towel. This inspired him with the “idea of doing a more important canvas”.

The following month, after receiving canvas supplies from Theo, he made two ambitious “double square” landscapes with a wider view of Daubigny’s garden. One is at the Hiroshima Museum of Art and the other is in the Rudolf Staechelin foundation collection in Switzerland.

Van Gogh’s Daubigny’s Garden (July 1890)Hiroshima Museum of Art

The stretcher of the reverse of Daubigny’s Garden is plastered with small labels recording the exhibitions where the painting was once displayed. Such labels were frequently used in the mid-20th century, although they are much less common nowadays.

Altogether Daubigny’s Garden has been lent to a total of 105 exhibitions since 1896. The labels record 17 of these venues.

Among the exhibitions which do not have labels were three in what may seem a surprising location: Indonesia. It was then very unusual for works by Van Gogh to be lent for shows outside Europe and North America. Indonesia was a Dutch colony at the time, which helps to explain the loans.

In 1938-39, Daubigny’s Garden, along with 13 other Van Goghs, was sent by the artist’s nephew (V.W. van Gogh) to shows in the capital Batavia (now Jakarta), Surabaya and Bandung.

The Van Gogh exhibition in Batavia (1938), with Daubigny’s Garden on the rightVincent van Gogh: letters, art, and context via Het Geheugen

The final Indonesian exhibition closed in January 1939, just a few months before the outbreak of the Second World War in September (which later led to the Japanese invasion of Indonesia in early 1942).

A label on the reverse of Daubigny’s Garden records its next journey. The painting, with the other Van Goghs, was sent directly from Indonesia to San Francisco, where it was included in a display of Masterworks of Five Centuries as part of the Golden Gate International Exposition world’s fair. The Indonesian exhibition had closed on 31 January, and the show in San Francisco opened on 18 February.

Labels on the reverse of Daubigny’s Garden recording its loan to exhibitions in San Francisco (1939) and New York (1945)Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)

The San Francisco show eventually closed on 29 October 1939, a month after the outbreak of the war. It was then too risky to return the Van Gogh paintings to the Netherlands. The 14 pictures, including Daubigny’s Garden, were hastily formed into a North American travelling exhibition.

Labels on the back of Daubigny’s Garden record its subsequent stops at the Toledo Museum of Art, the Art Association of Montreal (now the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts), the Syracuse Museum of Fine Arts (now the Everson Museum of Art) and New York’s Museum of Modern Art.

The wartime show would end up touring in no fewer than 39 cities across North America in 1939-45, bringing Van Gogh to a huge number of people during these difficult years.

James McNeill Whistler’s Arrangement in Grey: Portrait of the Painter (1872)Detroit Institute of Art (Bequest of Henry Glover Stevens; photograph © Detroit Institute of Arts/Bridgeman Images)

Amsterdam’s Van Gogh Museum last week opened Whistler: Dandy and Disruptor (until 10 January 2027), a version of which was shown earlier at Tate Britain, where it closed on 27 September. Van Gogh was a great admirer of James McNeill Whistler. In addition to the Amsterdam presentation, the Mesdag Collection in The Hague has a smaller show, Whistler: Loving the Netherlands, revealing the American artist’s links to the Dutch art scene.

Van Gogh’s Still Life: Can, Books, Wineglass, Bread and Arum, Sketch of Two Women and a Girl (front); Couple Walking (reverse) (June-July 1890)Christie’s

A Van Gogh sketch done at Auvers-sur-Oise sold at Christie’s Paris for €230,400 (including fees) on 23 October. The first side is a complicated series of partly overlapping images (some at different angles), entitled Still Life: Can, Books, Wineglass, Bread and Arum, Sketch of Two Women and a Girl. On the reverse is a smaller drawing, Couple Walking (June-July 1890).

Martin Bailey is a leading Van Gogh specialist and special correspondent for The Art Newspaper. He has curated exhibitions at the Barbican Art Gallery, Compton Verney/National Gallery of Scotland and Tate Britain.

Martin has written a number of bestselling books on Van Gogh’s years in France: The Sunflowers Are Mine: The Story of Van Gogh's Masterpiece (Frances Lincoln 2013, UK and US), Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence (Frances Lincoln 2016, UK and US), Starry Night: Van Gogh at the Asylum (White Lion Publishing 2018, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale: Auvers and the Artist’s Rise to Fame (Frances Lincoln 2021, UK and US). The Sunflowers are Mine (2024, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale (2024, UK and US) are also now available in a more compact paperback format.

His other recent books include Living with Vincent van Gogh: The Homes & Landscapes that shaped the Artist (White Lion Publishing 2019, UK and US), which provides an overview of the artist’s life. The Illustrated Provence Letters of Van Gogh has been reissued (Batsford 2021, UK and US). My Friend Van Gogh/Emile Bernard provides the first English translation of Bernard’s writings on Van Gogh (David Zwirner Books 2023, UKand US).

#9562. How to Build a Habit by Starting Ridiculously Small

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

In 75 minutes a week, I can reap the benefits of listening to uplifting music, getting out in nature, and getting morning outdoor light, all while exercising my dogs and getting enough cardio to measurably improve my health, happiness, and longevity.

And at times in my life, I have been a real runner. I ran a marathon in my 20s and a couple of half-marathons in my 30s. In my 40s, I mostly just made spectacular plans every January and September: I’d find exciting destination races to train for, join a gym and a yoga studio, sign up for running challenges, and pick out elaborate training plans. I’d run three or four days a week for a week or two, and then nada. Zippo. Zero runs per week.

Then, in 2020, I got into a real running habit. I’ve told the longer version of this story on a TED stage, so I won’t repeat it here, but suffice it to say that I did it by doing very, very little running. When I started going to Orange Theory classes, I kept running. I sustained this exercise habit for six years, through breast cancer and many other difficult life events.

Then the Orange Theory studio down the street from me closed. I tried other studios, but the classes I like are impossible to get into.

So I embraced working out on my own and getting back to running outside with my dogs. I bought very heavy dumbbells and set up a home gym on our covered porch. I spent an inordinate amount of time choosing a destination race, enlisting my adult children to join me. I set up a training schedule on my Garmin watch, and when I didn’t stick to it, I used Nike Run Club. I made a running playlist. I bought a double running leash.

Friends, I have done four runs in three weeks.

I know what I need to do. It’s so wildly unambitious that I’m embarrassed to tell you. I just need to get dressed to run first thing in the morning, put my dogs on their double leash, put on my playlist, and walk out the door, down the driveway, and to the mailbox. That’s it.

I know that most days, I’ll get a walk in, and once that walk is familiar, I’ll sometimes run a little. Some days I might run more, without even deciding to. But even when I don’t feel like doing more, the morning light I get while retrieving the mail and the walk back up our steep driveway are both good for me and genuinely enjoyable. It’s way better than nothing.

The mistake I make again and again is assuming that the size of my plan and the odds of my success are related: the more inspiring the goal and the more elaborate the plan, the better my results will be.

Ambition and results are related, of course, but not in the direction you think.

Creating a habit takes energy and focus, and we’ve only got so much of either, which is why ambitious plans produce a brilliant week and then…nothing. It takes between 18 and 254 days for a behavior to become automatic, and what predicts faster adoption isn’t ambition, self-discipline, or willpower; it’s repetition.

Repetition in a consistent context drives habit formation. Not just effort, intensity, or how badly someone wants it. Doing the thing, in the same place at about the same time, again and again, has the most impact.

Eli Susman, Ph.D., joins me in a webinar in a few weeks to talk about his book Micropractice.

Microhabits: The Science of Habits So Small They Actually Stick

Success is motivating. Doing what you said you’d do, even something absurdly small, builds the belief that you can do it. Failing repeatedly does the opposite; that’s a big part of why I spent my 40s making elaborate plans but not running.

Small behaviors make repetition more likely. What separates an actual habit from a nice couple of weeks is whether it holds up when you’re stressed, tired, busy, or not feeling 100%.

Missing a single day doesn’t meaningfully set most people back. We don’t need to be perfect here, folks. What won’t survive is a plan so ambitious that the off days outnumber the on days.

Micropractices, as researcher Eli Susman calls them, are very small behaviors that also have their own benefits; a tiny practice isn’t just a placeholder for a “real” one. Susman found that 20 seconds of self-compassionate touch (for example, sending kindness to yourself while placing your hand on your heart) per day improved mental health and lowered stress compared with a placebo finger tapping practice.

Across 280,000 meditation sessions in 103 countries, how consistently people meditated predicted their mood and resilience better than how long they sat. Similarly, a meta-analysis combining the results of many studies found that the benefits of practicing breathwork for stress didn’t depend on how long the session were. And breaking up six hours of sitting with brief bouts of walking improves energy, mood, and food cravings more than doing 30 minutes of walking all at once.

I hate the idea of abandoning my big plans. But the truth is that I am not choosing between the ambitious version and the tiny version. I am choosing between the tiny version and nothing.

Break the core behavior central to your habit down into something you can do in under five minutes, start to finish. Under a minute is even better. This isn’t the version that would impress your doctor or your neighbors; it’s the version you can do while exhausted, while traveling, while a little bit sick, and when you want nothing more than to stay on the couch.

Then, check it for resistance. If you feel any reluctance when you imagine doing it, it isn’t small enough yet. Cut it in half. Most people need to start with a micropractice: putting on your walking shoes and stepping out the front door, doing one pushup or 30 seconds of breathing, eating a single leaf of romaine, which, for the record, contains actual fiber and actual nutrients.

Do just that for a while. Resist the urge to do more. This is hard, but the moment you’re no longer willing to be unambitious is the moment you put the whole thing at risk. That’s when difficulty enters, and negotiation with yourself, and the possibility of failure. Your tiny habit doesn’t depend on motivation, which is precisely what makes it survive the days when you have none.

Expand only when you’re itching to, and only in absurdly small increments. Go one more minute, not 10.

Every time you repeat a behavior, your brain physically strengthens the connections that produce it, the way feet crossing a meadow gradually wear a path. Repeat it enough and the path becomes a groove your brain follows on its own, no willpower required. You’re carving a neural pathway for your habit, and everything you want is downstream from that.

At some point, it will become uncomfortable not to do this new behavior. You’ll do it without deciding to, without trying to. That’s the whole goal: repetition until the thing runs itself.

It’s hard to abandon our grand plans and great ambitions for something embarrassingly small. But, paradoxically, it is only in that tiny step that some of our grand plans are truly born.

Join Christine Carter and Eli Susman on Oct. 15 for a free live conversation, with a few tiny habits to try together.

Christine Carter, Ph.D. is a Senior Fellow at the Greater Good Science Center. She is the author of The New Adolescence: Raising Happy and Successful Teens in an Age of Anxiety and Distraction (BenBella, 2020), The Sweet Spot: How to Accomplish More by Doing Less (Ballantine Books, 2015), and Raising Happiness: 10 Simple Steps for More Joyful Kids and Happier Parents (Random House, 2010). A former director of the GGSC, she served for many years as author of its parenting blog, Raising Happiness. Find out more about Christine here.

#9561. In a friends-with-benefits relationship (FWB)? 6 tips to know

A friendship has turned physical, but everything else seems to be staying the same. You grab dinner, send memes, and share inside jokes, all with the understanding that it’s just casual. And yet, you can’t help but wonder where things are headed.

Friends-with-benefits relationships sit in the gray area between friendship and romance. These arrangements work out well for some people, but for others, they slowly become a source of anxiety or hurt.

Whether you're already in one or just curious what you'd be signing up for, here's a closer look at what a friends-with-benefits relationship involves — the risks and the rewards, plus how to navigate one with grace and self-awareness.

A friends-with-benefits relationship (often shortened to FWB) is when two friends are also physically involved with each other, without the commitment or expectations that come with a romantic partnership. There's no exclusivity agreement (unless discussed), no defined future together, and usually none of the relationship milestones that come with dating.

The idea is that the friendship stays intact while you enjoy the physical side of a relationship, no strings attached. It may sound straightforward, but in practice, it usually takes more communication and honesty than people expect going in.

Every FWB relationship looks different. Some see each other regularly, while others keep it more sporadic. What they generally have in common is a mutual understanding that neither person is looking for something more serious.

Not sure if you’re in one? Here are some signs that point toward a FWB dynamic:

You skip the things typical couples do, like meeting each other's families or planning trips together.

You haven’t talked about exclusivity or where the relationship is headed.

You call each other “friends” when describing your situation to others.

You’re dating, or open to dating, other people.

The relationship stays undefined, and one or both of you is comfortable keeping it that way.

Like any relationship structure, being friends with benefits has its upsides and its risks. If you're deciding whether to start a FWB relationship, this list is a good gut check for whether the upsides outweigh the risks for you.

Physical intimacy without the pressure of commitment

Closeness and companionship that come from an existing friendship

More freedom to focus on other priorities, like your career, personal growth, or social life

Low-stakes exploration if you’re not ready for something serious

Clarity about what you want (or don’t want) from relationships

One-sided feelings that go unnoticed or unspoken

Ambiguity about what the relationship actually is, even as time passes

Jealousy, especially if one of you starts dating someone else

Damage to the friendship if it ends badly

Lack of communication about needs due to unclear expectations

FWB relationships don't come with a rulebook — but there are common threads among the ones that work: honesty, self-awareness, and ongoing communication. These tips follow those threads.

FWB tension often comes from mismatched expectations that were never discussed. Before you get physically involved—or as soon as possible if you already are—have an open conversation about what you both want.

Get clear about what “casual” means to each of you, and make sure you're both comfortable with it. Talking through this early beats untangling confusion later.

💙 For more guidance, here’s how to set healthy boundaries in relationships.

Unless you've agreed otherwise, friends-with-benefits arrangements are usually non-exclusive, meaning either of you could be dating or getting involved with someone else. It's worth discussing up front how you'll handle that — will you tell each other when someone new is in the picture?

Your feelings about a FWB setup might shift over time. Take a moment every so often to check in on how you're feeling about the situation.

A few minutes of reflection, or a short meditation, can help you notice any uncomfortable feelings you've been avoiding.

💙 Try Checking In With Yourself with Prof. Megan Reitz on Calm.

Without active effort, the friendship side of FWB can slowly fade into the background until only the physical side is left.

Make it a point to spend time together without getting intimate. Ask about different parts of their life. Show up for each other the way you would have before your dynamic changed.

💙 Learn more about Mindful Friendships with Jay Shetty on Calm.

A FWB arrangement that works one month might not work the next. People's feelings and circumstances naturally evolve with time. The key is speaking up when you notice a change, whether it’s on your end or theirs.

This is where these relationships often get complicated. One of you has a change of heart, but stays silent, afraid of disrupting the dynamic or losing the other person.

Being upfront can be uncomfortable, but it’s one of the most respectful things you can do for yourself and your friend.

💙 Press play on Say What You Need to Say with Jay Shetty on Calm.

Any friends-with-benefits relationship could end at some point, and thinking ahead about how you'd handle it can reduce the fallout. Think about whether preserving the friendship matters to you. Either way, expect some awkwardness afterward.

It can be hard to end things with care and honesty, but it does less damage to the friendship than silence or avoidance.

Knowing what to do in a FWB situation matters, but it’s equally important to be aware of what can trip you up.

Don't assume you're on the same page without checking. Shared silence isn't shared understanding.

Don't use the arrangement as a way to stay close to someone you have feelings for. That's a recipe for getting hurt.

Don't ignore your feelings because they feel inconvenient. Feelings that get dismissed tend to resurface louder later.

Don't skip the conversation about seeing other people. Assumptions here can turn this arrangement messy fast.

Don't stay in it if you’re consistently left feeling worse. A casual relationship isn't worth more than your peace of mind.

Don't expect the friendship to survive constant unspoken tension. Even close friendships have limits, and unspoken hurt can gradually erode them.

Friends with benefits means you and your friend are physically intimate without the commitments of a romantic relationship. There's no assumed exclusivity and no defined future — just a dynamic that exists somewhere between friendship and romance.

Friends-with-benefits relationships get complicated when feelings become one-sided. One of you may develop deeper feelings while the other doesn't. It can also get tricky when expectations shift without a conversation, when one of you starts dating someone else, or when the physical side starts overshadowing the friendship.

There's no set timeline for a FWB relationship. Some arrangements last a few months, while others go on for years. How long yours lasts depends on whether you’re both comfortable with it, communication stays open, and your feelings stay compatible over time.

Friends with benefits may be a good idea if you and the other person are aligned on what you’re looking for. It can be a comfortable, low-pressure arrangement, or a source of confusion and hurt if expectations aren't discussed. Open communication and regular self-reflection tend to give the relationship the best shot at working.

Yes, some FWB arrangements do evolve into committed relationships, particularly when both people develop feelings around the same time and are open to more. That said, staying in the arrangement in hopes that it'll turn into something more comes with a risk. You may end up hurt if the other person doesn't feel the same way.

Jealousy is a normal reaction, even in FWB arrangements that are meant to be casual. This happens because intimacy can naturally lead to attachment. If you’re feeling this way, it might be a sign the situation no longer fits what you want.

The best way to end a friends-with-benefits relationship without ruining the friendship is to be direct and honest. Ghosting or avoiding the other person usually does more damage than an open conversation. Be clear about why things have changed, share appreciation for what you had, and give each other some space afterward.

#9560. Ozempic may have revealed the brain’s hidden “craving center”

For many people, the thought of a tasty burger or a cold pint of beer conjures up a vivid mental image and drives behavior.

This link between thinking and doing serves a clear function – it motivates us to get the necessities for life.

But for some, this process can malfunction. Preoccupation with these rewarding stimuli can lead to disorders of substance overuse, including overeating to the point of obesity and alcohol abuse.

Studies going back to the 1970s have linked vivid mental imagery with drug abuse.

Understanding this link between craving and consuming is central to understanding addiction. This has eluded neuroscience for decades, but the introduction of a new class of drugs for weight loss may have given us just the lever we need to understand it.

These new drugs – including Ozempic and Wegovy – mimic the GLP-1 hormone to stimulate insulin release, slow digestion, and increase feelings of fullness. They are known as GLP-1 agonists and were originally used to treat type 2 diabetes because they help control blood sugar.

As a side effect, people using these drugs also lost a lot of weight, in some cases almost as much as might be expected from bariatric surgery.

But there is another less well publicised effect. Human studies show that GLP-1 agonists reduce alcohol consumption. Preclinical animal studies suggest these drugs also reduce the use of cocaine, amphetamines, opiates and nicotine.

These drugs are changing how we think about the brain’s reward system. They may also open new treatment options for obesity, alcohol dependence and the consumption of other addictive substances.

We have a reasonable understanding of the brain’s “reward circuitry” associated with regions that produce the neurotransmitter dopamine.

These brain parts – the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and nucleus accumbens (NAc) – have been the subject of research on reward for decades. They are the obvious candidate regions to look for a mechanism for GLP-1 action in the brain. But they lack significant density of receptors for GLP-1 and are unlikely to be the direct mechanism.

We must, therefore, consider other brain regions to understand the anti-consumption effect of GLP-1 drugs.

One jump “upstream” from the dopamine-producing brain parts is a region called the lateral septum. This brain structure has been historically implicated in emotional regulation.

Back in 1953, pioneering US behavioural researchers Joseph Brady and Walle Nauta coined the term “septal rage” when animals with damage in the lateral septum showed increased aggression, while direct stimulation of this brain region reduced aggression.

Much more recent work has placed the lateral septum at the center of a neural connectivity network. This has reframed how we think about its function.

While a link between the lateral septum and another region called the hypothalamus is probably responsible for septal rage, the lateral septum links with many other regions with various functions.

The lateral septum inherits much of its primary input from a brain region called the hippocampus.

This region is well known as the place that lets us form long-term “episodic memories.” A famous case of hippocampal damage, Henry Molaison (patient HM), was unable to form new memories after his surgery for epilepsy. He effectively lived without a past, in permanent present tense.

The hippocampus also contains the remarkable “place cells” – neurons that fire corresponding to a person’s thoughts about their position in space and, as recent research has shown, time.

This “where and when am I” information gets forwarded to the lateral septum. Key research has recently shown the lateral septum also contains place cells, but these cells strongly respond to rewards. They effectively add “what is good in this place” to the “where and when am I” information from the hippocampus.

Critically, the lateral septum shares this information with the dopamine-producing regions we would normally associate with reward.

Neuroscientists now think of the lateral septum as the brain region that lets us “think about” rewards – our conscious perception of them – and communicates with the machinery in the brain’s reward system that produces dopamine to make us feel good about them.

There is one last reason to suspect the lateral septum as the mechanism behind the anti-consumption effect of GLP-1 agonists. It is absolutely loaded with GLP-1 receptors.

Emerging research points to this as the mechanism. GLP-1 activation directly in the lateral septum has recently been shown to reduce food consumption in mice. Earlier this year, another study showed the same for alcohol consumption.

My own lab has shown this year that GLP-1 drugs reduce a type of activity in the lateral septum that may prevent it communicating so effectively with other brain regions.

These findings are reshaping our understanding of how the brain processes rewards and have put the spotlight firmly on the lateral septum as the home of cravings.

#9559. What is a circadian rhythm disorder? Plus, 6 ways to treat it

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

You’re tired when you should be awake, or wired when you should be asleep. Whether it’s 2am and you’re staring at the ceiling, your body still hasn’t recovered from that red-eye flight, or the night shift is taking its toll, the struggle is the same: your internal clock and your life are pulling in opposite directions.

These are circadian rhythm sleep disorders (CRSDs), and they happen when your body's sleep-wake cycle doesn't match your daily schedule. And they're more common than you'd think — often mistaken for stress or brushed off as one more thing to deal with once life slows down.

The good news is that CRSDs are medically recognized and treatable. Below, we’ll cover the different types, why they happen, and how to get your sleep back on track.

Your body has an internal clock—the circadian rhythm—that regulates when you feel sleepy and when you feel alert. It runs on roughly a 24-hour cycle, shaped by external cues like light, temperature, and meal timing.

A circadian rhythm sleep disorder (CRSD) occurs when your internal clock consistently falls out of sync with your environment, social schedule, or desired sleep times.

There are several distinct types of circadian rhythm sleep disorders:

Delayed sleep phase disorder (DSPD): Sleep comes much later than usual (often in the early hours of the morning) followed by a struggle to wake up on time.

Advanced sleep phase disorder (ASPD): Sleep arrives early in the evening, and waking happens in the early hours of the morning — the reverse of DSPD.

Non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder: Sleep and wake times drift later or earlier each day instead of settling into a 24-hour rhythm. This pattern is most common in people who are blind.

Irregular sleep-wake rhythm disorder: Sleep is broken into several short stretches across the day and night, without a clear pattern.

Shift work disorder: Night or rotating shift schedules conflict with the body's natural sleep timing.

Jet lag disorder: A temporary misalignment between the body’s internal clock and local time after crossing time zones.

Symptoms vary based on the type of CRSD, but the core issue is the same: sleep happens at the wrong time.

trouble falling asleep at a normal bedtime

difficulty waking up in the morning, or waking too early

mood changes, including irritability, anxiety, or low mood

Circadian rhythm sleep disorders often stem from multiple factors at once, ranging from lifestyle and environment to biology.

Light exposure: Light entering your eyes is the strongest external cue for your internal clock to stay in sync with the outside world. Too much bright light at night, like from screens, or too little natural light in the morning can push your clock in the wrong direction.

Genetics: Your genes can set your natural sleep timing earlier or later than average. Certain gene variants have been linked to differences in circadian timing, which may explain a lifelong tendency toward being a night owl or an early riser.

Age: Your sleep timing usually changes with age. Teenagers drift toward later sleep and wake times, while older adults often feel tired earlier in the evening and wake earlier as a result.

Shift work and irregular schedules: Night or rotating shifts keep you awake when your body expects to be asleep. Irregular eating and exercise can add to that disruption.

Neurological conditions: Conditions such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, or a history of traumatic brain injury are tied to a higher risk of circadian disruption, including fragmented or irregular sleep. Researchers are still working out whether disrupted rhythms are a cause, an early sign, or both.

Blindness: Without light entering the eyes, the brain's clock loses its main external cue for staying aligned with a 24-hour day.

No matter which type of CRSD you're dealing with, you can get your internal clock back on track. Here's what works, and how to find the right approach for you.

In the morning: Bright daylight early in the day helps advance your clock, which is especially useful for delayed sleep phase disorder. During darker months, using a bright light therapy box (10,000 lux) for 20–30 minutes after waking can substitute for sunlight. If you have any eye conditions, it's a good idea to check with a doctor before starting.

In the evening: Reduce bright light 2–3 hours before bed to ease your body into sleep mode. Screens and overhead lighting can suppress melatonin production, while dimmer, warmer light helps your body settle down.

Traveling across time zones? The strategy for beating jet lag with light depends on which direction you're flying. Seek bright light in the new morning and avoid it in the new evening when flying east. Do the reverse when flying west. A day or two of light timing can speed up your adjustment.

💙 Pair your morning light with a Morning Meditation from the Daily Calm.

One of the most effective ways to steady your circadian rhythm is to maintain a regular sleep schedule. Wake up at the same time every day—even on weekends—to give your body a consistent cue to work with. It may feel hard at first, but with consistency, your body naturally adjusts to the rhythm.

Working nights or rotating shifts? "Consistent" doesn't have to mean conventional. Try anchoring your sleep to the same block of hours on workdays, and limiting how far you drift on days off.

💙 Build a sleep routine with Making Progress from the 7 Days of Sleep series on Calm.

Chronotherapy involves slowly adjusting your sleep and wake times in one direction, a little each day, until you reach your target schedule.

Dealing with delayed sleep phase disorder? This might mean going to bed a few hours later each day (moving all the way around the clock) until you land on your desired bedtime. It's a demanding process, and there's some risk of your schedule drifting further off track, so it's best done under a sleep specialist's guidance rather than on your own.

A sleep specialist can help tailor chronotherapy to your specific pattern.

Sleep difficulties often come with anxiety about sleep itself, which can make it harder to fall asleep. Mindfulness practices can help calm your racing mind and relieve that anxiety. Even a few minutes of mindful breathing or a short guided meditation can quiet your mind enough to help you drift off.

💙 Try this Wind Down (for Sleep) meditation on Calm.

Melatonin is a hormone your brain produces, and its levels naturally rise in the evening — signaling to your body that sleep time is approaching. Think of a melatonin supplement as a timing tool rather than a sedative that will help you fall asleep on the spot.

Dealing with delayed sleep phase disorder? Take a low dose (around 0.5–3 mg) three hours before your desired bedtime to help adjust your clock gradually. A doctor or sleep specialist can advise on the right amount for your situation.

Traveling across time zones? Melatonin taken around your target bedtime (about an hour before) in the new time zone is a well-supported way to adjust to jet lag faster.

💙 Discover the best time to take melatonin for restful sleep.

For persistent or severe circadian rhythm sleep disorders, professional support can make a real difference. A sleep specialist may recommend a formal evaluation, actigraphy (a wrist sensor that tracks sleep-wake patterns over time), or a combination of treatments.

Struggling with non-24-hour or irregular sleep-wake rhythm disorder? These patterns respond less predictably to light and schedule changes on their own. A sleep specialist can build a plan around your specific pattern.

Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is also sometimes paired with circadian-focused treatments. It’s a structured therapy that targets the thoughts and habits keeping you awake.

Several everyday habits can throw off your circadian rhythm, including irregular sleep schedules, shift work, jet lag, too much screen use at night, and inconsistent light exposure. Stress, alcohol, caffeine, and some medications can also throw off your body's timing.

Some circadian rhythm sleep disorders can go away on their own, but it depends on the type you're dealing with. Jet lag usually clears up within a few days as your body adjusts to a new time zone. But most chronic circadian rhythm sleep disorders don't resolve without changes to your sleep schedule, light exposure, or daily habits. The sooner you start addressing it, the more manageable the shift becomes.

Not quite, though circadian rhythm sleep disorder and insomnia can feel similar. Insomnia is trouble falling or staying asleep, no matter the time of day. A circadian rhythm sleep disorder is sleep happening at the wrong time. Someone with delayed sleep phase disorder, for example, might sleep just fine from 3am to 11am, instead of a more typical schedule.

The time it takes to reset your circadian rhythm depends on how far your body clock has shifted. Jet lag typically settles within a few days, but a significantly delayed or advanced sleep schedule can take several weeks of consistent habit changes to correct. Light therapy and melatonin can speed the process along, but there's no quick fix.

Melatonin can help with circadian rhythm sleep disorders, but the timing matters. For delayed sleep phase disorder, a low dose taken several hours before your target bedtime can help shift your clock gradually. For jet lag, taking it closer to your target bedtime tends to work better. A doctor or sleep specialist can help you figure out the right dose and timing for your situation.

If your sleep schedule has been getting in the way of work, relationships, or daily life—and adjusting your habits hasn’t helped—it's worth reaching out to a doctor or sleep specialist. They can assess whether you have a circadian rhythm sleep disorder and recommend a treatment plan.

💙 Learn more about the 7 most common sleep disorders.

In many cases, you can fix your circadian rhythm naturally. Focus on getting bright light in the morning and keeping consistent sleep and wake times. For milder patterns, these changes alone can make a noticeable difference, though more serious cases may need extra support.

#9558. Scientists discover a hidden brain rhythm that could improve Parkinson’s treatment

Deep brain stimulation (DBS) can reduce movement problems caused by Parkinson's disease, and new research is providing a clearer picture of why the treatment works. Scientists have found that its benefits appear to depend on stimulating a specific brain network that communicates primarily through a relatively fast beta rhythm (20 to 35 Hz).

The findings come from an interdisciplinary group of neuroscientists and clinicians at the University Hospitals of Cologne and Düsseldorf, Harvard Medical School and Charité Berlin. Published in the journal Brain, the study, 'The Deep Brain Stimulation Response Network in Parkinson's Disease Operates in the High Beta Band', is the first to bring together two approaches that have largely been studied separately: electrophysiology and brain imaging.

Pinpointing Where and How Brain Stimulation Works

"For the first time, we were able to characterize the DBS response network in Parkinson's disease in terms of space and time, simultaneously," says Professor Dr. Andreas Horn from the University of Cologne, who led the study and specializes in computational neurology. "We show that Parkinson's disease can best be treated if we stimulate a very precisely defined network. This network operates synchronized within a specific frequency band, and offers an explanation for how well patients respond to deep brain stimulation."

Deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus is already an established therapy for easing motor symptoms in people with Parkinson's disease. The treatment uses implanted electrodes to deliver small electrical pulses to areas located deep inside the brain.

Previous research has provided only part of the picture. Brain imaging studies have helped identify the locations where stimulation appears to work most effectively, while electrophysiological research has measured the frequencies of the electrical signals involved. Until now, researchers had not captured both the spatial location and timing of these signals at the same time.

To investigate this connection, the team studied a large multicenter group consisting of fifty patients and one hundred brain hemispheres. The scientists simultaneously recorded brain activity through the implanted DBS electrodes and with magnetoencephalography (MEG).

Using these recordings, they mapped functional connections between regions deep within the brain and areas closer to its surface.

Their analysis revealed that the important network connecting the subthalamic nucleus with frontal areas of the brain communicates largely at a comparatively fast frequency (20-35 Hz). Importantly, the strength of this connection was associated with how much individual patients' motor symptoms improved following electrode implantation.

A Brain Rhythm That May Shape Treatment Response

"These results suggest that a certain rhythm of the brain acts as a communication channel between the subthalamic nucleus and the cerebral cortex and may mediate the therapeutic effects of deep brain stimulation," explains Dr. Bahne Bahners, first author of the study, who works at Düsseldorf University Hospital. "By stimulating regions that are connected to the identified network, we will probably be able to adjust DBS settings more precisely in the future, especially in patients who have not yet benefited optimally from deep brain stimulation."

The findings could therefore provide a foundation for making deep brain stimulation more precisely tailored to an individual patient's brain network, particularly when existing DBS settings do not provide the desired level of symptom relief.

Researchers now plan to investigate more directly how deep brain stimulation causes changes within brain networks. Studies examining these causal effects are currently underway.

The study was largely funded by the Professor Klaus Thiemann Foundation.

Materials provided by University of Cologne. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9557. Body doubling: what it is, how it works, and tips to try

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

If you’ve ever opened your laptop to begin your workday from home or checked your mountain of a to-do list and felt zero motivation to tackle it, you’re in good company. On days that you just can’t find the energy or focus to get started, it can help to have a little boost of accountability.

Body doubling, a phrase that means working alongside another person, has gained popularity over the years and is especially popular among people with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Body doubling (either in person or virtually) is said to help motivate people to stay focused and accountable for the tasks at hand. And while it isn’t a formal treatment or backed by robust clinical research, plenty of people have spoken to its effectiveness.

So, what does body doubling involve, and why do so many people swear by it? More importantly, will it work for you? Pull up a seat and let’s explore what you need to know about the technique, plus a few simple ways to try it out for yourself.

Body doubling is the practice of working alongside another person to stay focused and complete a task, either in the same space or virtually. According to the ADDA, the term “body doubling” was coined in the late 1990s by ADHD coach Linda Anderson.

The rationale behind body doubling is that having someone else present and engaged in their own task can make it easier to start and stay on track with yours. To be clear, there’s no coaching or collaboration involved. You’re just working next to each other, because a shared presence can create a sense of structure and accountability.

If you sit at your kitchen table while your roommate does homework, join a silent Zoom session where everyone works on their own projects, or even fold laundry while a friend cleans their space on FaceTime, those are all examples of body doubling.

Many people feel that body doubling helps them break through procrastination and maintain momentum,  especially during overwhelming tasks.

Getting started: Sometimes the hardest part is just beginning. Having someone else nearby can help create a sense of gentle urgency.

Staying on task: When another person is focused, it can be easier for you to stay engaged with your own work.

Feeling less isolated: This practice can reduce the emotional friction that builds when you’re feeling alone in your head.

Creating structure: Knowing someone will be present at a specific time gives your day a natural rhythm. Plus, it can add a layer of accountability.

This technique has gained popularity within the ADHD community. While it’s important to note that this isn’t a clinically recommended treatment—and there’s limited research to support it—many people with ADHD do say that it helps them function more consistently. The idea is that having someone nearby provides external structure and co-regulation.

When your executive functioning is impaired, simple tasks can feel overwhelming. But body doubling creates a soft sense of accountability, which can make it easier to begin and stay engaged in tasks.

With that said, some people find it distracting or feel pressure to “perform,” especially if their partner’s energy doesn’t match theirs. Additionally, if your body double doesn’t understand ADHD, their presence can sometimes feel more frustrating than supportive.

If you’re navigating ADHD, body doubling could be another great tool to add to your toolkit. But only if it feels natural to you.

Disclaimer: Please note that body doubling isn’t a substitute for medication or therapy for people with ADHD.

If you find it hard to begin or stay engaged with tasks, body doubling could be the flexible tool you need. To get started, look for someone who matches your energy and who also makes you feel comfortable.

Here are nine ways you can mindfully add body doubling into your life.

If you’re new to body doubling, try it during something that feels manageable, like folding laundry or organizing your desk. This can give you space to experiment without the pressure of a high-stakes deadline or an environment that isn’t familiar to you, like a coworking space or coffee shop.

Have a quick conversation about what you both want. Ask the other person if you’ll talk, stay silent, or check in at the end.

Clear expectations help make the experience smooth and more supportive.

💙 Stay on the same page with your coworking partner with guidance from Jay Shetty’s Expectations.

Working alongside others in total silence can be helpful for concentrating and removing social pressure, while still giving you the benefits of shared presence.

Try scheduling a Zoom session where you say hello, then mute yourselves and work independently. You could also start a silent group video call with coworkers and only use the chat to check in.

If real-time body doubling feels overwhelming or isn’t accessible, consider searching for helpful videos on YouTube or TikTok.

Search for “study with me” or “body doubling,” and you’ll find creators who film themselves doing everyday tasks. By watching someone else stay focused, it may help you do the same.

Whether it’s a weekly Sunday cleaning hour with a friend or a daily Zoom session at 9am, a recurring slot can build structure into your routine. This can be especially helpful if you struggle with executive function challenges.

Related read: Meditation for ADHD: 9 tips and techniques

You and your body double don’t need to be doing the same thing. One of you could be writing emails while the other is meal prepping or baking a cake.

What matters most is that the energy feels aligned, focused, and respectful.

Related read: How to focus better: 8 tips to improve concentration

Make whatever task you’re doing as manageable as possible. Choose a specific task to start with, and try doing it for 15–30 minutes at first.

This reduces overwhelm and helps give you a clear finish line.

Some people feel vulnerable doing tasks in front of others, especially ones tied to shame or executive dysfunction.

So, choose a body double who won’t judge or try to fix you.

💙 Learn how to build relationships with people you trust during this Mindful Friendships session with Jay Shetty.

If you prefer asynchronous support, text a friend when you start a task and again when you finish. On the flip side, if you’re more motivated in groups, explore coworking in community accountability spaces.

Remember, there’s no one right way to body double. The key is to experiment and adjust based on what feels good to you.

Yes. Body doubling only needs one other person who is working at the same time as you. They can be in the room or on a video call. They don’t need to share your task or give you feedback.

Whether it works varies from person to person. Research on body doubling is limited, and many reports come from people who have tried it. Start with one short session and notice if it’s easier to begin and stay on task.

Body doubling works by providing subtle social accountability and structure. When another person is present, your brain registers the shift in environment. This presence can make it easier for you to start a task or stay with it.

And the accountability can be enough to kickstart momentum, especially if you’re someone who tends to overthink or avoid certain tasks.

It can. Procrastination often stems from overwhelm, perfectionism, and decision fatigue. But body doubling can add a sense of time and presence. You can see that there’s someone else there doing their own thing. And, as a result, it can become a little easier for you to start doing your own thing.

It allows the pressure of the task to lift, even though it may still feel hard.

There can be cons of body doubling. Some people find it distracting, especially if the other person wants to talk and you don’t. Additionally, if you have social anxiety or a history of trauma, being observed might make you feel emotionally charged.

In general, this practice isn’t for everyone. If you’re curious, check in with yourself. Ask if it’s something that would feel supportive and safe. If not, then it’s okay to step back and try a different format.

Anyone can try body doubling. While the term does have roots in ADHD communities, the technique can be applied to anyone. If you struggle with focus or motivation, this practice might be the thing for you.

Plus, if you’ve ever gotten more done in a coffee shop than at home, or felt a boost from working silently next to a friend, you’ve already experienced a version of body doubling.

You don’t need someone in the same room to try body doubling. Virtual options can be just as effective. You could join a coworking session on Zoom or even stream a “study with me” video in the background.

That being said, if you’d rather keep it low-contact, text a friend when you’re about to start a task. Then text them again when you finish. The key isn’t the format; it’s the feeling of shared effort and accountability. So, do whatever feels right to you.
