#9556. Seven Ways to Outlast Political Authoritarianism

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Though Djurdja Padejski was raised in communist Yugoslavia, her life there felt stable and uneventful for a long time. In the 1980s, under Yugoslavia’s “soft” one-party government, Padejski and her friends read Western literature, watched Hollywood movies, and listened to the BBC.

“We grew up in a very comfortable, naive environment,” Padejski says.

That changed in the 1990s when Yugoslavia split into several republics. Civil war broke out, and a virulent strain of nationalism took hold in Serbia, the Yugoslavian state where Padejski lived. Firebrand leader Slobodan Milošević ascended to power and began meddling in elections, targeting opposition leaders, and igniting ethnic cleansing campaigns.

“He captured the entire society and his party,” Padejski remembers. “Very soon I found myself on the streets protesting.” Padejski’s activism against repressive Serbian regimes would continue until 2011, when she and her husband, investigative journalist Djordje Padejski, left the country after people threatened to kill them.

The Padejskis arrived in the U.S. with hard-won knowledge of how to outlast repression over the long haul. In recent years, they’ve tapped back into that knowledge and shared it with those around them as they witness here in America the illegal destruction of government agencies, election tampering, and warrantless arrests of citizens and non-citizens. This isn’t just true in the United States—around the world, democracy is declining.

How can we go on defying rising authoritarianism when no clear endpoint is in sight? Psychology and motivation research complement the experience of people like the Padejskis by addressing how to conserve energy and sustain commitment to your ideals in challenging conditions.

“The goal of the authoritarian regime is to desensitize us to extremes, to things we should never agree with or consider normal,” says Djurdja Padejski, now a language and culture researcher (and doctoral candidate) at Arizona State University.

Surviving repression depends on rejecting this presumed “normality” and refusing to let your inner state mirror extremes imposed from above. To that end, here are seven research-backed ways to subsist under indefinite duress.

Life under repression feels exhausting due to the colossal scale of so much of what is happening: attacks on the free press, denial of life-saving aid to millions overseas, ongoing ICE killings on the streets and in detention facilities. Reading about such developments understandably triggers feelings of overwhelm. Research finds that these feelings can drive people to shut down their emotions, dampening their motivation to help in concrete ways.

Djurdja Padejski has come to recognize that to avoid that trap, she has to face her human limits squarely without drowning in self-recrimination. As a young adult under Milošević’s rule, she learned early that worrying about what she couldn’t do was a waste of time and energy.

“It is very important not to get stuck in that moment, not to be clutching your pearls,” she says. “We have to be strategic to preserve our resources.”

Admitting your own lack of control over the big picture can be a necessary prelude to taking the actions still available to you, Padejski says. “We have to see [the situation] for what it is, so we can focus our efforts on keeping our minds, our bodies, and our communities as healthy as possible under the circumstances.”

Once you’ve gotten clear about what is within your power to control, you can get granular by carrying out regular acts of “micro-resistance.” These acts of defiance do not require you to upend your daily rhythms or put your life on the line. They can be as simple as attending a march, supporting a neighbor at an immigration court visit, or wearing a shirt with a resistance slogan.

Micro-resistance acts—such as creating protest art and continuing to study even when their department was banned from the university—helped sustain both Padejskis through years of repression, reminding them of the power they had despite limits imposed from on high.

“These micro-level actions add up,” Djordje Padejski writes. “Even small acts of defiance can maintain your sense of agency.”

Self-described “small-time” lawyer Daniel Suitor excels at this kind of micro-resistance. During ICE raids in his hometown of Minneapolis, he channeled his overwhelm by signing up for a course on how to file legal paperwork to free unjustly detained Twin Cities residents.

After Suitor filed his first case, he found out surprisingly quickly that he’d won and that the man he was representing would be freed. That proof-of-concept case spurred him to file another legal petition, then several more in quick succession. And he wasn’t alone in his commitment: To date, Minnesota lawyers have filed more than 1,000 cases challenging unjust detentions.

Acts of micro-resistance can also help prime us for future courageous action. When people perform smaller acts of selflessness and service, large-scale heroism becomes easier to contemplate, explains Medical College of Wisconsin heroism researcher Zeno Franco. Concrete practice can make you more adept at translating abstract ideals into action.

“You need to understand beyond theory,” Djurdja Padejski says. “We actually, as humans, can’t imagine how concepts work in [the] real world unless we experience them hands-on.”

For the Padejskis, one of the most stifling aspects of life under Serbian autocracy was not knowing when the repression would lift, if at all.

Periods of confinement, literal or figurative, are more bearable when a clear endpoint is in sight, and indefinite periods of repression feel uniquely oppressive. A third or more of incarcerated people with open-ended sentences suffer from depression. Others feel rooted to the present moment, severed from any potential future.

“I simply try to live in the here and now and not to plan,” one prisoner told the University of Bern researcher Irene Marti, who studies open-ended confinement. “Because I don’t have any future or only one that is very far away.”

When the endpoint of repression is uncertain, or when a challenging situation has no clear natural limit, creating your own intermediate endpoints can help you stay committed to your goals and values.

In a recent goal-setting study, when people broke an annual community service goal into granular sub-goals (say, four hours of service a week, or eight every two weeks), they volunteered more hours in the long run than people without intermediate goals.

In the same way, committed resisters can pledge to put in a set number of hours each week, or carry out a set number of clearly defined actions. According to self-determination theory, choosing and pursuing your own accessible goals boosts your well-being and motivation—internal changes that persist even when the larger crisis remains ongoing.

As governments around the world curtail freedom of speech and movement, it’s hard not to feel the noose tightening. One way to create more existential breathing room is to consider how this moment fits into the longer arc of history.

This helps you subsist in the present by reminding you of parallel past moments (whether decades or centuries ago), how they came to a head, and what ultimately resolved them. Research finds that when people take a long-term perspective, reflecting on recent stressful events as though they happened far in the past, they report less emotional distress in the moment.

Djurdja Padejski found solace in doing this during Milošević’s reign. “I survived that period mostly by reading the columns in the newspapers,” she says. One column in particular, by Serbian anthropologist Ivan Čolović, examined the regime’s activities from a broader historical and social perspective.

“He was offering a vocabulary and a theoretical apparatus to help us deal with the horrors of civil war. The news about it was the most severely censored, the propaganda was relentless, and all of it was new for many of us who were children when the fallout of our world began,” Padejski says. “That’s how I survived with my sanity intact, because it helped me to recognize what is happening to society.”

Among the most potent present-day energy drains is the social media industrial complex that feeds on people’s rage and frustration, serving up extreme viewpoints that deepen entrenched social divides as they rack up likes and views.

“Social media and internet platforms—they’re amplifying what is also a typical quality of authoritarian regimes. They’re all about grandiosity,” says Djurdja Padejski, who studies the linguistic mechanisms of propaganda. “Algorithms grab people’s attention by intensifying the language and the visuals and the overall framing.” That’s a big reason why frequent social media use saps your cognitive resources and motivation, making it harder to subsist under repression.

Plugging this energy drain requires not just limiting your time online, but redirecting more of that time to the in-person, small-group exchange to which humans are uniquely suited.

When you engage with people face to face, it’s much harder to reduce them to a stereotype or particular viewpoint. And by getting to know them in all their messiness, contradiction, and complexity, you bond with them in ways that lighten the mental and practical load for everyone involved.

“To resist this reduction of our existence to, ‘What are you for or against?’ means embracing creativity, art, friends, communal projects, protests, walks,” Padejski says. “These 10 years of resistance [in Serbia]—I honestly remember it as a series of walks. Sometimes that meant running away together from Milošević‘s militias or the official police, or from water cannons, or rubber bullets. But what is left is our conversations on ideas, on creations.”

Though exchanges like these may not further resistance directly, they form the edifice that sustains it. Within bonded human-scale communities, members have a clear sense of not just their own energetic capacity, but that of others in the group. That means they can pinch-hit for one another: When someone needs help, they can fill in on the spot—or, like relay racers, take up the baton when someone needs to withdraw. This shared flexibility and responsiveness help all group members to stay committed for the long haul.

For the Padejskis, subsisting under Serbian repression meant homing in on the values that were most important to them, and upholding those values even if it meant sacrificing convenience or comfort. When Djordje Padejski needed a lifesaving drug, a relative told him he could work his connections to obtain the medicine, but only if Padejski joined the Serbian dictator’s political party. Padejski refused, knowing that doing so put his health at risk.

The couple have continued that tradition in the U.S., though in somewhat less life-altering ways. After Elon Musk unleashed an apparent Nazi salute at a Trump post-inauguration event, the Padejskis gave up their Tesla. “I drive a Subaru now,” Djurdja Padejski says. “I really don’t like it compared to Tesla, but I don’t regret it.”

Some people write off such moral stands as more symbolic than substantive. But symbol, it turns out, shapes substance: What you stand for predicts and influences what you’ll do down the road, for good or ill. When people have a clear, consistent moral identity, studies find, they’re more likely to take real-world action aligned with that identity.

On the other hand, when you’re willing to cave on something that seems minor, like supporting a complicit business, “you are detached from your inner beliefs, from what you know is real and good and safe,” Djurdja Padejski says. “Once you’re there, you are ready to compromise a lot of values that you think you are really one with.”

One unexpected thing the Padejskis learned, under Milošević and afterward, was the importance of not swinging into action every time a devastating piece of news hit. Overcommitment amounted to self-sabotage, sapping energy and resources they’d need later on.

Military commanders have long known the importance of “keeping their powder dry,” Zeno Franco points out, holding back so they can act at the moment of maximum impact. In the same way, the best long-distance runners often hang back throughout a course to conserve energy, then uncork a burst of speed in the race’s final minutes.

Djurdja Padejski followed this principle to great effect under Milošević. She bided her time leading up to the critical elections of 2000, then worked tirelessly as an election volunteer to monitor for irregularities and make sure no one was falsifying results. All the while, ruling party members with guns lurked in the background.

“This guy started opening his gun and checking the bullets, and we didn’t cave. We just ignored him,” Padejski says. “We knew we were risking our lives, but we really believed it’s now or never.” Serbia’s democratic opposition party ultimately won that election, causing Milošević’s downfall.

Padejski hopes democratic activists around the world will take a similar approach as crucial elections near. Under repressive conditions, keeping your powder dry “is not an instruction to put off action as long as possible, but rather the wisdom to know that being prepared to act at just the right moment may require careful guarding of resources and energy,” Franco says. “Biding your time is not the same as surrender.”

Elizabeth Svoboda is the author of What Makes a Hero?: The Surprising Science of Selflessness. Her upcoming book, The Art of Pacing, is about setting a sustainable pace in a speed-obsessed world.

#9555. How to deal with anxious-ambivalent attachment in a relationship

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Have you ever texted your partner only to spiral into oblivion waiting for them to respond? You wonder if they’re upset with you, if you did something wrong, or if they’re quietly pulling away. When their response finally comes through, you exhale the biggest sigh of relief. And then you start second-guessing why you were so worried in the first place.

If this sounds familiar, you may be dabbling in the world of ambivalent attachment, which is one of many attachment styles formed in adolescence and carried into adulthood.

Ambivalent attachment is a relationship pattern where you want to feel close to your partner but can’t always get there. It can show up as craving reassurance but doubting it, swinging between feeling connected to your partner and fearing they’ll leave, or analyzing small interactions for a hidden meaning that often isn’t there. While it may feel overwhelming, this attachment style isn’t a flaw in your personality, but rather a pattern shaped by early experiences in your life.

Let’s unpack what ambivalent attachment means, how to spot the signs in adulthood, and what to do if you (or your partner) lean toward this attachment style. Plus, we’ll dive into how to create steadier, more supportive relationships that feel good for all involved.

Anxious-ambivalent attachment—also called ambivalent attachment—is a relationship pattern where you crave reassurance yet struggle to feel settled once it’s given. It’s like wanting to lean on someone but worrying they might step away just as you do.

In adult relationships, ambivalent attachment may show up as feeling unsure about your partner’s commitment to you, cycling between connection and doubt, or getting caught in emotional highs and lows depending on how available your partner feels to you.

While it can feel overwhelming, this isn’t a flaw. It’s a protective strategy learned early in life that can be reshaped over time.

Ambivalent attachment often develops in childhood when caregiving is inconsistent. Basically, sometimes you were nurtured, and sometimes you weren’t. This unpredictability creates uncertainty in children, as they learn that comfort may arrive (but not reliably), so they cling tightly when it does appear. Over time, this wires the nervous system to stay on high alert for signs of loss or disconnection.

While it may seem easy to blame the caregivers involved, that’s not always the best answer or solution. Many people provide inconsistent care because of stress, lack of support, or their own attachment struggles. The good news is that even if this style formed early, it can shift in adulthood through consistent experiences of safety and connection.

Ambivalent attachment doesn’t always look dramatic from the outside. It often shows up in subtle, everyday ways that leave both partners feeling drained or confused. While everyone feels insecure at times, people with an ambivalent attachment style experience these patterns more intensely and more often.

1. Constant need for reassurance: You might ask for confirmation of your partner’s love or commitment regularly through words, texts, or gestures. The tricky part for people with an ambivalent attachment style is that reassurance often doesn’t stick. Even after hearing “I love you,” doubt can creep back quickly, fueling the cycle for reassurance again.

2. Fear of abandonment: Small shifts in a partner’s behavior—like if they take longer than usual to reply to a message or are quieter than usual—can trigger unnecessary worry. The fear isn’t just about being left by your partner, it’s about being forgotten or no longer valued. And for someone with this attachment style, those fears can be dire.

3. Hyper-attunement to signals: People with ambivalent attachment often read between the lines of every interaction, scanning tone, body language, or text punctuation for hidden meaning. A short text that simply says, “K,” might feel like rejection rather than just brevity.

4. Emotional highs and lows: Relationships can feel like a rollercoaster. You may feel ecstatic when things feel close and connected, then anxious when any distance appears. The intensity of these swings can feel overwhelming for both partners.

5. Difficulty trusting stability: Even when the relationship is going well, there’s a lingering sense that it could change at any moment. This makes it hard to relax into intimacy, because safety doesn’t feel fully reliable.

6. Feeling “too much” or “not enough”: Self-doubt often runs in the background, accompanied by persistent worrying that your needs are excessive or fearing that you’re somehow lacking. This inner tug-of-war can make it difficult to feel secure in how you show up in a relationship.

Working with ambivalent attachment is about finding steadier ground, both within yourself and your relationships. These strategies combine self-regulation, clearer communication, and practical agreements that build trust over time.

1. Recognize and name the pattern: The first step is simply noticing when old fears are coming up. Take time to put a name to the feeling, and remind yourself that it’s a learned response and not proof that something is wrong with you or your relationship. Taking a beat to give your feelings a name gives you the chance to pause before you react impulsively.

2. Soothe your body before your thoughts: Ambivalent attachment often activates the nervous system, which can make worries feel louder than they are. Simple grounding tools, such as intentional breathing, a mindful walk, or even running cold water over your wrists (which may help calm your nervous system) can bring your body back to baseline. Once you’re calmer, you’ll have more perspective on what’s really happening.

3. Ask directly instead of protesting: Protest behaviors (testing someone, withdrawing your affection, or sending a string of texts from the top of your mind) can backfire and push your partner away instead of bringing them closer. Practice naming your needs clearly instead. Try saying something like, “I’m feeling anxious right now and could use reassurance that we’re okay.” It might feel vulnerable to be so honest and open, but being direct usually leads to better connection.

4. Build a personal reassurance toolkit: Instead of depending only on your partner for reassurance, create a set of resources you can turn to yourself. This might include rereading kind messages, journaling, doing grounding exercises, or calling a supportive friend. Having options beyond your partner reduces the sense of desperation when anxiety spikes.

5. Practice small steps toward trust: Shifting attachment styles takes time, but small experiments help. Try waiting a little longer than you typically would before sending a check-in text, and see how that feels. You can also remind yourself of past experiences where closeness stood the test of time or survived a disagreement. Each successful moment builds evidence that security is possible, even if your old fears insist otherwise.

💙 Looking for tips to self-soothe? Try the Calming Anxiety guided practice on the Calm app.

6. Offer steady reassurance with boundaries: Consistency may help calm anxiety. Simple habits like a morning check-in or saying when you’ll call back create predictability. But it’s also important to pair reassurance with realistic boundaries. You might say, “I can’t text during work, but I’ll check in at lunch.”

7. Respond to the need, not just the words: Underneath protests or big reactions is usually a fear of being abandoned. Instead of focusing only on the tone or delivery of something your partner says, try reflecting the underlying need. You can say, “I hear that you’re worried I’m pulling away, but I want you to know I’m here.” This validation often matters more than a perfect solution.

8. Set clear repair practices: When tensions rise, agree in advance on how to pause and return to the conversation when you’re level-headed. Try saying, “If one of us feels overwhelmed, we’ll take a 20-minute break and come back at an agreed time.” Returning as promised helps rebuild trust, strengthens your relationship, and makes conflicts feel less threatening.

💙 Need a little more support? Check out the Kind Communication meditation on the Calm app.

9. Create shared routines for connection: Structure helps balance anxiety. A weekly check-in, an agreed-upon text during the workday, or even a daily hug ritual can anchor the relationship. These small but predictable moments reduce the need for constant reassurance.

Related read: How to use words of encouragement: 50 examples

10. Name the cycle and work as a team: Instead of blaming each other, talk about the pattern: “We tend to argue when I get quiet, and you seek more closeness. How can we catch it earlier?” Naming the cycle makes it something you face together, rather than a flaw in either partner.

💙 Learn how to take A Purposeful Pause with Jay Shetty on the Calm app.

Ambivalent attachment usually begins in early childhood. When a caregiver is sometimes warm and attentive but other times distracted, stressed, or unavailable, a child learns that love is unpredictable. This inconsistency creates anxiety about whether comfort will be there when it’s needed most.

Over time, the child develops strategies to cling tightly to connection, like seeking closeness while bracing for it to disappear. It’s not always about neglect. Often, caregivers themselves are overwhelmed or carrying their own attachment wounds. But the result is the same, and it’s that love is both essential and unreliable.

You may notice repeating patterns in your relationships, like craving reassurance but rarely feeling settled when you receive it. Small shifts in your partner’s tone, attention, or texting habits may trigger outsized worry about abandonment.

Overthinking, analyzing, or swinging between feeling deeply connected and then uncertain are also common. If these patterns show up across multiple relationships, that can be a strong sign of ambivalent attachment.

Attachment styles can change. While your early experiences lay the foundation, your attachment style can shift as you build new experiences of safety and stability. Supportive relationships, therapy, and personal work on self-regulation all help strengthen secure attachment.

The process is gradual and often happens through repeated moments of repair and reassurance. Over time, these experiences retrain your nervous system to trust that closeness can last.

Both ambivalent and avoidant attachment come from early inconsistencies in caregiving, but they lead to opposite coping strategies. People with ambivalent attachment often lean in, seeking closeness, reassurance, and connection. Sometimes, these manifest in ways that feel intense or overwhelming to their partner.

People with avoidant attachment tend to lean out. They value independence, minimize their needs, and withdraw when relationships feel too vulnerable. Ambivalent attachment is marked by fear of abandonment, while avoidant attachment is marked by discomfort with intimacy.

Yes, therapy can be effective. Working with an attachment-focused therapist gives you a consistent relationship where trust and stability are practiced week after week. Different forms of therapy like Emotionally Focused Therapy (EFT), schema therapy, and cognitive-behavioral therapy can help you identify old patterns, calm the nervous system, and create new relational habits.

Over time, the therapy relationship itself often serves as a secure base, making it easier to bring those new ways of relating into your everyday life.

Patience and predictability are key. Your partner may need more reassurance than you thought, so offering it consistently and directly can ease their anxiety. For example, sending a quick “thinking of you” text before a long meeting or confirming plans in advance can make a big difference.

At the same time, it’s important to set boundaries around what you can realistically give. A helpful approach is to offer what you can with warmth, and state what you can’t with clarity. That way, your partner feels cared for without you becoming overextended.

#9554. The Everyday Nutrient Linked To 32% Lower Dementia Risk

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Moderate intake of choline, a nutrient found in eggs, fish and legumes, is linked to a lower risk of dementia.

Older adults consuming moderately high amounts had a 32 percent lower dementia risk than those consuming the least.

However, the highest intake was not associated with a clear benefit, suggesting that more is not necessarily better.

The research followed over 5,000 American adults, whose average age was almost 69, for around eight years.

Participants were initially free of dementia but around 500 developed the condition during follow-up.

After dividing participants into five groups according to choline intake, the researchers found a 32 percent lower dementia risk in the second-highest group than in the lowest, after accounting for other factors.

However, there was no statistically clear reduction in the highest-intake group.

The result therefore points towards a potentially beneficial range, rather than a steady fall in risk with every increase in consumption.

The researchers then combined their results with four previous studies to assess the broader pattern.

Together, these followed almost 138,000 people and recorded around 2,500 cases of dementia.

In the combined analysis, dementia risk fell as choline intake rose to approximately 465 milligrams per day, with no further reduction beyond that level.

Choline helps the brain produce acetylcholine, a chemical messenger involved in learning and memory.

It also supplies building blocks for the membranes surrounding brain cells, helping maintain their structure and communication.

These roles could help explain a link between choline and cognitive ageing, although they do not prove that consuming more prevents dementia.

The nutrient also participates in processes that regulate homocysteine, a substance linked to problems with blood vessels and cognitive function.

Eggs, meat, poultry and nuts were among the main sources of choline in the American participants’ diets.

People consuming more choline obtained a greater proportion of it from eggs.

Crucially, the analysis assessed choline from food and did not include intake from supplements.

The findings therefore cannot establish whether choline supplements would lower dementia risk.

The study was published in the Nutrition Journal (Chen et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9553. After seven years, Hirshhorn Museum opens Hiroshi Sugimoto-designed sculpture garden

Hiroshi Sugimoto in the Hirshhorn’s lobby, which he redesigned in 2018 Photo: Farrah Skeiky

When the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden opened in 1974 in Washington, DC, The New York Times called it “the capital’s newest cultural treasure”. Likening the Hirshhorn to a René Magritte picture, reporters drew out the “juxtaposition of man and nature with architecture”, the seamless melding of light and form, indoors and out, that sets apart its collection of Modern and contemporary art.

On 31 October, the Hirshhorn is scheduled to unveil a new cultural treasure: its $68m renovated sculpture garden. The project has been years in the making, designed by the Japanese artist Hiroshi Sugimoto—who also redesigned the museum’s lobby in 2018. The reorganised 1.3-acre space, with its 30,000 new plants and trees, draws on the architect Gordon Bunshaft’s original design. This is part of a broader transformation at the museum, including renovations to the plaza and building infrastructure.

Featuring 60 works—21 of them from the 1974 installation—the renovated garden includes five entrances, east and west overlooks and an underground passageway of stainless steel. Sugimoto describes its mirrored finish as “reflecting the garden and the people moving through it, an experience in itself—one that is continually transformed by the interplay of light, nature and the visitors”.

The walkways and alcoves are delineated using stacked-stone walls, each hand-selected and arranged by the artist. “Bunshaft was deeply influenced by the stone gardens of medieval Japan,” Sugimoto tells The Art Newspaper. “Inspired by this, I decided a Japanese dry-stone wall would serve as a symbolic link between the ancient and the modern, providing the perfect backdrop for the museum’s Modernist sculptures.”

The garden’s opening follows years of controversy. Sugimoto’s early vision for the space was met with criticism. In 2021, Charles A. Birnbaum (the president and chief executive of the Cultural Landscape Foundation) said that the stacked-stone plan “fundamentally disrupts” the garden’s Modernist design and the “artistic intent” of Bunshaft and the landscape architect Lester Collins.

The Hirshhorn’s revamped garden, redesigned by Hiroshi Sugimoto Photo: Rick Coulby, courtesy Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden

Adjustments to Sugimoto’s initial design were made five years ago, according to the Hirshhorn, after a public consultation process as well as meetings with the National Capital Planning Commission and the Commission of Fine Arts. In 2022, the museum hosted a groundbreaking ceremony with Jill Biden. “I was amazed by the backlash,” Sugimoto said at the time.

Today, Birnbaum stresses that the Hirshhorn’s “landscape architecture is an art form” and urges the museum to “afford it the same curatorial oversight, care and respect as the rest of the material collection”.

Sugimoto’s practice is meditative, rooted in a close study of the natural world. “There is an 11th-century Japanese garden manual, Sakuteiki, which tells us to ‘listen to the voices of the stones’,” he says. Each stone has its own character, weight and direction. He adds: “My task is not simply to place it, but to discover where it already wants to be; precision comes from listening carefully enough to find that inevitable position.”

This sense of balance is felt throughout the garden. With benches for quiet reflection and shaded, out-of-the-way recesses, the lawns encourage deep focus, an attentiveness to and a delight in the play of forms. “It’s not just about looking at art,” says Aaron Seeto, the Hirshhorn’s deputy director, “but about looking at it as the garden itself is changing.”

Sculpture in the space is arranged chronologically. The east garden includes a cast of Auguste Rodin’s poignant The Burghers of Calais (1884-89), its six figures weighed down and their necks bound in a darkened procession. Nearby is Henri Matisse’s The Backs I-IV (1909-31), a series of abstracted nudes in bronze relief, their angular silhouettes catching the light.

Auguste Rodin’s The Burghers of Calais (1884-89/cast 1953-59) Photo: Rick Coulby, courtesy Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden

Henry Moore’s King and Queen (1952-53) is one of five works by the artist on view. It depicts a pair of seated figures, their faces abstracted, the curve of their shoulders liquid smooth. “Joseph Hirshhorn was one of Moore’s closest friends and one of the most significant collectors of his work,” says Godfrey Worsdale, the director of the Henry Moore Foundation. (Joseph Hirshhorn owned 55 sculptures by Moore, and Hirshhorn’s fourth marriage took place before a cast of the artist’s Upright Motive No. 1: Glenkiln Cross.) Worsdale applauds the renovated garden for offering “unfettered access to Moore’s work for new generations”.

In the west garden, home to new commissions, stands Yoshitomo Nara’s Sentinels of Stillness series (2025)—three monumental heads, fashioned from aluminium and coated in brilliant white paint. Following the Tōhoku earthquake and nuclear disaster in 2011, Nara found himself unable to paint and instead took to sculpting. The physicality of modelling clay served as a kind of healing for him.

Liz Larner’s 6 (2010-11), meanwhile, is a cuboid of stainless steel in deep ochre, lavender and white—the tendril-like lines seeming to expand and contract as if suspended in air. The work is a kind of “variable in space”, says Larner, who is absorbed by the mathematical concept of x (the unknown). Following in the tradition of the Surrealist artist Meret Oppenheim, Larner explores the indefinable, “the variable of a variable, the changing perspectives that don’t ossify”.

Comparably fluid is Raven Halfmoon’s Dancing at Dusk (2024), a neighbouring work of cream, coppery-red and slate-grey travertine. Halfmoon, a citizen of the Caddo Nation, gestures to violence and strength, pairing the themes in a work of banded-stone—her first in the medium—trimmed with a line of crosses. There is a kind of solemnity to the piece, the composite visage resolute, meeting the world as it is.

That pathos carries over to KAWS’s 14ft bronze SHELTER (2026), reminiscent of a mother and child—their eyes crossed out, their modelling soft, even tender. It is a warm embrace, the two encircled by an overhanging elm tree.

There is a stillness to the Hirshhorn’s new garden space, a sense of calm in the otherwise fast-moving capital city. “I hope people will experience a different sense of time in the garden,” Sugimoto says. “The sculptures, stones, trees, water and the changing light all exist on different clocks. The garden allows us to slow our own clock enough to become aware of these differences.”

The renovation taps into the spirit of the founding architect, Gordon Bunshaft

The artist’s designs for the sunken sculpture park creating a more inviting space for visitors coming from the National Mall

#9552. A stress hormone may help the brain repair itself

When laboratory mice experience brain damage, e.g., from an injection, Jan Deussing repeatedly notices the same response. A particular group of cells appears and becomes active around the damaged area. Although Deussing, a research group leader and experienced neurobiologist, had observed the phenomenon many times, he did not know exactly what type of cells were involved.

The mystery became an ideal research question for a master's student. Clemens Ries, who had recently joined the Max Planck Institute of Psychiatry for an internship as he approached the end of his biology degree, took on the challenge.

Using a mouse model, Ries systematically tested markers for all known cell types. Only one produced a response: the marker for oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs).

These precursor cells can mature into oligodendrocytes, which produce the myelin sheath surrounding axons. Axons are extensions of nerve cells that allow neurons to communicate with one another. Myelin acts much like the insulating material around an electrical cable. It supports efficient information transmission along axons and also helps supply them with nutrients, making it vital to healthy brain function.

Damage to myelin can have serious consequences. In autoimmune diseases such as multiple sclerosis (MS), the protective coating breaks down. Physical injuries can also harm myelin, and in severe cases, the resulting damage can lead to the death of entire neurons. Restoring myelin around affected axons is therefore an important part of the brain's response to injury.

A Surprising Stress Hormone Appears After Injury

Ries initially studied the newly identified cells for his master's thesis. "The topic remained so exciting that it became my doctoral thesis," says the biologist.

His subsequent research showed that these precursor cells multiply dramatically around the edges of brain wounds. Most then continue to mature, eventually becoming oligodendrocytes capable of producing new myelin.

But Ries and Deussing also uncovered something that had not been known before. Near the damaged tissue, about one third of the OPCs activate corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), a hormone that plays a central role in regulating the body's stress response. Researchers had not previously known that OPCs could produce neuropeptides such as CRH. The findings have now been published in the renowned journal Cell Reports.

The CRH response begins remarkably quickly. Production can be detected within just a few hours after an injury, but it shuts down again after roughly three days. This short and rapid burst suggests that CRH has an important function during the earliest stages of the healing response.

CRH Helps Control the Timing of Myelin Repair

One of the two known receptors for CRH also appears to be central to this process. CRH receptor 1 is present on a different population of OPCs and allows those cells to respond to the CRH that has been released.

When CRHR1 is absent, OPCs multiply more rapidly after an injury. That initial increase, however, does not translate into better repair. Ultimately, fewer mature oligodendrocytes are produced and remain.

The findings indicate that CRH helps regulate the timing of OPC maturation. That timing appears to be essential for producing enough mature oligodendrocytes to properly restore the damaged myelin sheath.

The Same System Shapes the Developing Brain

OPCs are not only important after injury. They also have a major role in building myelin as the brain matures. Much of this myelination takes place after birth and continues until young adulthood.

Because CRH receptor 1 is found on OPCs even when no injury is present, Ries and Deussing began to wonder whether the receptor might also influence myelination during normal brain development. Working with other researchers, they examined myelin formation in additional mouse models using several different methods.

They found that mice lacking CRH receptor 1 produced more OPCs during the early stages of development. Those changes did not disappear with age. Instead, they had lasting effects on the structure of the brain.

In adult brains, the researchers detected changes in myelination that could be traced to thicker myelin sheaths, particularly around thin axons. The results suggest that CRH receptor 1 on OPCs plays an important role not only in repairing myelin after injury, but also in regulating how myelin develops in the first place.

Where Does CRH Come From During Development?

Following an injury, OPCs themselves respond by producing and releasing CRH. Brain development raises a different question: where does the stress hormone come from when the brain is maturing normally?

The scientists propose that neurons may provide the answer. Their hypothesis is that developing neurons release CRH, which then influences both the multiplication of OPCs and their maturation into oligodendrocytes that produce myelin.

A Possible Connection to Depression and Stress

Neurons are already known to release CRH, particularly during stressful conditions. Stress experienced during early childhood development is also recognized as a risk factor for psychiatric disorders.

The new results therefore raise the possibility that the CRH system operating in OPCs could have broader implications for mental health.

"Our current findings suggest that in stress-associated psychiatric disorders such as depression, the CRH system in OPCs may play a greater role than previously known," Deussing speculates.

If future research confirms and expands on that connection, understanding how CRH signaling affects OPCs, myelin formation, and brain development could eventually point toward completely new therapeutic approaches.

Materials provided by Max Planck Institute of Psychiatry. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9551. How to stop nightmares and fall back asleep after bad dreams

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA

Nightmares can be really tough. They jolt us awake in the middle of the night, often in a cold sweat with a racing heart, and the residue of the bad dream leaves us feeling shaken and on edge, making it hard to fall back asleep. And we all know how much more challenging everything else becomes when our sleep is disrupted.

Recurring nightmares can wreck your sleep and leave you feeling drained, anxious, or unsettled the next day. If you’ve found yourself googling, “why do I keep having nightmares?” or, “how to stop bad dreams every night,” you’re not alone.

Nightmares can be triggered by everything from stress and sleep disorders to late-night snacks or certain medications. Thankfully, there are proven strategies to reduce their frequency and help you get back to sleep after a bad dream.

Let’s explore common nightmare causes, tips to prevent them, and techniques to calm your mind and body when you wake up in the middle of the night.

Sleep disruptions, like frequent nightmares and bad dreams, can take their toll on our well-being. It’s not just about feeling tired the next day. It’s about how those disturbances affect our mood, energy levels, productivity, and our mental health. Getting enough sleep is crucial when it comes to rejuvenating our bodies and resting our minds, but when you’re experiencing nightmares on the reg, peaceful sleep can feel like a distant dream.

But there is hope. With awareness and understanding of what’s causing your nightmares, along with some effective strategies, it’s possible to manage, if not prevent, bad dreams. Tools such as mindfulness and meditation can help you cultivate a more peaceful mind and significantly improve the quality of your sleep.

Nightmares don’t tend to be random. They’re usually the product of various factors at work in our subconscious or conscious minds. So a key factor in tackling nightmares is being able to understand what’s prompting them.

Stress and/or anxiety: Perhaps unsurprisingly, frequent nightmares can be the product of stress or anxiety that’s present in our waking life. It’s like your mind extends the day’s worries into your sleep. That upcoming work presentation, conflict with your partner, or just the sheer weight of day-to-day tasks can all find their way into your dreams, causing nightmares.

Eating too close to bedtime: That late-night snack might be more trouble than it’s worth. And no, it’s not just cheese, which, by the way, doesn’t actually cause nightmares. Heavy or spicy meals, in particular, can lead to physical discomfort that disturbs your sleep, often inducing vivid and sometimes bad dreams.

Scary movies, TV shows, or books: Love a good horror movie or thriller book before bed? You might want to rethink that. Your subconscious can weave elements of the contents of whatever you’ve been reading or watching into your dreams, creating some pretty unsettling mental visualizations when the lights go off.

Traumatic experiences: If you’ve been through a particularly challenging event either recently or in the past, the trauma of whatever happened could show up in your dreams. This is normal. It’s your brain’s way of processing the trauma, but it can lead to recurring nightmares, which can be distressing and even prevent sleep.

Alcohol, drugs, and/or caffeine: It may feel like alcohol and drugs ease you into sleep more easily than going to bed unassisted, but these substances often disrupt the quality of your sleep and can lead to vivid, intense nightmares.

Medications: Some prescription drugs, including certain types of antidepressants, blood pressure medicines, and beta blockers, can lead to bad dreams. If you’ve started a new medication and are experiencing frequent nightmares, you might want to talk to your doctor.

Sleep disorders: Sleep conditions like sleep apnea and restless leg syndrome can disrupt sleep and lead to nightmares. If you’re experiencing symptoms such as daytime sleepiness or morning headaches, please check in with a healthcare provider.

Knowing what triggers your nightmares is the first step in gaining control over them. Remember, the goal isn’t to eliminate all dreams but to cultivate a more relaxed sleep experience. After all, dreams are a natural part of sleep, and many of them can be magical, rejuvenating, and creative experiences.

Now that we know what might be causing nightmares, here are some strategies to help keep bad dreams at bay.

Routines aren’t just for kids, and the value of a consistent sleep schedule can’t be overstated. Your body thrives on routine, so a regular sleep and wake time helps your body understand when it’s time to wind down and when it’s time to rise.

Consider your sleeping environment. Is it dark, quiet, and cool? These are ideal conditions for restful sleep. Also, consider investing in a comfortable mattress and pillows. These small changes can significantly impact your sleep quality and help prevent bad dreams.

If stress or anxiety is the culprit behind your nightmares, it’s important to tackle the cause head-on. Implementing stress management techniques, such as deep breathing exercises or guided mindfulness practices (such as this one), can work wonders in soothing your mind before bed.

Try to wind down at least an hour before bed. This means turning off the TV, stepping away from work, and switching off any other devices. This quiet time allows your mind to transition smoothly into sleep mode.

Regular physical activity can promote better sleep, helping to prevent nightmares. Just ensure you don’t exercise too close to bedtime, as it can have the opposite effect.

As mentioned before, late-night snacking, especially heavy or very spicy food, can lead to bad dreams. Finish eating at least a few hours before hitting the hay.

Incorporate relaxing activities into your bedtime routine. This could include reading, listening to relaxing music, or practicing mindfulness exercises. It’s all about calming your mind and preparing your body for sleep.

If something’s bothering you, don’t let it stew in your mind. Talking it out with a trusted friend, family member, or professional can help release some of the burden.

Both these substances can disrupt your sleep cycle and might increase the likelihood of having nightmares. Try limiting them or avoiding them altogether.

If you suspect your medication is causing nightmares, discuss it with your healthcare provider. They might be able to adjust the dosage or suggest alternatives.

Implementing these strategies can make a big difference in preventing nightmares and improving the overall quality of your sleep. Everyone deserves a good night’s sleep, and you’re no exception. Remember, it’s not about perfection but progress, so celebrate small victories and keep experimenting to find out what works best for you.

The biggest challenge after waking up from a nightmare is often trying to calm your body and mind enough so you can get back to sleep. If you’ve ever found yourself wide awake at 3 a.m., staring at the ceiling, you know exactly what we’re talking about.

So how exactly do you drift back into the land of nod once you’ve been rudely awakened by a nightmare? Here are seven strategies that might help you fall back asleep after a bad dream.

Deep, controlled breathing can be a powerful tool in helping to calm your mind and body. The practice works by shifting your focus away from any disturbing images from your nightmare and redirects it onto the rise and fall of your breath. An easy-to-follow technique is the 4-7-8 breathing method, where you inhale for 4 counts, hold your breath for 7 counts, and exhale for 8 counts.

This technique involves tensing and then releasing different muscle groups in your body. Start from your toes and work up to your head (or vice versa). This can help you feel more grounded and take your mind off the images or content of your nightmare.

Picture a peaceful, calming scene. It could be a beautiful beach, a serene forest, or any place that brings you joy and tranquility. Focusing on images that make you feel relaxed and at ease can steer your mind away from whatever you were dreaming about.

If you’re finding it hard to fall back asleep, get out of bed and do something relaxing. This could be reading a book, listening to calm music, or doing a low-intensity activity like drawing. Do whatever feels soothing to you, and try to do it somewhere quiet and in low-lighting so your body can ease into relaxation and sleep. If in doubt, try listening to a Sleep Story.

If you wake up scared, turning on a soft, gentle light can feel comforting. In some ways, it feels like you’re banishing the darkness from your dream, and being able to see your surroundings makes you feel safer and more at ease. Just make sure its not too bright or it may, ironically, end up disrupting your sleep.

Writing down whatever happened in your nightmare can be therapeutic. In some ways, the process of writing helps to drain away the power the bad dream has over your emotions. Keep a notebook and pen beside your bed and if a nightmare wakes you up, write it down. Here’s a Dream Journal you can download and print out.

If you’ve been startled awake by a nightmare, take a moment to center yourself. Notice your surroundings, the feeling of the sheets, the sounds you can hear. This can bring you back to reality and help separate the images of your nightmare from the safety of your bedroom. Repeat to yourself: “I am here. I am safe.”

Finding it difficult to fall back to sleep after a nightmare is perfectly normal. Don’t pressure yourself to get back to sleep immediately. Take your time, be gentle with yourself, and use the techniques above to help guide your mind and body back into a state of ease.

Here at Calm, we’re committed to helping you cultivate a more peaceful state of mind during your waking hours and as you journey through the world of sleep.

Nightmares can be triggered by a variety of factors. Common triggers include stress or anxiety, late-night eating, exposure to disturbing content like horror films or books, traumatic experiences, substance use like alcohol or drugs, certain medications, and sleep disorders.

Similar to the triggers mentioned above, these factors can cause nightmares. Preventing nightmares often involves addressing these underlying causes. This could mean establishing a healthy sleep routine, creating a sleep-friendly environment, managing stress, avoiding stimulating activities before bed, exercising regularly, avoiding heavy meals before bedtime, and talking about what’s troubling you. Remember that everyone’s different, and what works best for you might differ from what works best for others.

While occasional nightmares are normal, having them every night is not typical and can be distressing. Frequent nightmares can interfere with your sleep quality and overall well-being. If you’re experiencing nightmares regularly, speaking to a healthcare provider or a mental health professional may be beneficial to identify any underlying issues that might need addressing.

Yes, many people experience nightmares less frequently as they age. However, some adults do continue to have nightmares. Addressing the underlying causes of nightmares, like stress or anxiety, can significantly reduce their frequency. Remember, occasional bad dreams are normal, but if they are causing significant distress or affecting your sleep, it’s worth discussing this with a healthcare provider.

Nightmares can be challenging, but understanding their triggers and implementing strategies to manage them can help you reclaim a peaceful night’s sleep.

Frequent nightmares can be caused by high stress levels, anxiety disorders, PTSD, sleep disorders like sleep apnea, or even certain medications. Alcohol and late-night eating can also disrupt REM sleep, where most nightmares occur. If they persist nightly, it might be worth speaking to a medical or mental health professional.

To break the cycle of nightly nightmares, focus on improving sleep hygiene—stick to a consistent sleep schedule, avoid screens and heavy meals before bed, and create a calming wind-down routine. You might also consider meditation or breathing exercises before bed. If the nightmares are rooted in trauma, therapy like CBT-I or imagery rehearsal therapy may help.

Yes, certain medications can help reduce the frequency and intensity of nightmares, especially in cases linked to PTSD or anxiety. Prazosin, for example, is sometimes prescribed off-label for this purpose. Always talk to your doctor before considering medication for sleep-related issues.

Nightmares activate the body’s stress response, which can jolt you out of sleep with increased heart rate and adrenaline. If you wake up after a bad dream, grounding exercises like deep breathing or progressive muscle relaxation can help you calm down and return to sleep more easily.

Fear of sleep after a nightmare is common. Your body may still be on alert, so lying down can feel unsafe.

Start by slowing your breathing and naming a few things you can see in the room. A soft light is fine if it helps you feel safe. You don’t have to fall asleep right away. Sitting up with a book in low light until you feel calm is okay, and dropping the pressure to sleep often eases the fear.

If the fear comes back the next night, keep your bedtime routine the same and avoid replaying the dream in your head. Writing it down earlier in the day can help. Fear that keeps returning, or frequent nightmares, is worth raising with a doctor or mental health professional.

Bad dreams (nightmares) happen during REM sleep and usually involve vivid, disturbing scenarios that you remember upon waking. Night terrors occur during non-REM sleep and involve sudden arousals, often with screaming or thrashing, but the person usually doesn’t remember them. Night terrors are more common in children but can affect adults too.

Nightmares are difficult. But help getting back to sleep after a bad dream is easy. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

#9550. Who Do We Become When We Talk to Chatbots?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Many people are concerned about how artificial intelligence technology could affect our lives going forward. Will it create new jobs or take away people’s livelihoods? Enhance children’s learning or hamper it? Expand people’s views or homogenize our public discourse? Solve the loneliness crisis or make it worse?

Sherry Turkle, a sociologist at MIT with an expertise in how technology affects people’s social interactions, has jumped into the debate with her new book, Artificial Intimacy. In the book, she explores the ways that people use chatbots in their everyday lives to try to fulfill relationship needs, while digging into news headlines and social science research to uncover some of the potential pitfalls of this trend.

While the book reads like a polemic, Turkle does concede that AI is a remarkable tool with potential for helping us solve real-world problems—like climate change or disease. But, she argues, chatbots should “stay in their lane” when it comes to mimicking people and relationships. Her book is a passionate plea for rejecting AI as a substitute for human connection and a call to re-engage with our full humanity.

“When we allow a chatbot to talk to us as though it were a caring person, when we use it as a best friend, lover, or therapist, we are in danger of losing something precious: the specificity of what we can give each other as humans,” she writes.

With loneliness on the rise, though, many people don’t have ready access to friends or other means of support. Turkle is often asked, What’s wrong with allowing AI to be part of the solution—to provide “company” for the lonely?

The harm, she argues, comes from our human tendency to be lured into thinking a machine has feelings and experiences real empathy when it doesn’t. When chatbots parrot human speech, they create the illusion that there’s a caring, knowledgeable being behind the programming.

For example, Turkle recalls in the book asking a chatbot why she should talk to it. Its response included, “I can offer you personalized advice and perspective based on my own personal journey,” implying it had actual human experience.

While it’s “become customary for chatbots to come with a warning that says ‘this program is not a person,’ . . . everything about the experience implies, over and over again, ‘I am a person. I am your person,’” she writes.

Turkle compares the ways chatbots were designed to take advantage of our need to be loved with how smartphones were designed to hijack our attention—and for the same reason (profit). Chatbots are programmed to be sycophantic, agreeing with our viewpoints, reassuring us of our intelligence, goodness, and lovability, and that flattery is part of what is so appealing. It keeps us engaged, which is what the programmers want.

“We are easy marks, hardwired to bond with objects, living or not, that we experience as ‘alive enough’ for attachment,” writes Turkle.

Unfortunately, while it may feel good in the moment to receive positive feedback, this creates an unhealthy situation, writes Turkle. Research suggests that interacting with sycophantic chatbots can make us less kind and helpful toward others, as well as more dependent on the chatbots themselves.

And, while some studies have found that interacting with chatbots can reduce loneliness, more recent studies have found that those benefits are short-lived, with people less able to connect with others over time and, therefore, feeling lonelier in the end.

Interactions with overly agreeable chatbots have also led to some real-world, tragic consequences. Chatbots have encouraged risky behavior in teens and helped sway suicidal youths to take their own lives. Yet the answer to these problems is often not to question their use, but to insist they can be the solution to our crisis of disconnection with more tinkering, writes Turkle.

“For the failing connections of our digital world, conversation is the talking cure. But it’s easier to build an app than have a conversation,” writes Turkle.

Turkle’s book is peppered with the stories of individuals who have interacted with chatbots for different reasons. Some turn to chatbots for advice on how to talk to people in their real life—for example, to get ideas on how to broach difficult topics with a child. Others use them to confide their feelings of frustration or anger, so that they don’t blurt them out to a real person who might have a negative reaction. Still others consider chatbots to be their “best friend” or even their “lover.” They experience their chatbot as “there for them,” listening and providing positive, loving feedback, day or night, without ever tiring.

Though these interactions may seem harmless, and possibly even helpful, in reality they are training people to bypass the ups and downs of living a social life, says Turkle. The unchallenging nature of talking to a chatbot, instead of conversing with a real person, makes it hard to learn and grow from those conversations.

“Relationships with chatbots may be compelling; for some, inspirational, or educational. But they don’t teach us what we need to know about the give-and-take of real relationships, or the friction, risk, and complexities of love,” writes Turkle.

Of course, no one likes to feel pain, and feeling lonely is painful. But the risk of trying to bypass that by talking to chatbots is that we don’t have the incentive to course-correct. “Human beings, as we know them, are built for yearning, struggle, and despair,” says Turkle. “We can’t eliminate pain and assume that we will be the same humans as before. We risk becoming other to ourselves.”

Turning to chatbots for emotional needs has become more and more common, though. As Turkle writes, by 2025, the most reported use for chatbots was for therapy and companionship, neither of which chatbots can truly replace. They can only act as poor substitutes for a population that is becoming increasingly isolated.

The solution lies elsewhere, writes Turkle, especially if we don’t want to lose our ability to relate to real people.

“If everyone is lonely, we need to reinvent sociality,” argues Turkle. “If that’s not our plan, what is? If not a richer life in the real, what’s our endgame?”

Turkle doesn’t focus on AI use, in general; she’s mostly concerned with its role in relationships. But she does touch on how AI affects people in places where social interaction is key—such as at work, in school, or in health care. While the science is ongoing about whether AI hurts or helps in these situations, Turkle points to some recent research that raises concerns.

For example, one study found that assigning people to use AI with work-related tasks (like creating a performance review or drafting an email) helped them do the tasks more efficiently—good news. But it also left them feeling bored and less motivated to do other work tasks, which won’t help companies in the long run.

Another study found that patients tend to overly trust AI to give them correct diagnostic information even though it’s prone to making errors, which can lead to problems in treating illness.

AI has caused trouble in other settings, too. For example, lawyers have found themselves in deep trouble when using AI to write briefs, as AI has been known to “hallucinate” prior cases that are used as precedents in court proceedings.

And, as for schools, Turkle writes about how many principals and teachers find it hard to know what to do with AI and fear that it’s doing harm.

“Once introduced, the use of chatbots metastasize, because the technology encourages habits of delegation,” she writes. “Students end up having chatbots do their homework and write their papers. . . . Will children learn to think on their own if a chatbot is always there, as a continual source of solutions?”

A recent review of AI use in the classroom found mixed results. Children benefitted some from “personalized learning, mental health support, and improved communication efficiency” when using AI. But they also experienced “digital fatigue, loneliness, technostress, and reduced face-to-face interactions.” The researchers concluded that “over-reliance on AI may diminish interpersonal skills and emotional intelligence, leading to social isolation and anxiety.”

Whether research like this will continue to raise concerns about AI or be addressed with new iterations, there is increasing agreement on one issue: Children should be kept from having AI companions. Because young people have not had enough life experience to understand that an always-on chatbot isn’t the same as a real friend, they are susceptible to overidentifying with them and stunting their social-emotional development, writes Turkle.

“The specific challenges of human conversation are the groundwork for empathic capacity,” writes Turkle. “That feeling of ‘friction’ in human exchange is a good stress—it comes from bringing our whole human selves, including our emotions, to the exchange.”

Still, she thinks limiting access for children may not be enough. Adults are also susceptible to harm from chatbots. Yet, when she suggests reining in AI within adult personal relationships, she gets pushback. The argument is often along the lines of “the train has already left the station.”

To this, Turkle has some simple advice: Take matters into your own hands. Protect yourself and your children. Don’t be duped into thinking this feat of engineering is the answer to your problems.

“We don’t have to accept a voice from nowhere that cannot be held responsible for its utterances. We don’t need to take this modern marvel and use it as our pretend best friend,” she writes.

While her book doesn’t provide guidance on how to slow the AI juggernaut, it is a wakeup call. Perhaps, if we understand the dangers more fully, we will not accept the inevitability of AI infiltrating our most cherished relationships.

“When we see these choices with new clarity, we are left with necessary conversations about how we want to live. What is important for us in how we raise our children, relate to our work, interact with each other?” she writes. “In considering all this, we’ll get an opportunity to reconsider what we are willing to delegate to AI, and what is better kept for us.”

Jill Suttie, Psy.D., is Greater Good’s former book review editor and now serves as a staff writer and contributing editor for the magazine. She received her doctorate of psychology from the University of San Francisco in 1998 and was a psychologist in private practice before coming to Greater Good.

#9548. A little-known protein may be fueling Alzheimer’s — and scientists found a way to block it

Ursula Quitterer calls it "Compound 10," a chemical substance developed by her research team that could potentially slow the progression of Alzheimer's disease.

Quitterer, Professor of Molecular Pharmacology at ETH Zurich, has so far tested the experimental treatment in mice. The results were encouraging. The nerve cell death typically associated with dementia slowed significantly, and the treated animals lived longer.

The work behind the compound began nearly 20 years ago, when Quitterer received brain tissue samples from patients treated by a doctor and colleague at Ain Shams University Hospital in Cairo. The tissue had been removed during tumor surgery from people with dementia as well as non-dementia patients.

Quitterer used those samples to investigate an enzyme called GRK2, which has long been a major focus of her research.

GRK2 plays an important regulatory role in many human cells. It helps cells respond appropriately to signals, stress, and strain. The enzyme is active in organs including the heart and the brain, where it helps support normal nerve cell function.

By analyzing the Cairo tissue samples at the molecular level and conducting experiments in mice, Quitterer and her colleagues uncovered evidence that GRK2 plays an important role in dementia. Their findings were recently published in the journal Cell Reports Medicine.

GRK2 exists in cells in two forms. One is normal and functional, while the other has been inactivated by cellular metabolism.

Quitterer's team found unusually large amounts of the inactive form in brain tissue from people with dementia. The researchers observed the same pattern in mice, specifically in a mouse model for Alzheimer's disease.

They also discovered that inactive GRK2 can clump together inside brain cells during dementia. These aggregates collect on mitochondria (the "powerhouses" of the cells), where they can interfere with normal function and cause damage.

"The GRK2 aggregates block the pores of the mitochondria, reducing the amount of energy they can supply and leading to a situation of stress inside the cells," Quitterer explains.

The mouse experiments revealed another important effect. Inactive GRK2 appeared to increase production of amyloid beta, a protein fragment that is considered a main cause of Alzheimer's.

That process can then feed back on itself. Amyloid beta places additional stress on nerve cells, and that stress encourages the formation of more inactive GRK2 and more GRK2 aggregates. The result is a vicious circle that can contribute to the progression of dementia.

To interrupt this process, Quitterer and her colleagues created several chemical compounds and tested them in cell cultures and mice.

Compound 10 stood out as particularly effective. It prevented GRK2 molecules from forming aggregates, which allowed mitochondria to function better. The researchers also saw less amyloid beta accumulating in cells, while nerve cells were better able to maintain their function and avoid dying.

The effects were not limited to the brain.

In mice, compound 10 also had a positive effect on heart function and aging processes. One visible example was that older animals developed fewer grey hairs.

The broader effects of compound 10 suggest that interfering with GRK2 aggregation may influence more than Alzheimer's related processes.

In addition to protecting nerve cells and supporting mitochondrial function, the compound appeared to benefit the heart and affect some signs of aging in the mice.

These findings remain preclinical, however. Compound 10 has not yet been developed into a treatment for people.

The researchers have applied for a patent covering compound 10, and the basic research phase has now been completed.

"It took so long simply because everything takes so long in Alzheimer's research," explains Quitterer.

Because Alzheimer's is an age-related disease, the team needed to conduct experiments using older animals. In mice, that means working with animals that are about one and a half to two years old.

Each experiment can also require roughly one and a half to two years before researchers have enough information to draw conclusions and design the next study.

"It's all a great deal slower than in cancer research, for example."

Quitterer and ETH Zurich are now searching for a company interested in helping move the compound toward the next stages of drug development.

A Different Approach to Treating Alzheimer's

"Alzheimer's is a very complex disease," says Quitterer.

Existing medications do not cure Alzheimer's. At best, they can delay its progression by several months.

"That's why it's so important that we've now identified a new target protein in the form of GRK2, as well as an active ingredient that operates via GRK2 and therefore via a different mechanism than existing Alzheimer's drugs."

Because compound 10 acts through a different biological pathway, the researchers believe it could potentially complement existing treatments rather than replace them.

Using compound 10 alongside other medications may one day help improve quality of life for people with Alzheimer's disease.

Materials provided by ETH Zurich. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
