#9535. A major Alzheimer’s risk gene may shrink brain cells years before symptoms

Millions of people carry APOE4, the strongest known genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease. New research suggests the gene variant may begin altering brain activity well before memory problems become noticeable.

Researchers at Gladstone Institutes have now mapped out a molecular sequence that could help explain these early effects. Their findings also point to a possible way to reverse some of the changes.

In a study using mouse models, published in Nature Aging, the researchers found that APOE4 increases production of a protein called Nell2. Higher Nell2 levels caused neurons to become smaller and unusually active. Mice with the greatest brain hyperactivity when they were young later developed the most severe memory problems.

The team then reduced Nell2 production. Even in adult mice carrying APOE4, neurons returned toward their normal size and firing behavior. The result raises the possibility that future drugs targeting Nell2 could help people with APOE4 who face an elevated risk of Alzheimer's disease.

"To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study that has directly examined what APOE4 does to the function of neurons at different ages," says Misha Zilberter, PhD, principal staff research scientist at Gladstone and a senior author of the study. "We found fundamental changes in brain circuits occurring in young mice that still had normal learning and memory, and importantly, that those changes predicted the development of cognitive deficits at older ages."

A Major Genetic Risk Factor for Alzheimer's

APOE4 is one of three common forms of the APOE gene, but it has a much stronger connection to Alzheimer's risk than the others. Roughly one in four people carry APOE4, and the variant is estimated to occur in 60 to 75 percent of people with Alzheimer's.

"This study is a big breakthrough for the field of Alzheimer's research," says Yadong Huang, MD, PhD, associate director of the Gladstone Institute of Neurological Disease and a senior author of the study. "It opens the door to a better understanding of how APOE4 alters the function of neurons at a young age to increase risk of cognitive decline, and to the development of therapies that could block the detrimental effects of APOE4 early on."

APOE4 Makes Memory Circuits Hyperactive Early

Earlier research had already found signs of unusually high brain activity in human APOE4 carriers before middle age. That early hyperactivity has also been associated with later cognitive decline. What remained unclear was how APOE4 produced these cellular changes and why they might contribute to memory problems later in life.

To investigate, the researchers studied recordings of brain activity in young mice and examined individual neurons from their brains. Young mice carrying APOE4 showed excessive neuronal activity in two areas of the hippocampus, a brain region central to memory.

Notably, those same hippocampal regions have also been found to be hyperactive in people carrying APOE4.

"We found that the extent of hyperactivity in young mice predicted how poorly they performed on spatial learning and memory tests later in life," says Dennis Tabuena, PhD, a scientist co-mentored by Zilberter and Huang, and first author of the new paper.

The scientists also compared these animals with mice carrying APOE3, a version of the APOE gene associated with a lower risk of Alzheimer's disease in humans.

Neurons in the affected brain regions were smaller in APOE4 mice than in mice with APOE3. Smaller neurons tend to respond more easily to stimulation, making them more likely to fire excessively.

The hippocampal neurons of APOE3 mice eventually became more excitable as well, but that shift did not appear until the animals were old.

"This suggests APOE4 accelerates a process that resembles normal aging, and could explain why people with the gene variant are more likely to develop Alzheimer's disease earlier in life," Huang says.

The Effect Comes From APOE4 Inside Neurons

Most APOE4 in a healthy brain is produced by astrocytes, cells that help support neurons. Because of this, researchers had long suspected that astrocytes were largely responsible for the connection between APOE4 and Alzheimer's risk.

The new results point in a different direction. According to the researchers, the hippocampal hyperactivity associated with APOE4 was entirely driven by APOE4 produced within neurons themselves.

"When we deleted the APOE4 gene from astrocytes, nothing changed," Zilberter says. "But when we deleted it from neurons, the cells became larger and started functioning normally again."

Nell2 Emerges as a Possible Treatment Target

The researchers next searched for the molecular process responsible for making APOE4 neurons smaller and more excitable. They examined patterns of gene activity in individual cells across several types of cells in the hippocampus.

That analysis highlighted Nell2. The molecule appeared at unusually high levels in neurons carrying APOE4.

The researchers then used CRISPRi, a method that lowers the activity of a gene without permanently changing DNA, to reduce Nell2 in hippocampal neurons from adult APOE4 mice.

After Nell2 levels fell, the neurons became larger and less excitable. The finding indicates that elevated Nell2 is responsible for the excessive neuronal activity seen in brains carrying APOE4.

Nell2 had not previously been investigated specifically in connection with APOE4. However, earlier research found elevated levels of the protein in the brains of Alzheimer's patients, with higher amounts associated with poorer cognitive function.

"What's exciting about Nell2 is that we were able to reverse the disease manifestations in adult mice by lowering its level," Huang says. "That tells us the damage is not irreversible, and that there may be a window for intervention even after disease processes have been triggered."

The research was supported by the National Institute on Aging (R01AG061150, R01AG087323, R01AG092390, R01AG085468, R01AG055682, R01AG071697, P01AG073082, F32AG0859612), the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (K99NS134734), and the National Center for Research Resources (C06 RR018928).

#9534. Calm launches Shift to help people feel better in the moment through sound

Shift is a new dedicated in-app experience designed to help people relieve stress, wind down, focus, and feel better through bilateral audio, an audio-based approach inspired by a technique therapists use that moves sound intentionally between your ears.

Shift offers four states to move into, grounded in everyday needs: Focus, Release, Uplift, and Sleep, each through its own custom bilateral track. It also includes a 7-day guided program and 20+ additional tracks to browse, including an exclusive track from popular duo, Daisy the Great.

Shift is one of Calm's largest expansions into a category since Sleep Stories, following increased user and cultural demand since it began developing this content in 2022.

SAN FRANCISCO, CA – October 27, 2026 – Calm, a trusted leader in mental wellness with the #1 app to help you sleep more, stress less and live mindfully, launches Shift – a new in-app offering designed to help people shift how they feel in the moment using bilateral audio, an audio-based approach inspired by a technique therapists use. At launch, Shift provides a 7-day guided program and more than 20 custom bilateral tracks, including an exclusive song by popular New York-based duo, Daisy the Great.

Bilateral audio intentionally moves sound between the left and right ear, creating a natural rhythm designed to help shift your mood, whether that’s finally settling into sleep, releasing the day’s tension, or clearing afternoon fog. No special skills required, just headphones and a few minutes.

Calm added bilateral audio content to its music library in 2022 and has since seen user and cultural demand build. It’s one of the top search terms on Calm, Google search for “bilateral audio” is up over 5000% in the past year, and across the internet, concepts like “brain flossing” have gone viral, pointing to bilateral stimulation to “clear mental clutter”.

“Calm’s origins are rooted in making meditation accessible, but we never intended to be a meditation-only app,” said Dun Wang, CEO of Calm. “We want to be a place people can come to feel better, in whatever way they need. At first it was meditation, then it was sleep, which led to the launch of Sleep Stories, an innovative format that is now one of our most popular offerings. Shift is next, leveraging bilateral sound and music to meet people with approachable, trusted, and deeply human support that leaves them feeling better than when they came.”

7 Days of Shift – a 7-day guided program narrated by Calm meditation teacher Rose Nisker, pairing a few minutes of grounding wisdom with a bilateral track each day.

Shift Your State – 4 new bilateral tracks paired with looping visuals, each composed to shift people into one of four goal states: Focus, Release, Uplift, and Sleep.

Shift Music – an expanded library of new bilateral audio tracks for users to explore any time.

Among the new music is an exclusive bilateral remix of “The Record Player Song” from Daisy the Great. Originally released in 2018, the song became a breakout hit for the duo and has amassed more than 200 million streams across two versions. More recently, Daisy the Great reimagined the track using hocketing, a musical technique in which a single melody is split between two or more voices or instruments, alternating notes and rests, and the new version has gained massive traction across TikTok. It's the first of multiple tracks Calm and Daisy the Great will create together for Shift, continuing Calm’s long-standing approach of partnering with artists to create content that resonates with people.

“We started to make a lot of videos online singing with a technique called hocketing where we split up the melody line and pass it back-and-forth, and it makes a really awesome vocal effect. We did it with our song ‘The Record Player Song,’ and that one really seemed to resonate," said Daisy the Great. "That song already has a bit of a built-in bilateral quality with the melody passing between us, and the overlapping vocals, so it made a lot of sense for Shift. We're so, so excited to be working with Calm and their production team to not only share our music in a new way, but hopefully to help people feel good and connected to themselves too.”

Calm also collaborated with outside consultants certified by the EMDR International Association throughout Shift's development to ensure the content is credible, safe, and suitable for everyday, self-guided use.

“With Shift, Calm takes its already impressive collection of self-soothing programs to another level, thoughtfully integrating guided imagery, relaxing music, and gentle bilateral stimulation,” said Roy Kiessling, LISW. “As an experienced EMDR clinician and trainer, I appreciate the care Calm has taken to emphasize relaxation, emotional comfort, and positive resource enhancement. Shift offers a welcome, accessible way to incorporate soothing bilateral stimulation into everyday emotional well-being.”

#9532. The name of a 3,500-year-old Egyptian dog depicted in a tomb painting has been revealed—and it has a unique link to the god Anubis

The dog’s painted presence and name meant that he would survive after death

A researcher has identified the previously unknown name of an Ancient Egyptian dog, painted in the tomb of a noble 3,500 years ago. The name, Duaty, is the first to feature an epithet of the canine-headed god Anubis, raising fresh questions about the role of dogs in Ancient Egyptian society.

“The name is entirely unique among the known corpus of dog names from Egypt,” the archaeologist Chelsea Kaufman of Johns Hopkins University, United States, tells The Art Newspaper. “We only know about 100 dog names from Egypt, several of which are duplicates, but Duaty is entirely new.”

The tomb, located in a necropolis at Luxor, 500km south of Cairo, had previously been investigated by Egyptologists, but the dog’s name, Duaty, couldn’t be read without modern digital imaging software.

Ancient artisans painted three dogs in User’s tomb. Each wears a collar and sits upright beneath User’s chair. Egyptologists had already read the names of two of these dogs: one was Kenii, “Strong One” and the other was Maaty, which means “Trusty”. But the third remained anonymous.

When re-examining photographs of this tomb scene, Kaufman noticed that there was a faint painted inscription above the third dog’s head. She then used digital imaging software to enhance the blue pigment in these faded hieroglyphs, which made it possible to read the name more clearly.

Kaufman’s investigation, published in The Journal of Egyptian Archaeology, revealed that the dog’s name, which means “He-of-the-Underworld”. This is usually an epithet of Anubis, a god associated with the dead and funerary rituals.

“The significance of the name remains an open question,” Kaufman says. “It’s tempting to interpret it as a direct reference to Anubis, but we just can’t be certain this was the intention. It is worth considering that the name alludes to the dog having already died by the time the tomb was painted, but of course this remains speculation.” The dog’s painted presence and name meant, however, that he would survive after death, and enjoy the food and drink that Egyptians offered to the dead in the tomb.

Duaty also differs from the other dogs in the tomb, and every other dog in Egyptian art, by his unique coat pattern, which is red and rippled—intriguingly similar to the clothing worn by User above.

Speaking to The Art Newspaper, the Egyptologist Salima Ikram, who was not involved in the study, says of the discovery: “Pets, particularly dogs, are often shown in Egyptian tomb paintings. Dogs are frequently named, unlike cats, which are called the male cat or the female cat. On the whole, pets are shown as a record of actual companion animals of the deceased, but they might have alluded to the gods as well, such as Anubis, Re, Bastet, and Hathor, with only Anubis being evoked by canines.”

Kaufman meanwhile says it is an extraordinary feeling to have made this discovery. “As far as I know, I am the first person in 3,500 years to read Duaty’s name. We spend so much time studying the people of ancient Egypt, but as someone who is passionate about dogs, it is an honour to give Duaty some of his identity back as well.”

#9531. Speaking Faster Can Make You More Persuasive — Until This Happens

Your best argument may lose its edge if listeners struggle to keep up with how quickly you deliver it.

Your best argument may lose its edge if listeners struggle to keep up with how quickly you deliver it.

Speaking at a lively pace can make a strong argument more convincing, but rushing can weaken its impact.

Very fast speech makes it harder for listeners to weigh up what they hear, reducing the advantage that good reasons have over weak ones.

The findings suggest that persuading someone depends partly on giving them enough opportunity to think.

The conclusions come from six experiments involving almost 4,000 people who listened to persuasive messages delivered at different speeds.

Across the experiments, increasing the pace from very slow speech initially improved impressions of the speaker’s confidence and encouraged closer consideration of the message.

However, these benefits eventually weakened or reversed as the delivery became faster.

This helps explain why simply telling someone to speak more quickly is incomplete advice.

A faster delivery can make an argument easier to engage with until the listener begins struggling to keep up.

Crucially, the consequences depend on whether the reasons being offered stand up to scrutiny.

In the two main experiments, listeners heard a proposal that would allow university students to pay lower tuition fees in exchange for working part-time.

Some heard strong arguments emphasising benefits such as smaller classes and better services.

Others heard weak arguments that included reduced leisure time and superficial improvements to the campus.

The recordings were digitally altered to change speaking speed while keeping other vocal features, such as pitch and intonation, unchanged.

Participants then rated their support for the proposal, with some also recording the thoughts that had occurred to them while listening.

The combined results showed that strong arguments gained an increasing advantage over weak ones as speech became faster, but lost some of that advantage at higher speeds.

In other words, delivery affected how effectively listeners distinguished a convincing case from an unconvincing one.

A central part of persuasion is how carefully people consider the reasons they are given.

When listeners examine a message closely, they have more opportunity to recognise its strengths, spot its weaknesses and form their own reactions.

This benefits a strong argument, while exposing the shortcomings of a weak one.

Very fast delivery can interfere with that process, making the merits of the message less influential.

The analyses suggested that changes in how easily listeners felt they could follow the reasoning helped explain this pattern.

Although speaking speed also affected how confident the speaker sounded, confidence alone did not adequately explain the overall pattern.

One possible reason very slow speech is less effective is that it makes sustaining attention more demanding, while excessively fast speech leaves too little time to absorb the content.

The experiments tested seven speaking speeds, ranging from 113 to 218 words per minute, but did not establish one ideal pace.

The most effective delivery is likely to depend on factors including the complexity of the message, the audience and the presence of distractions.

The findings also concern recorded persuasive messages, so they do not establish a universal rule for every conversation or public speech.

For someone presenting a strong case, the findings suggest keeping the delivery lively while giving listeners time to follow the reasoning.

Rushing may reduce the very scrutiny that would otherwise make a good argument convincing.

The study was published in the Journal of Nonverbal Behavior (Guyer et al., 2025).

#9530. What Bystanders Can Do to Stop Sexual Violence

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

As an undergrad student decades ago, I attended a dorm presentation describing the importance of giving and receiving sexual consent. The workshop leaders explained that if your partner said “no” or “stop” but you proceeded to have sex anyway, it was considered rape.

A high-profile athlete on campus raised his hand and said, in utter disbelief, “That can’t be right. By that definition, everyone I’ve ever had sex with I’ve raped.”

I was horrified by his comment, but most students laughed. He clearly saw nothing wrong with the view he’d expressed, presumably believing it was widely shared.

I immediately thought of this experience when I heard about the alleged sexual assault committed by seven fraternity members at Cornell University. As a social psychologist, and the author of a book examining why so-called good people stay silent in the face of problematic behavior, what I find most tragic about the events at Cornell is that reportedly over 50 men on a group chat learned about the assault as it was happening. Yet there’s been no public report that any of them tried to stop the assault, help the victim, or contact campus or local police departments.

This type of inaction is very common. In about one-third of sexual assaults, at least one other person is present who potentially could intervene but in most instances chooses not to. Why?

Data suggests a minority of men actually commit sexual assault. Researchers estimate about 6.5% of male college students in the United States and Canada have committed rape. Yet many men who find sexual violence offensive mistakenly believe that other men do not.

Undergraduate men in one study reported their beliefs about common rape myths, such as “If a girl doesn’t physically fight back, you can’t really say it was rape,” and “If a girl goes to a room alone with a guy at a party, it is her own fault if she is raped.” Researchers then asked participants how they thought both their close friends and average male college students would answer these same questions.

The results provided clear evidence that college men have skewed views of what those around them are thinking. Most students saw their classmates and friends as more supportive of rape myths than they themselves were.

Unfortunately, believing that other men generally accept sexual violence—even when this belief is wrong—inhibits their willingness to intervene to stop such behavior when they encounter it. In fact, men’s beliefs about their peers’ attitudes are a stronger predictor of their willingness to intervene than their own stated attitudes about sexual aggression.

Men who underestimate their peers’ discomfort with sexually aggressive behavior often fear the consequences of calling out problematic views or intervening in the face of inappropriate behavior. The most common reason male college students give for failing to intervene in situations involving sexual violence is a fear of being laughed at or ridiculed—in particular, a desire not to appear weak to other men.

Men who actually commit assault also tend to overestimate support for such behavior. Not surprisingly, men who report having committed sexual assault believe that other men are more accepting of such behavior and have engaged in such behavior themselves.

This assumed support leads them to feel comfortable describing problematic behavior, which leads other men to believe that sexual violence is more common, and more accepted, than it actually is.

Given the consistent evidence that men wrongly believe that most men are more comfortable with sexual violence than they themselves are, the challenge is not to change the social norm. It’s getting people to see what it actually already is.

Correcting such misperceptions can go a long way toward reducing sexual violence. First-year male college students who participate in a 90-minute sexual assault prevention program—focused on refuting rape myths, increasing awareness of the importance of consent, and correcting misperceptions about other men’s attitudes and behaviors—report reduced levels of sexual aggression themselves four months later.

These programs work in two ways. First, men who receive accurate information about what other men actually believe are less inhibited about speaking out and intervening. Second, men who are at risk of engaging in sexual aggression may change their intentions after learning that their peers do not support such behavior.

At the same time, men in tight-knit groups feel considerable pressure to show loyalty to other group members, which may lead to ignoring bad behavior committed by their peers.

But the underlying dynamics of peer influence can help shift group norms from protecting group members by staying silent to stepping in to prevent bad behavior. One college football player described looking out for his teammates, even if that meant interrupting a potential sexual encounter: “Maybe you don’t get the girl, but you’ll keep your scholarship and still be on the team.”

Another approach for preventing sexual assault is to learn strategies for intervening. Bystander intervention programs emphasize the importance of stopping bad behavior before it escalates, teach specific skills for intervening, and remind people that everyone has a responsibility to prevent sexual violence.

Students who participate in such programs are more confident in their ability to intervene and more willing to do so. Most importantly, rates of sexual violence are markedly lower on campuses that have implemented these programs. For example, one study found that experiences of sexual harassment and stalking were 11% lower and that instances of unwanted sexual activity with women who were too drunk or high to stop them were as much as 17% lower.

It’s tempting to read about the Cornell case and assume the apparent inaction in the face of problematic behavior is uniquely a problem at one college, or only with members of fraternities, or only with college students. But the reality is that pretty much everyone has been in situations where they’ve seen potentially problematic behavior and failed to speak up.

Understanding the very normal psychological factors that lead people to misperceive what others are actually thinking and feeling—and learning specific strategies for intervening—can make a real difference.

#9529. Depression may shut down the brain’s ability to make new neurons

Most of the brain's roughly 100 billion neurons are produced before birth. However, the small number of new neurons that continue to form in the adult hippocampus may play an important role in protecting against depression, according to new research from Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons.

The findings provide the first evidence that neurogenesis, the process of producing new neurons, stalls in the brains of adults with major depressive disorder. Researchers also identified molecular programs involved in controlling this process, offering potential clues for developing new treatments.

"Historically, depression was thought to be a disease of neurotransmitter deficiency, especially serotonin, but we now think that depression stems from multiple issues that affect our neurons' ability to adapt to stress and changing environments," says Maura Dupont, professor of psychiatry, who led the research.

"Without the ability to create new neurons, people with depression may not have the resilience to effectively adapt to the environment."

How New Neurons May Shape Memory and Emotion

The researchers focused on the hippocampus, a brain region that plays a major role in episodic memory and emotional responses to the environment. It is also one of the few areas of the adult brain that continues to generate new neurons.

Although the hippocampus is not the only brain region involved in depression, its influence over both memory and emotion has made it an important area of study. Researchers believe changes there may contribute to the tendency of people with depression to interpret experiences more negatively.

"The hippocampus is important for our ability to distinguish between similar but different memories and separate the emotional connotation of past memories and current events," Dupont says.

This ability is known as pattern separation. When it becomes impaired, individual memories and the emotions attached to them may become less distinct, allowing separate experiences to blend together.

"You may be out with a friend for lunch, but she's tired and doesn't talk much. With intact pattern separation, you remember this as a unique event. With impaired pattern separation, it becomes mixed with previous memories of feeling rejected, leading you to think, 'They're upset with me'," Dupont explains. "And I see this a lot in my patients, where they can only retrieve negative information from their memories."

Research in mice has shown that adult neurogenesis is necessary for pattern separation. A recent study involving patients with brain tumors, in whom neurogenesis was eliminated by radiation therapy directed at the hippocampus, suggests that the same relationship may exist in humans.

"It's important to emphasize that we do not yet know the complete mechanism, particularly in humans, but the newborn neurons seem to enhance pattern separation because they are especially responsive to new experiences and can be incorporated into new memory circuits more easily, allowing new memories to be stored separately from the old ones," Dupont says. "Turning neurogenesis back on may be a way to treat depression in some people by rewiring their hippocampus circuit."

Depression Affects More Than New Neuron Growth

The researchers found that the changes linked to depression extended well beyond neurogenesis. New neuron formation operates within a larger hippocampal circuit that stores episodic memories along with their emotional significance, and molecular disruptions appeared throughout that system.

The affected genes included those involved in building new connections between neurons, supporting communication among brain cells, supplying cellular energy, and moving materials within cells.

The trisynaptic circuit, the hippocampus's primary pathway for establishing new emotional memories, also displayed evidence of inflammation and cellular stress in people with depression.

To identify these changes, researchers studied nearly half a million brain cells collected from people with depression and control subjects shortly after each donor's death.

Using an array of recently developed techniques, the team measured the activity of every gene within individual cells and examined whether cellular proteins had been altered. This enormous dataset allowed researchers to see what individual cells were doing and determine exactly where affected cells were located within the hippocampal circuit.

Genes, Environment, and the Biology of Depression

The analysis revealed altered activity in several genes whose genetic variants have previously been associated with major depression.

Other disrupted genes showed epigenetic changes that may reflect the influence of environmental factors. Epigenetic mechanisms can adjust how strongly genes are turned on or off without altering the underlying DNA sequence.

"These are like dimmer switches that control how active genes are, and they are affected by life experiences such as stress, learning, aging, chemicals, etc.," Dupont says.

The diversity of molecular changes may also help explain why depression can look so different from one person to another.

"Overall, the wide range of effects we found could reflect different pathogenetic mechanisms, perhaps indicating that depression is not just one disease," she adds.

Researchers still have only a limited understanding of depression's underlying biology, according to Dupont. By defining the disorder more precisely at the cellular and molecular levels, studies like this one could eventually provide new targets for treatment.

Dupont and her colleagues hope that depression could eventually be classified according to its molecular characteristics, much as cancer increasingly is today.

"We want to reclassify depression based on its molecular features, similar to what has been done in cancer," Dupont says. "Classifying cancers based on their cellular characteristics, not their locations, has led to new and improved treatments. We hope the same will be true for depression and other psychiatric or brain diseases."

The study, "Dysregulated adult hippocampal neurogenesis in major depressive disorders," was published Aug. 21, 2026, in Nature Medicine.

All authors from Columbia University and/or New York State Psychiatric Institute unless noted: Madeleine S. Peng, Jialin Jiang, Lucia Polizzi, Tiancheng Shi, Rakshitha Ramkumar, Victor O. Anosike, Giulia Guasoni, Alexandra M. Wamalwa, Madeline B. Mariani, Cheick A. Sissoko, Alexandria N. Tartt, Camille Fulmore, Gorazd B. Rosoklija, Yung-yu Huang, Victoria Arango, Shujuan T. #9528. Is sharenting safe? 7 ways to mindfully post about your kids online

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Your kid loses their first tooth or says something hilarious at dinner, and your thumb is already halfway to the share button. For a lot of parents and caregivers, posting these moments feels like second nature.

Believe it or not, there's actually a name for this habit: sharenting. And while it’s often a simple way to stay connected, it also puts your child’s story online before they can choose to share it. If you’ve started to wonder about the risks, it’s a good time to take stock of your posting habits.

Here's a look at why parents share and what’s worth knowing about the risks, plus seven small shifts to help you post with confidence.

Sharenting is when parents or caregivers post about their kids on social media. It could be a single birthday photo, or years of posts documenting a whole childhood. Think videos, funny quotes, school updates, potty-training wins, and even ultrasound pictures from before the baby arrives.

It's also widespread. Research reviews estimate that about three in four parents share photos, stories, or videos of their kids online, and most use their children's real names.

Parents have always shared news about their kids through holiday letters, birth announcements, and photos mailed to relatives. Social media just made the audience much bigger, the posts more public, and the record harder to remove.

Most sharenting comes from a good place. You're proud of your kid and you want the people in your life to know. Studies on parents who post about their kids point to the same reasons:

Staying close: Photos and videos let faraway family and friends watch your child grow.

Celebrating and remembering: Posts mark your child’s milestones and give you something to scroll back through later.

Finding community: Other parents and caregivers can offer advice and a “me too” at 2am, when parenting feels isolating.

Feeling seen: A kind comment on a rough day reminds you that you’re doing okay.

💙 Feeling alone as a parent? Here’s how to deal with loneliness.

Sharing your kids online isn’t necessarily harmful. Still, a few risks are worth knowing about:

A lasting digital footprint. Screenshots, reshares, and archives mean a photo can outlast the original post. Many kids have years of photos online before they're old enough to understand who can see them.

Personal information. Someone could piece together a full name, birth date, hometown, and school from a handful of posts. Over time, details like these may be misused for identity theft.

Location and background details. Location tags and details like a house number, school logo, or regular park in the background show where your child spends their time. On a public account, that can make their routine visible to strangers.

Facial recognition and AI. Photos on public accounts may be saved, scanned, or collected by AI tools and facial recognition software. Some of those tools turn ordinary photos into fake images.

💙 Want to bring more intention to parenting, online and off? Start here.

Before you hit share, take a breath and think about whether you want to post this moment. If you do, scan the photo and caption for anything that gives away too much, like a full name or a street sign.

For some structure, a short breathing exercise or meditation can help.

💙 Listen to Pause to Breathe with Prof. Megan Reitz on Calm.

A couple of settings are worth checking before your next post. If your account is public, anyone can find and save your posts. Photos taken on your phone may also include the location where you took them.

Switch to a private account and remove followers you don’t know.

Turn off geotagging in your camera and app settings.

Platforms can change their defaults without warning, so it’s worth redoing this check every couple of months.

You can share the moment without giving away your child’s identity. Skip birth dates, school names, and daily routines. Use a nickname or first initial instead of your child’s full name.

Posting a day or two later makes it harder for anyone to know where your child is in real time.

Once your child is old enough to weigh in, show them the post and ask if they're okay with you sharing it. This shows them that their opinion matters. If your child is too young to decide, the next tip can help you decide for them.

Imagine your child at 25, seeing what you’re about to post. Does it give away something private about them, such as a health issue or a hard time at school? What seems relatable now may feel too personal to them later.

If you're unsure, keep the more personal moments in a private family group or an offline album.

💙 Explore Shift Your Perspective with Jay Shetty on Calm.

Your past posts felt right at the time, and it’s okay if some show more than you’d share today. Scroll back through your posts for details like full names, school names, or locations.

Delete the post, archive it, or move it to a private album if it feels too revealing.

You're not the only one with a camera. Grandparents, co-parents, babysitters, and friends may post photos of your child too, usually out of love and pride. A conversation up front about family boundaries keeps everyone on the same page.

leave full names and birth dates out of captions

skip location tags and recognizable landmarks in the background

use private groups or shared albums instead of public posts

💙 Calm’s Kind Communication session can help you find the words for a warm, open conversation.

Sharenting means posting about your child on social media, and the word blends "sharing" and "parenting." It covers anything from baby photos to regular updates as they grow up.

Common sharenting examples include ultrasound pictures, birthday posts, funny quotes, and health or milestone updates. Even a photo that seems harmless can reveal more than you intended, like a club sign or a team jersey in the background.

Many parents share to stay connected and celebrate their kids. Sharenting keeps faraway family members in the loop and connects you with other parents who get it. During hard stretches, it can help you feel less alone.

The main risks of sharenting include a lasting digital footprint and exposed personal details. Photos can be saved, reshared, or collected by AI tools, which is why child safety groups encourage private accounts.

That said, many posts don’t lead to harm, and small habits like turning off location tags help lower the risks further.

Sharenting shapes your child’s public image before they’re old enough to agree to it. Names, schools, and tagged locations can also reveal their routines to strangers, and a handful of details may be used for identity theft.

If you keep personal moments offline now, your child has more room to shape their own image as they grow.

There's no set age for when kids should have a say in what you post. Young kids may not fully understand what sharing means, so the decision starts with you. You can start asking as soon as they’re able to weigh in, and give their yes or no more weight as they grow.

#9526. Your brain may not actually “make” decisions

What we experience when making a decision may be very different from what actually happens inside the brain, according to Indiana University Professor Tom James.

For decades, both scientific theories and everyday intuition have tended to describe decision-making as a sequence. First we perceive something, then we think about it and make a choice, and finally we act. Each step is often assumed to correspond to a distinct brain function, moving from sensory processing to cognition and then to motor activity.

Many scientific approaches, particularly model-based cognitive neuroscience, are built around this same linear framework. It also matches how decision making feels from the inside. As James notes, "Our actions feel like they are caused by decisions based on desires, beliefs, and intentions."

Rethinking the Brain's Decision Making Process

James argues that this familiar explanation, sometimes called the "sandwich model," does not fit neatly with what scientists know about the brain. Sensation has identifiable sensory mechanisms, and action has identifiable motor mechanisms. But the supposed cognitive stage between the two does not appear to have a corresponding neural process that functions as a distinct decision maker.

Rather than proposing a dedicated decision-making system that directs behavior, James suggests that sensory, sensorimotor, and motor processes together produce what he calls 'action selection.' In this view, behavior emerges through ongoing interactions among the brain, body, and environment. These processes can occur simultaneously and feed back into one another rather than unfolding as a simple sequence.

That does not mean James believes decisions are unreal.

As James says, "Of course they do. We use this language all the time and it's very helpful in terms of describing behavior. The leap, I think, is to say that the brain works by having decision-making or control processes. It produces behavior that is well described in that way. But it doesn't need a process that does that to make it look that way."

James, a professor in the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences in the College of Arts and Sciences, presents the argument in "Sensorimotor Mechanisms of Decisions and Actions," an article just published in the Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience.

What Happens in the Brain When We Make a Decision?

James develops his argument using a "physicalist" framework associated with philosophers such as Daniel Dennett. The approach makes explicit what James sees as a basic assumption underlying science: physical phenomena can cause both physical and nonphysical phenomena, while nonphysical phenomena cannot themselves cause physical events.

Sensory and motor processes, for example, are physical. Decisions, in this framework, are nonphysical. If that is the case, James argues, a decision cannot literally cause a physical action.

To make the idea easier to understand, he uses several analogies.

Drawing on Daniel Dennett's comparison between the self and a center of mass (CoM) or center of gravity, James suggests that decisions may function in a similar way. A center of mass is a useful mathematical concept, but it cannot independently exert a physical force. (i.e., you cannot move an object's center of mass without moving the object) In the same sense, James proposes that a decision may be an abstract description rather than a physical entity that directly causes something to happen.

Another analogy shows how useful concepts can become less informative when scientists need to understand events at a more detailed level.

We routinely use the phrase "the university" to describe the activities of an institution. The term conveniently represents a collection of people, buildings, departments, and processes. Saying that "the university took certain actions during a campus protest," however, tells us little about the specific events involved. A detailed explanation might instead require examining meetings between administrators, phone calls to state police, and other individual actions.

James argues that decisions present a similar problem for neuroscience. They may provide a useful high-level description of behavior without revealing the physical mechanisms producing it.

As James maintains: "As mental phenomena, they are defined on too abstract a level for the goals of cognitive neuroscience."

In other words, simply saying that someone made a decision does not explain what happened inside the brain.

James uses a third example to push the argument further.

He points to a robot constructed from a small number of sensory, motor, and sensorimotor modules. The machine demonstrates "wall-following" behavior that can appear purposeful. From the outside, it seems to have goals, strategies, and perhaps even something resembling intentions.

But the robot contains no system designed to make decisions.

"The robot does not have decisions built into it," James explains. "It just senses its environment and moves around accordingly. And based on the environment, wall-following turns out to be a good thing. It looks intentional. It looks strategic. It looks like the robot is making decisions. And yet, it is not. The reason we know it is not is that there are no systems built into it to do that."

That raises a provocative question. If a relatively simple machine can produce behavior that looks intentional without possessing a decision-making system, could human behavior also appear to result from centralized decisions even if no such central process exists?

James argues that this explanation is more parsimonious than assuming the brain contains what he calls "a higher-level, central controller that monitors and regulates sensory and motor processes."

The idea of a central controller also creates a philosophical problem that has been discussed since the time of Descartes.

If some higher-level entity inside the brain is responsible for observing information and deciding what to do, scientists still need to explain how that controller itself works.

"Explaining that the brain works by way of a central controller suggests that you haven't figured out how the brain works, because you've just put a person inside your brain," says James. "Dennett called this idea the Cartesian Theater. That person inside your brain would need another person inside its brain, which would need a person inside its brain and so on, in an infinite regress. So the problem is never solved. It's just passed on."

Instead of invoking an internal decision maker, James proposes focusing directly on the interacting sensory and motor systems that generate behavior.

If decision making emerges from continuous interactions among the brain, body, and environment, studying it will require experimental methods capable of capturing that complexity.

James acknowledges that this creates both exciting opportunities and difficult methodological challenges. Researchers would need to move beyond strictly linear models and examine processes that happen simultaneously, influence one another, and change as a person interacts with the surrounding world.

His own laboratory has begun exploring this direction by drawing on ideas from embodied cognition and ecological psychology.

James believes this approach could help cognitive neuroscience uncover the mechanisms that give rise to what we describe as decision-making. It may also offer new ways to investigate many other cognitive and mental phenomena that have traditionally been treated as distinct processes inside the brain.

Materials provided by Indiana University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9525. Structures found on Peruvian coastline highlight underwater secrets of the Inca

El Huarco’s cliff structures, made by the Inca in the 15th century, were designed to be seen from the sea Rocío Villar Astigueta/Ministerio de Cultura de Perú

Near the desert cliffs of Cerro Azul, 170km south of Lima, visitors are likely to stumble on El Huarco. This is a place where architecture was not merely the result of conquest but served as an aggressive form of visual propaganda, designed to overwrite the history of a vanquished society. Recently, maritime and coastal archaeological research has revealed that an imposing imperial structure, erected by the Inca in the 15th century, was not intended to be seen from land but instead to scare off enemies approaching by sea.

To secure their dominion, the Inca undertook a radical aesthetic transformation of the cliffs, creating a landscape specifically designed to both impress and intimidate. “Recent studies along the bluffs have identified 17 architectural elements,” the archaeologist Rocío Villar Astigueta tells The Art Newspaper, “including walls and orderly lines of stone that provide evidence of the intense modification of the cliff face overlooking the sea.”

She adds that this architecture was deliberately planned to be viewed from the ocean: “Its visibility from the sea acted as a political marker for sailors, communicating the presence and power of the Inca Empire on the central coast,” linking this architecture to a system of ports or paths that formed part of the network of the Qhapaq Ñan (the Inca road system).

El Huarco Archaeological Site Rocío Villar Astigueta/Ministerio de Cultura de Perú

Prior to the expansion of the Inca Empire in the 15th century, the lower part of the Cañete Valley belonged to the Huarco Confederation. The Huarco were master fishers, hydrologists and architects of the landscape. Their architectural language was defined by tapial—massive walls of rammed earth that reflected the dusty shades of the cliffs—and small sun-dried adobe bricks. For centuries, this organic architecture served a proud society that tenaciously defended their autonomy.

In his Crónica del Perú (1553), the Spanish conquistador Pedro Cieza de León describes the war between the Inca and the Huarco as one of the most brutal chapters in the pre-Hispanic history of the Andes. The Inca forces faced stubborn resistance for four years, and their victory ultimately came not through a direct military advance but trickery.

As the story goes, the Inca emperor’s wife used the area’s spiritual traditions to devise a deadly trap. She sent a mission to propose a great ritual ceremony of joint fishing to honour the goddess of the sea, promising the Huarco that the Inca would recognise their sovereignty over the valley in exchange for their participation. The Huarco agreed, abandoning their clifftop fortresses to board the ceremonial rafts. Once the hidden Inca army had left the Huarco defenceless at sea, it entered the valley, took control and captured the population. The Inca hanged the Huarco leaders and most of the local inhabitants.

To create the imposing cliff structure after their successful conquest, the Inca introduced elite stonework techniques to an environment built entirely of earth. Villar stresses that the architectural styles found on the cliffs include imperial masonry with finely rounded and assembled stones, comparable to what is found in the palaces of Cuzco—the historic capital of the Inca Empire. For anyone sailing along the coast, the sight of these enormous stone structures, perfectly fitted together and gleaming on the desert cliffs, held an unmistakable message.

A ceramic sculpture recently found in the waters off El Huarco Rocío Villar Astigueta/Ministerio de Cultura de Perú

Recent archaeological research in the waters just off El Huarco’s cliffs followed reports from local fishers of strange objects and shapes spotted beneath the waves. Peru’s cultural ministry organised groups of divers to see if they could find anything. They discovered submerged stone walls, once part of the coastal settlement (now underwater because of changes in sea level, erosion and earthquakes) as well as Inca artefacts tied to early navigation and fishing. Many of the surfaced artefacts are now held at the nearby Municipal Museum of Cerro Azul.

“The museum’s entire collection consists of objects that residents have voluntarily contributed,” says the archaeologist Astrid Suárez. “The fishermen’s associations also support fieldwork aboard their boats. Children play a crucial role, insisting to their parents that they hand over objects discovered by their grandparents or aunts and uncles and passed down from generation to generation, after learning that this is cultural heritage and we are all responsible for protecting it. The children also act as museum guides in exchange for tips.”

As Peru’s cultural ministry uses some of these new findings as proof of the importance of the site—an effort to eventually declare it Cultural Heritage of the Nation—the cliffs of Cerro Azul continue to bridge the gap between myth and reality. The site remains an enduring monument to the way empires, water and stone can rewrite human history.

The incident at Chan Chan, the largest adobe city in the Americas, has drawn attention to the lax security at the 600-year-old Unesco World Heritage Site

#9524. 128 graduation wishes and messages for every graduate

Graduation is so much more than a diploma. It’s often the beginning of a big, uncertain shift into the unknowns of adulthood, a new career, and a life that’s far less defined than it was when you were a student. For some grads, this shift is an exciting one. For others, it’s terrifying. And many feel both.

If someone you love is graduating, you may want to write them a message that honors this journey. You want your note to feel personal, thoughtful, and maybe even a little inspiring — but finding the right words isn’t always easy.

The good news is you don’t need to be poetic or profound to share a meaningful sentiment on your loved one’s special day. A simple, warm message that acknowledges the moment and the person is more than enough. Whether you’re writing to a high school senior, a college grad, or someone finishing their doctorate, we’ve pulled together graduation wishes that are thoughtful, grounded, and easy to make your own.

The best wishes are the ones that make the graduate feel seen and loved. You recognize all the effort they’ve put in and offer encouragement without adding expectations.

Here are four aspects of a great graduation wish:

It’s genuine: A heartfelt “I’m proud of you” means more than a forced life lesson.

It reflects your relationship: Speak the way you typically would with them. If you’re usually lighthearted, stay lighthearted. If you’re more heartfelt and earnest, go that route.

It acknowledges the transition: Graduation is a moment of change, which can be both exciting and uncertain. Acknowledging this can help bring relief to the graduate.

It avoids pressure: Avoid mapping out their future or telling them what’s next, as this can add pressure. Instead, aim for something like, “Whatever comes next, I believe you’ll succeed.”

Graduation cards can have a tendency to lean on phrases like “Wishing you all the best!” and “The future is yours!” On the surface level, these messages can be sweet, but they don’t always reflect the depth of the relationship you’ve built.

If you want the graduate in your life to feel seen by you, here are 72 wishes that can help you out.

How you deliver it matters too. In person, a hug and “I’m so proud of you” mean a lot. In a card or text, you might write, “Congratulations on your graduation! I’ve loved watching you work toward this day.” Skip questions about what comes next. Many grads are still figuring that out, and today is for celebrating what they’ve done.

Start with congratulations, then add one thing you've loved watching her do. A line or two is plenty for a card. Here are short graduation messages for a granddaughter, whether she's finishing high school, college, or another program:

"So proud of you, my granddaughter. Congratulations on your graduation!"

"Watching you become who you are has been one of the great joys of my life. Congratulations, sweetheart."

"You're a very special young woman, and I'm so proud of all you've worked for. Congratulations!"

"You made it through high school, and I couldn't be prouder. Whatever comes next, you have my love."

"A college degree! Granddaughter, you've made me so proud. Congratulations."

"Being your grandma has been one of the best parts of my life. Congratulations, graduate!"

Congratulate the achievement and acknowledge the time it took. A doctorate often means years of research and writing, so mentioning that effort shows you see it. A line or two is enough. Here are a few short messages for a PhD or doctorate degree:

"Congratulations on completing your PhD. I've loved watching you work toward this day."

"You earned this doctorate through years of hard work. So proud of you!"

"Congratulations on your doctorate degree. I hope you take time to enjoy this one."

#9523. Childhood trauma may leave a lasting “scar” inside brain cells

Severe stress during childhood can increase a person's vulnerability to anxiety, depression, and other mood disorders when new challenges arise later in life. Scientists at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis and Princeton University have now identified a biological process that may help explain how early trauma can have such long-lasting effects on the brain.

Researchers have known that stress during early development can alter gene activity in the brain. The new findings suggest that these changes stem partly from the way brain cells package their DNA. By making certain stress-related genes easier to activate, early adversity may leave the brain more reactive and less able to tolerate future stress.

The study was published Aug. 7 in Neuron.

"We have uncovered a new biological process linking experience of early-life adversity to this long-term vulnerability to mental illness," said Meaghan Creed, PhD, an associate professor of anesthesiology at WashU Medicine and the study's co-corresponding author. "This finding reveals a physical scar left by trauma experienced during development inside brain cells, providing scientists with a concrete biological target to develop new treatments and interventions."

How Childhood Stress Changes DNA Packaging

More than half of children worldwide experience some form of early-life stress, including abuse, violence, or drug use within the household, and other traumatic events. Experiencing four or more of these adverse events is associated with a sharply higher risk of physical and mental health problems later in life.

To understand how these experiences can physically alter the developing brain, the researchers focused on the ventral tegmental area. This brain region contains neurons that produce dopamine, a chemical messenger involved in processing important experiences, including rewards and adversity. When stress causes these neurons to become abnormally active, reward processing can be disrupted, potentially increasing vulnerability to anxiety and depression.

The team then examined the epigenome inside these dopamine-producing neurons. The epigenome consists of molecular tags that help control whether genes are switched on or off, ultimately influencing how cells behave.

Catherine Jensen Peña, PhD, an assistant professor at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute and the study's senior and co-corresponding author, compared DNA inside cells to a coiled slinky. DNA is wrapped around proteins called histones, which help control how tightly or loosely it is packed. When this genetic slinky is tightly compressed, genes are less accessible and remain switched off. When the structure loosens and opens, the genes become easier for the cell to activate.

SETD7 Primes Brain Cells for Future Stress

In young mice exposed to stress, the researchers found elevated levels of an enzyme called SETD7 in dopamine neurons compared with mice raised under typical conditions. SETD7 helps add a chemical marker called H3K4me1 to the DNA packaging system. According to Peña, this tag encourages the genetic structure to open, making the cell more responsive to what is happening in its environment.

To test whether SETD7 itself could produce these changes, the scientists artificially increased the enzyme in young mice that had not experienced early-life stress. As the animals matured, their dopamine-producing brain cells developed a more open DNA structure, making stress response genes easier to activate.

These mice also became less tolerant of stress as adults. Animals that had elevated SETD7 levels when they were young developed more reactive dopamine neurons and showed more anxious behavior than mice whose SETD7 levels remained normal throughout life.

The researchers then tested the opposite approach. After early-life stress, they prevented SETD7 from adding excessive amounts of the H3K4me1 marker. This kept the DNA structure more tightly closed and protected the mice from becoming unusually sensitive to stress later in life.

Even after experiencing stress both early in development and again as adults, mice with reduced SETD7 activity behaved much like unstressed animals. They remained similarly social and exploratory, while activity in their dopamine neurons stayed at normal levels.

The results suggest that SETD7 and the changes it produces in DNA packaging may help create a lasting molecular memory of early adversity. They also give researchers a specific biological pathway to investigate as a possible target for future interventions.

"There are currently no treatments for what early-life stress does to the brain, partially because we have not had a clear picture of what molecular mechanisms to target," Peña said. "This work is exciting because it reveals a clear mechanism, and also helps explain why the impact of stress is both latent and broad. Additionally, if we can step in with supportive care, therapy or social resources to buffer children during those sensitive windows of development, we may be able to protect the epigenome -- preventing the genetic slinky from locking into an open position and perhaps giving the developing brain a chance to build natural resilience."

Materials provided by WashU Medicine. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9522. For How Long Do You Need to Meditate?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Picture this: 71 adults signed up for a study comparing brief to longer mindfulness practice. Many had never meditated, while others had dabbled years before.

Participants were divided at random into three groups: One group got 20 minutes of mindfulness meditation, a second group got five minutes, and the control group relaxed with audiobook excerpts from Bill Bryson’s A Short History of Nearly Everything, Bryson’s soothing recounting of the cosmos and our place in it.

In studies like these, “mindfulness meditation” typically means sitting quietly, eyes closed or softened, resting nonjudgmental attention on your breath or bodily sensations, gently noticing when your mind wanders (as it will), and just as gently bringing it back.

Now, you might expect that longer meditations would deliver greater benefits. After all, we’re conditioned to believe that more is better—especially when it comes to self-improvement. But this research and many other studies find that more minutes don’t necessarily mean more benefit: Shorter practices can work just as well—and sometimes better—while consistency may matter more than duration.

In this first study, each participant attended four 25-minute sessions over two weeks. In every session, the time not spent on audio-guided mindfulness-of-breath practice was filled by Bryson’s eloquence. To ensure the results reflected only the study activities, participants were asked to avoid any formal mindfulness practices outside these sessions.

After those two weeks, the five-minute meditators actually showed greater improvements in stress and mindful awareness (the tendency to stay present in daily life with less judgement) than the 20-minute group. Even depression and anxiety improved just as much—if not more.

Was the extra time with Bryson the magic ingredient for those five-minute meditators? The control group, who luxuriated in 25 uninterrupted minutes of his charm, showed no meaningful improvement. So while his voice may soothe, it wasn’t what moved the needle.

One five-minute meditator put it this way: “I always thought that to do mindfulness, I’d need a long time to dedicate to this, which seemed too challenging to even start. But I’ve learned that five minutes can help!” In contrast, a 20-minute participant admitted, “I think a shorter one would be better for me to learn mindfulness.”

There’s more. The facilitator observed that participants in the 20-minute meditation sessions more often fidgeted, shifted in their seats, and peeked through half-closed eyes, as if tranquility were just out of reach. Meanwhile, the five-minute meditators appeared more at ease and less prone to these signs of discomfort. Five of them even requested recordings to continue at home. The 20-minute group? Not a single request. For these beginners, less really did seem to be more.

Now, before you dash off to cancel that meditation retreat, remember that this study focused on people with little to no meditation experience. So if you’re a seasoned meditator, those longer sessions might still pack more punch for you, as we’ll explore later. And both the five-minute and 20-minute groups showed improvements in mindful awareness, depression, anxiety, and stress compared to the control group. The five-minute meditators just improved more when it came to mindful awareness and stress.

The takeaway? For beginners, a quick dip into mindfulness might be more refreshing than a long soak.

You might be wondering, Isn’t this just one study? Could it be a fluke? But multiple randomized controlled trials have explored how the length of meditation shapes its impact.

I join Christine Carter, Ph.D, in a webinar next week to talk about my book Micropractice.

Microhabits: The Science of Habits So Small They Actually Stick

In the largest of these studies, researchers recruited 372 adults online—about half of them new to meditation—to see how the “dose” of mindfulness meditation affected mindful awareness and emotional well-being. Participants were randomly sorted into one of four groups: Some meditated for 10 minutes, others for 20, and the rest listened to a 10- or 20-minute National Geographic article on sequoia trees. (Because nothing soothes stress like a deep dive into bark thickness.)

What did the researchers find? The 10-minute meditators showed greater improvements in mindful awareness than those who listened to the 10-minute sequoia lecture. Surprisingly, the 20-minute meditation group didn’t outperform any group—not even the tree enthusiasts. In fact, the 10-minute group showed slightly greater improvements in mindful awareness than the 20-minute meditators, although the difference wasn’t statistically significant, meaning it could have occurred by chance. Still, it suggests that for boosting mindful awareness right after practice, 10 minutes might be at least as effective as 20.

But that was just one session. What happens with consistent practice? In another study, 77 college students were randomly assigned to meditate daily for 10 or 20 minutes. After two weeks, both groups showed similar improvements in stress and, again, mindful awareness. But those assigned to the 20-minute group experienced a slightly greater boost in self-compassion, the skill of meeting your own struggles with the kindness you’d offer a dear friend.

So if you’ve poured hours into longer meditations, you can rest easy—it wasn’t for nothing. The evidence suggests that whether your sessions are short or sustained, they can offer meaningful benefits.

Another notable finding is that the 10-minute group practiced more consistently, logging about 82 minutes total. The 20-minute group missed more days and didn’t always finish, ending up with just 103. Double the goal, barely a quarter more practice.

If you’ve ever tried meditating, you might be nodding along. Some sessions are bliss, while others are a tug-of-war with time. Maybe you’ve battled that nagging frustration, trying to keep your mind steady for more than a fleeting moment. Or felt the magnetic pull of distraction, your mind wandering just when you need it to stay put. As the minutes crawl, doubt can creep in: Am I even doing this right? Is it worth it? These tough moments can teach you a lot, but they can also make meditation feel intimidating—and make you less likely to stick with it, especially when you’re just starting out.   Another study looked at even longer sessions, comparing 10 minutes of meditation to 30 minutes. This experiment split 161 adults into four groups: 10 or 30 minutes of daily sitting meditation, or the same amount of mindful movement. The mindful movement was a stretching practice that brings mindful awareness into motion—less stillness, same presence.

After two weeks, everyone saw benefits: Mindful awareness increased, well-being improved, and distress levels dropped. But there were no significant differences among the groups. Whether they meditated for 10 minutes or 30, sitting or moving, all the groups seemed to benefit equally.

So, here’s the bottom line: One study found that longer sessions more strongly boosted self-compassion. Another showed that shorter ones more effectively reduced stress. But across studies, most of the key benefits—mindful awareness, mental health, well-being—weren’t tied to how long people practiced.

Why? Because as we’ll keep exploring, the nervous system learns through repetition, not duration. It’s consistency that reshapes patterns. Not heroic efforts once in a while, but showing up, again and again, however you can.

The benefits of consistency over length show up in observational studies, too, where people choose how often and how long to meditate. While observational studies can’t pin down cause and effect, they offer a richer view of how shorter practices play out in the real world.

Imagine it’s early morning. You reach for your phone and open Insight Timer, a free meditation app. Before your meditation, it asks, “How are you today?” You tap an icon—maybe “OK,” maybe “great”—capturing a snapshot of your mood in seconds.

Now imagine doing this regularly, for 14 months straight. That’s exactly what 10,409 people from 103 countries did in a groundbreaking study. Many were new to meditation, using the app to track their emotional ups and downs in real time. It’s like taking your emotional temperature—not with a thermometer, but with a single tap that sums up how you feel.

The findings? Consistency (four to seven days a week)—not duration—was the strongest predictor of better mood, resilience, and equanimity, the ability to stay cool under pressure. Think of it like watering a plant: A little each week keeps it happy and growing. Forget all month and drown it after four weeks? It wilts anyway.

For beginners in the Insight Timer study, short sessions—five to 10 minutes—outshone longer ones in improving mood over time. But after 20 sessions? Longer practices—21 to 30 minutes—began to take the lead in mood improvement. It’s like your brain needs to build its meditation muscles before longer sessions feel better than short ones—like a marathon that only gives you the high once you’ve earned it.

But do shorter sessions lose their impact as you gain experience? Not at all. They might just become your secret weapon. After 80 sessions, shorter practices make a late-game comeback, boosting equanimity and showing that even seasoned meditators can benefit from briefer sessions.

The idea that consistency beats duration is backed by a meta-analysis challenging the belief that longer equals better. Think of a meta-analysis as a “study of studies,” combining data from multiple research papers to uncover clearer, big-picture insights.

When researchers analyzed 203 randomized controlled trials totaling 15,971 participants, they found no association between meditation session length and better outcomes. In fact, a trend emerged in favor of shorter practices for reducing depression symptoms, although it wasn’t statistically significant. Still, shorter sessions were at least as effective as longer ones, calling into question the assumption that more minutes always mean more benefits.   So what’s the takeaway? When you’re starting out, don’t sweat the long stuff. Quick sessions might do more to lift your mood early on. As you settle in, longer practices might bring deeper emotional gains. But even if you’re a pro, short sessions don’t lose their value—they just shift their superpower, helping you stay steady when life throws you curveballs. Different strengths, different stages. And who doesn’t love a shortcut that actually works?

Eli Susman, Ph.D., is a UC Berkeley-trained psychologist, former Harvard researcher, and author of Micropractice: A Science-Backed Approach for Calm, Clarity, and Joy in 30 Seconds or Less, forthcoming in 22 languages.

Using animal characters, educators can help children navigate big feelings with mindfulness and self-compassion.

A study of 38,000 people around the world finds that people who feel connected to nature are more hopeful, purposeful and resilient.

Whether we’ve been trying to improve our exercise, eating, sleep, or happiness, self-reflection is one of the most practical tools we have.
