#9481. Ten TV Series That Highlight the Best in Humanity: 2026

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Every year, we invite staff and regular contributors to nominate TV series for Greater Goodies, the awards we give to stories that exemplify or illustrate kindness, community, empathy, and more keys to well-being. Here’s what we came up with this year: The Boroughs, Death by Lightning, Envidiosa, The Hawk, Heated Rivalry, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, Lucky, Murderbot, Pluribus, and Shrinking.

Name the last show you’ve seen that features a hero over the age of 60. Drawing a blank? It’s not your fault—the media’s modus operandi is to equate heroism with youthfulness. Netflix’s The Boroughs flips this stereotype on its head.

With a star-studded lead cast, all 70 or older, we follow Sam Cooper’s (Alfred Molina) experience as he reluctantly moves into a senior living community in New Mexico after the death of his wife. But a series of strange events suggests that this is no ordinary retirement community.

As Sam navigates grief, new friendships, and a new identity, he joins forces with his neighbors to solve and resolve the community mystery. Overcoming obstacles like age discrimination and self-doubts, the group peels back the layers of the strange occurrences. At the root of the mystery is a societal fear of aging.

The show highlights what researcher Margie Lachman calls “crystallized intelligence”: the culmination of life experience, memory, and know-how. In The Boroughs, that turns out to be just as heroic as super human strength or the ability to fly. — Shanna B. Tiayon

History has already told us how Death by Lightning ends: Charles Guiteau will assassinate President James Garfield in 1881. But why? That’s one of the questions explored by the series, and it finds motivation in a sense of purpose–how purpose forms and how people come to cross-purposes.

Garfield (Michael Shannon) is principled and drawn reluctantly into a presidential contest he entered to nominate someone else. Guiteau (Matthew Macfadyen), meanwhile, is disturbingly sympathetic: charming, articulate, and desperate to do something meaningful with his life. Despite failed ventures, including a stint at the Oneida free-love commune, he remains convinced greatness awaits him. Believing his campaigning secured Garfield’s victory, he expects a government position to confirm his worth.

As their stories converge, Garfield finds purpose in his presidency: fighting corruption while supporting education and equal opportunity. Guiteau pursues a reward he feels he deserves, an entitlement that leads to tragedy.

In these ways, Garfield and Guiteau offer sharply contrasting answers to what makes a life meaningful, and watching their stories unfold side by side, we see how differently the desire to matter can play out.

Who you really ought to be watching closely is Garfield’s Vice President, Chester A. Arthur (Nick Offerman). A comfortable beneficiary of the political machine, he becomes an unlikely source of hope as the story goes on. Offerman makes him funny, flawed, and increasingly affecting as the demands of office begin to collide with old loyalties.

In a political landscape that can leave us cynical–in both the 19th century and the 21st–the series makes room for something more hopeful: the possibility that even an unlikely person can rise to the occasion, if they know why they need to rise. – Aurelia Santos

When almost-40-year-old Vicky (Griselda Siciliani) breaks up with her long-term boyfriend, she is driven to embark upon a journey of self-discovery.

At first, Vicky is just looking for a replacement for her boyfriend—but the problem is that her compulsive comparisons with other women sabotage attempts to connect with other people. (Indeed, the name of this Argentinian show, Envidiosa, means “envious.”) Vicky is self-absorbed and yet at the same time she doesn’t have a strong sense of her own self.

We see this vividly in her hilarious sessions with her therapist. When, for example, she goes on an envious rant about a friend’s milestone, she is forced to confront the quiet, uncomfortable realization that she never once asked how her friend actually felt. In short, Vicky is not a polished role model—and over the course of four seasons, we see her empathy grow through the painful process of unlearning self-centeredness.

Personally, I see Envidiosa as an opportunity to question how we show up for others’ joys and struggles, and I take it as an invitation to reflect: How can I empathize with the ups and downs of those around me? Envidiosa is a funny and at times embarrassingly relatable story about trying to become a more empathic human being and friend. — Criss Cuervo

In The Hawk, washed-up professional golfer Lonnie “The Hawk” Hawkins (Will Ferrell) has made a miracle comeback into the PGA tour—this time around, facing a tough competitor in his son, Lance (Jimmy Tatro).

It’s a screwball comedy, full of dirty jokes and a rapid-fire rapport between Lonnie and his not-quite-ex-wife, Stacy (Molly Shannon). A makeshift-caddy he “picked up at Walmart” (while chatting up the parking lot, from his camper van) adds to the fun, serving up an unlikely duo that seem happy just to be alive.

Even when he’s pretty down and out, Lonnie is looking on the bright side of things. Everything is done with gusto—he chats up the golf ball before each swing, he devours plates of Buffalo Wild Wings, he plays mini golf with his son and makes it a full-on competition.

“Son, never play golf angry,” he tells Lance. For Lonnie, life is all about golf—and golf is all about fun. Why spend all your time on something if you aren’t doing it for the joy of it?

I especially love Lonnie’s adoration for his estranged wife, a firecracker in her own right. In episode four, when the Hawk crashes his son’s engagement party–yes, you read that right–and then attempts a getaway with his caddie in the van, Stacy hurls the cake at them, along with a string of expletives.

It doesn’t even faze him. “You gotta love the passion!” Lonnie gushes. “That is one hot tamale!” — Hope Reese

Heated Rivalry follows stick-crossed lovers Shane and Ilya as they figure out how to be intimate within the highly competitive, homophobic environment of professional hockey.

At first, Shane and Ilya swap fluids more readily than emotions. But over the course of six episodes, the two learn to love across gaps in culture, language, and experience. In one pivotal scene, Shane invites Ilya to speak vulnerably about family dynamics in Ilya’s native Russian—despite not understanding a word of it.

That works because Shane does not focus attention on himself. Instead, he stays present on the phone, serving as a witness to Ilya’s visceral emotions. Their connection lies in felt care, in hearing the texture of another’s heartbreak.

In similar fashion, Ilya grounds Shane in stressful encounters. He supports Shane through panic without wallowing in his lover’s fear and entices Shane to relish pleasures outside of straight standards. As a couple, they help each other explore complex parts of themselves. We see a similar process unfold in another couple in the show, as they learn to respect each other’s different needs.

People might tune into Heated Rivalry for locker room towel drops and HBO’s glossy cinematography. They should stay to see a couple learn to love each other’s differences. The show exemplifies how bridging differences, at its best, means supporting others to more fully encounter themselves, and how in the process our relationships can grow.

With plenty of additional homoerotic stick-and-ball games to pull on from the novels of Rachel Reid, the next season of Heated Rivalry is expected to air on HBO Max and Canada’s Crave in Spring 2027. — Luke Brown

The monstrously successful HBO series Game of Thrones famously tossed out a lot of good-and-evil fantasy tropes to tell a morally complicated story of how power corrupts even the best people. A prequel called House of the Dragon shares that worldview.

That’s why a new prequel called A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms came as something of a surprise to fans. Unlike the other two series, this is not a story about a struggle for power. Instead, it focuses on a rather naive, not-too-bright “hedge knight” named Duncan (Peter Claffey) seeking to be hired by whatever lord will take him. Though Duncan is taller and stronger than most, he’s touchingly childlike as he tries to find his place in the merry old kingdoms of Westeros.

The first two episodes are funny and charming, as Duncan acquires a squire in the form of a little bald boy going by the name Egg (Dexter Sol Ansell), and fumblingly tries to enter a jousting tournament. And then Duncan finds himself on a collision course with the great and powerful of Westeros. When violence finally comes, there’s nothing casual about it. We feel the force of every blow, the tragedy of every death, and the erosion of Duncan’s innocence.

I’m giving A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms the award for integrity, but I can’t tell you why without spoiling the ending. Let’s just say that the series turns out to be the story of how one simple young man discovers what is most important to him—and finds the courage to stick to that path even in the face of isolation, temptations, and threats. — Jeremy Adam Smith

How do you exit a life you were born into?

That’s the question behind Lucky, starring Anya Taylor-Joy. Lucky was raised by her con-artist father and taught the “family business” from a young age—but when we meet her, she navigating internal conflict with the life she’s been told to live and the life she wants for herself.

Her desire to quit is complicated by her marriage to Cary, the son of a ruthless mob leader, who was also socialized into a life of crime. The couple plan one final con as their exit strategy, but it goes terribly wrong. Lucky sets out to resolve the botched plan, reconcile her marriage, and protect both her life and her father’s.

Her intelligence is put to the test as she puts the pieces together, connects the dots, and outsmarts her rivals. In the process she discovers her own virtue—and that the intelligence which made her a successful con artist can also set her free.

Through the course of the series, she realizes that she does not have to pay for the sins of her father. Having never been given the opportunity for self-determination, she makes peace in the best way she knows how and chooses a new path. — Shanna B. Tiayon

The Murderbot Diaries are a series of science-fiction novellas by Martha Wells, about a genderless, robotic soldier who manages to achieve free will. Since discovery will result in deactivation and since it doesn’t like humans very much anyway, Murderbot conceals its freedom of mind and consumes a lot of human-made entertainment inside its own head, even as it externally follows every order given to it by the evil corporation that owns it. Murderbot even has a favorite TV show: the Star-Trek-like Rise and Fall of Sanctuary Moon.

As a result of this isolation, the novellas are built almost entirely around its memorable inner monologues, with a voice that is by turns snarky, vulnerable, cold-blooded, disgusted, and puzzled. One of the things that makes these books distinctive is that Murderbot is not Pinocchio—it has no wish to become a “real boy.” It doesn’t want a gender, or the same feelings and drives as people. It just wants to be itself—and to have that difference respected.

While the Apple TV show based on the books is not quite that original or interesting, Murderbot retains its focus on finding the balance between belonging and difference. When we meet Murderbot (Alexander Skarsgård), he’s been hired to protect a group of polyamorous hippie scientists who hail from a utopian colony that exists independently of the corporations that rule the rest of the galaxy.

They are Murderbot’s first encounter with humans not shaped by dehumanizing hyper-capitalistic values, and they observe Murderbot in a way the corporate humans cannot. Over the course of the first season, they begin to realize that there is more to Murderbot than meets the eye, and they learn to see and appreciate Murderbot on its own terms. But what’s crucial is not that they perceive the humanity in Murderbot—it’s that Murderbot sees the humanity (and the goodness) in them.

In time, it becomes an accepted part of their society—without becoming more like them. Even so, the first season concludes on a tough-minded, melancholy note, as Murderbot itself can’t quite feel like it belongs. Will it someday find a place among these crunchy idealists? Stay tuned: The second season is coming in 2027. — Jeremy Adam Smith

Have you ever been among people but you didn’t feel part of the crowd? Like they were in on a joke that you just couldn’t get?

Welcome to Carol Sturka’s world. The science-fiction premise of Pluribus is that an alien virus transforms humanity into one big happy hive mind—everyone except Carol and 13 other people who seem to have immunity.

Even among those remaining individuals, though, Carol stands out as a malcontent. We sense that she’s been a fish out of water for her whole life.

Indeed, not every viewer will find Carol relatable or likable. When we first meet her, she’s at a bookstore event promoting her highly successful romantasy series. With her fans, she’s charming, funny, and kind. When she gets into a limo after a big sendoff by readers, the drivers asks if she’s famous.

“That depends,” Carol replies. “Are you a big fan of mindless crap?”

In short, Carol hates herself, her work, and her readers. And as we discover, her personality is snarky, uptight, stubborn, and uncompromising. When the virus hits, it’s an apocalyptic event, but Carol doesn’t change one bit—and her traits become both a blessing and a curse. The whole world wants to be kind to her, but Carol can’t accept kindness. That drives her to fight back. And that’s what ultimately makes her the hero of the story.

In the end, Pluribus is a very Greater Good thought experiment. It takes prosociality to its limits and finds that a total togetherness, empathy, and cooperation to the exclusion of selfishness, crankiness, and boundaries is a self-destructive dystopia, not a utopia. The show seems to argue that humanity needs difficult people like Carol to survive, and so invites us to appreciate what the Carols of the world have to offer. — Jeremy Adam Smith

In Shrinking, talking and listening are the name of the game. Jimmy (Jason Segel) is a widowed psychotherapist who helps patients navigate anxiety, OCD, PTSD, and other ailments as he himself is floundering.

But he’s not alone. His teenage daughter, overbearing-but-lovable neighbors, and coworker-friends (with Harrison Ford as the curmudgeonly head of the practice) are all there to help him when his life goes off the rails after his wife was killed by a drunk driver.

In its three-season run, the series is heavy-handed with its use of therapy-speak among the whole gang, whether between therapist-to-patient, therapist-to-daughter, or therapist-to-therapist. Characters “feel seen.” More times than I can count, they tell each other “I hear you.” We witness, in detail, exchanges inside the therapy office—and outside of it, in a rogue practice known as “Jimmying,” where therapy takes place at such venues as, for instance, the boxing ring.

In other words, there’s a lot of “deep listening”: the practice of being present, open, and empathic with another person, in a way that goes beyond just hearing and understanding words. In his grief, Jimmy himself is not always a perfect deep listener. He tends to talk more than a typical therapist, and frequently injects himself into the discussion. Shrinking isn’t about perfection—it’s about struggling to connect and growing in the process. – Hope Reese

#9480. Brain scans reveal which disorders are linked to faster brain aging

People with dementia, mild cognitive impairment, alcohol addiction, and psychiatric conditions such as schizophrenia may show signs of accelerated brain aging, according to a study published in the open access journal PLOS Medicine. The research, led by Shile Qi of the Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, China, found that different conditions appear to be associated with distinct patterns of aging across the brain.

Researchers can estimate whether a person's brain appears older or younger than expected for their chronological age. One way to do this is with predictive age difference (PAD), which compares a person's actual age with an age estimated from brain imaging. A positive PAD means the brain appears older than would typically be expected.

To investigate how different brain conditions might influence this measure, the researchers analyzed structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data from 45,900 controls drawn from several brain imaging databases. They compared those scans with data from 2,698 people with a range of conditions and differences, including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), alcohol or tobacco addiction, Alzheimer's disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or major depressive disorder.

Alzheimer's and MCI Show the Strongest Associations

Among the conditions examined, the neurodegenerative disorders AD and MCI showed the strongest associations with higher PAD values, suggesting the greatest degree of accelerated brain aging.

Addiction and psychiatric disorders were also associated with increased PAD. By contrast, the researchers found no overall differences in PAD between controls and people with ADHD or ASD.

Different Disorders Affect Different Brain Regions

The team also examined PAD across individual brain regions and looked at patterns of gene expression associated with the different conditions.

One area that stood out was the prefrontal cortex, which showed higher PAD across multiple brain disorders. Psychiatric disorders were associated with elevated PAD in the frontal and temporal lobes, while dementia was linked to higher PAD in the frontal and occipital cortex.

Addiction showed a different pattern. Higher PAD was observed in the default mode network, as well as in the salience network, putamen and thalamus.

The researchers also identified differences in gene transcription associated with particular conditions and divergences, suggesting that the patterns of brain aging may be linked to distinct underlying biological processes.

The findings do not show that these conditions directly cause accelerated brain aging. The study is correlational, and some conditions, particularly psychiatric disorders and addiction, frequently occur together, which can make their individual effects difficult to separate.

Even so, the researchers suggest that studying PAD more closely could eventually help identify biomarkers associated with common brain disorders and provide new clues about the biological pathways involved.

The authors add, "Different neurological disorders appear to leave different signatures on the brain aging clock, which may help researchers better understand the neural and biological pathways involved in these conditions."

This work was supported by the Key Research and Development Plan of Jiangsu Province, China (BE2023668) to S.Q., and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (62376124) to S.Q. The funders had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript.

Materials provided by PLOS. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9477. Could quitting ultra-processed food boost your mental health?

A small preliminary study from UC San Francisco adds to mounting evidence that eating fewer ultra-processed foods may help reduce symptoms of depression.

Published Sept. 23 in JAMA Psychiatry, the study was funded by the National Institutes of Health. Researchers believe it is the first study to compare depression symptoms in the same participants before and after they moved from their usual ultra-processed diet to healthier foods.

The pilot study included only 20 people, but senior author Andrew Krystal, MD, Ray and Dagmar Dolby Distinguished Professor in UCSF's departments of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and Neurology, said it "successfully established the viability of carrying out this research in a larger-scale trial."

Depression Symptoms Improved After a Major Diet Shift

Participants cut their intake of ultra-processed foods by more than 85%. After doing so, they showed moderate to large improvements across three different measures of depression. Anxiety scores also improved modestly.

Ultra-processed foods include products such as packaged snacks, fast food, sugary drinks, and other industrially manufactured foods. These products may contain ingredients including preservatives, artificial coloring, flavor enhancers, and emulsifiers.

"Reducing the amount of ultra-processed food in our diet can be challenging, because it's highly palatable, cheap, and convenient," said corresponding author Nyasha Chagwedera, MD, PhD, assistant professor in the UCSF Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences. "Ultra-processed food triggers dopamine, the pleasure hormone, which promotes craving. Food companies work with scientists to find just the right amount of sugar, salt, and fat that make you want to eat more and more."

The participants had an average age of 44, and 70% were female. Along with depression, 14 participants also had anxiety. Everyone in the study had a high BMI and at least one metabolic disorder -- such as hypertension, diabetes, or elevated LDL cholesterol.

Researchers divided the participants into two groups. One group stayed on its usual diet for four weeks, while the other switched to a diet low in ultra-processed foods. Participants selected and bought their own food with guidance from the research team. After four weeks, the groups switched diets.

Chagwedera, who founded the UCSF Metabolic and Mental Health Program, said one possible explanation for the connection between ultra-processed food and depression involves what she described as a "leaky, out-of-balance gut." According to this idea, ultra-processed foods may damage the protective lining of the gut.

"This gut damage can create low-grade, chronic inflammation throughout the body that either directly causes depression or makes people more vulnerable to it."

"In other words, junky processing may harm your gut in ways that ripple up to your brain."

Because the study was small, the findings are still preliminary. The researchers now plan to investigate the effect in a larger group, with enrollment for phase 2 expected to begin in 2028.

Authors: Additional UCSF authors include Eliana Kim, MD, Dorothy T. Chiu, PhD, Chengshi Jin, PhD, Catherine Lee PhD. Other authors are Susannah Tye, PhD, of the University of Queensland, Australia, Mayo Clinic, and Emory University.

Funding: National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences, National Institutes of Health, through UCSF-CTSI Grant Number UL1 TR001872; NHLBI grant R38AG070171, NIMH grant R38AG070171, and the UCSF Weill Institute of Neurosciences.

#9476. What It Takes to Be Free

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. For two decades, it has remained free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If it makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider aiding its sustenance with a one-time or loyal donation. Your support makes all the difference.

You can also become a spontaneous supporter with a one-time donation in any amount:

Need to cancel a recurring donation? Go here.

We spend our lives trying to find our power and our freedom. It is not easy: We live in a culture that has distorted the meaning and measure of power, confusing visibility with value, status with substance, attention with love; we live in a universe where free will may be an illusion, where chance deals the vast majority of the cards — the family and epoch we are born into, the body and biochemistry we live in, the people we cross paths with, the accidents of chemistry and happenstance we call love. The great double-edged question is how to keep power from becoming a prison and how much freedom we can find between the narrow parameters of our givens. But somewhere deep down, in the marrow of our language, we seem to know: The word power shares its Middle Latin root with possibility — its only measure is that which liberates the possible in us; our only power is our freedom.

“Nothing is more unbearable, once one has it, than freedom,” James Baldwin wrote. It is unbearable largely because it demands a shedding of the self with all of its attachments — to ways of being, to ideas about how the world ought to be, to particular interpretations of reality. Such attachments are shackles best broken by what Iris Murdoch has so splendidly termed unselfing, key to each of the five kinds of freedom she identified in literature and life. For Murdoch, freedom takes radical unsefling — only then are we truly free to both be ourselves and love each other:

Freedom is exercised in the confrontation by each other, in the context of an infinitely extensible work of imaginative understanding, of two irreducibly dissimilar individuals. Love is the imaginative recognition of, that is respect for, this otherness.

This is why, for Octavio Paz — who thought deeply about freedom — love is “a knot made of two intertwined freedoms.” And if love is our fulcrum of belonging, then belonging itself is woven of the same paradox — something Maya Angelou articulates in one of her finest interviews:

You only are free when you realize you belong no place — you belong every place — no place at all.

In this sense, freedom is the hinge between being and belonging that swings open the door to being ourselves — which, yet again paradoxically, must include the freedom to change, to confront the illusory solidity of the self, its ceaseless mutability. Psychoanalyst Karen Horney formulates this perfectly in her pioneering work on the fundaments of personal growth:

We do not need an inner strait jacket with which to shackle our spontaneity, nor the whip of inner dictates to drive us to perfection. There is no doubt that such disciplinary methods can succeed in suppressing undesirable factors, but there is also no doubt that they are injurious to our growth. We do not need them because we see a better possibility of dealing with destructive forces in ourselves: that of actually outgrowing them. The way toward this goal is an ever increasing awareness and understanding of ourselves. Self-knowledge, then, is not an aim in itself, but a means of liberating the forces of spontaneous growth… And as we lose the neurotic obsession with self, as we become free to grow ourselves, we also free ourselves to love and to feel concern for other people.

Then, and only then, can we contact the soul beneath the self, which is the only real locus of our freedom. Vassily Grossman — who spent a thousand days as a correspondent on the frontlines of the Holocaust — captures this beautifully in a passage from his almost unbearably poignant reckoning with life and death:

What constitutes the freedom, the soul of an individual life, is its uniqueness. The reflection of the universe in someone’s consciousness is the foundation of his or her power, but life only becomes happiness, is only endowed with freedom and meaning when someone exists as a whole world that has never been repeated in all eternity. Only then can they experience the joy of freedom and kindness, finding in others what they have already found in themselves.

#9475. This diet may slow brain aging by 2.5 years

A diet that combines elements of the Mediterranean diet with an eating plan designed to lower blood pressure may help slow some of the structural changes that occur as the brain ages, according to research published online in the Journal of Neurology Neurosurgery & Psychiatry.

Greater adherence to the MIND diet was linked to less brain tissue loss over time, particularly in grey matter, which plays an important role in memory, learning, decision making, and information processing. It was also associated with less enlargement of the brain's ventricles, fluid filled spaces that tend to grow as brain tissue shrinks.

The Mediterranean-Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension Diet Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay diet, or MIND for short, has previously been associated with better cognitive health, according to the researchers.

The eating pattern emphasizes green leafy vegetables; other vegetables; berries; nuts; whole grains; fish; beans; olive oil; and poultry, along with moderate wine consumption. It also recommends limiting butter/margarine, cheese, red meat, pastries/sweets, and fried fast foods.

Although previous research has connected the MIND diet with cognitive benefits, its relationship with age related changes in brain structure has remained less clear. Those structural changes are also relevant to neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases.

Researchers Tracked Brain Changes for Years

To investigate, researchers studied 1647 middle aged and older adults (average age 60 at the start of the study) from the Framingham Heart Study Offspring cohort (FOS).

Participants underwent regular health evaluations every 4-8 years. Starting in 1999, they also received MRI brain scans every 2-6 years.

Diet was assessed through at least 1 food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) completed during check ups between 1991-5, 1995-8, and/or 1998-2001. Each participant also had at least 2 brain MRI scan assessments between 1999 and 2019 and showed no evidence of stroke or dementia at the time of their first MRI scan.

The average MIND diet score was just under 7 out of a possible 15, with 15 representing the strongest adherence.

People in the highest third for MIND diet adherence were more likely to be women and college educated. They were also less likely to smoke or have obesity.

They were also less likely to have conditions that can affect brain health, including type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and cardiovascular disease.

Higher MIND Scores Linked to Slower Grey Matter Loss

Over an average follow up period of 12 years, MRI scans showed the expected age related changes across the group. These included decreases in total brain, grey matter, white matter, and hippocampal volumes.

At the same time, cerebrospinal fluid and ventricular volumes increased, as did white matter hyperintensities, which appear as bright spots on MRI scans and can indicate tissue damage.

However, people with higher MIND diet scores experienced slower loss of grey matter.

Each 3 point increase in MIND diet score was associated with slower grey matter loss of (0.279 cm³/year). According to the researchers, that corresponded to 20% less age related decline and the equivalent of 2.5 years of delayed brain aging.

A similar pattern appeared in ventricular enlargement. Each 3-point rise in MIND diet score was associated with slower expansion of total ventricular volume by −0.071 cm³/year, equivalent to 8% less tissue loss and about 1 year of delayed brain aging.

Some foods appeared to contribute more strongly to the favorable associations.

Higher berry intake was linked to slower increases in ventricular volume. Poultry was also associated with slower ventricular enlargement, along with a slower decline in grey matter.

In contrast, higher consumption of sweets was associated with faster ventricular enlargement and greater hippocampal atrophy. Fried fast foods were also linked to a larger decline in hippocampal volume.

"MIND-recommended foods rich in antioxidants, such as berries, and high-quality protein sources like poultry may reduce oxidative stress and mitigate neuronal damage," suggest the researchers. "Conversely, fried fast foods, often high in unhealthy fats, trans fats, and advanced glycation end-products, may contribute to inflammation and vascular damage," they add.

Not every food produced the expected pattern.

Higher whole grain intake was associated with several unfavorable structural changes, including faster losses of grey matter and hippocampal volume, as well as faster ventricular enlargement.

Cheese showed the opposite pattern. Greater cheese intake was associated with slower declines in grey matter and hippocampal volume, less ventricular enlargement, and fewer white matter hyperintensities.

Benefits Appeared Stronger in Older Adults

The overall associations remained consistent across several additional analyses and were stronger among older participants.

The researchers say this may suggest that the MIND diet could be especially relevant for people at greater risk of faster brain aging or those who show more variation in the pace of brain atrophy.

Stronger associations were also seen among participants who were more physically active and among those who were not overweight or obese.

That pattern raises the possibility that combining a brain healthy diet with other healthy lifestyle habits could help reduce the risk of neurodegenerative disease, the researchers say.

The findings come from an observational study, so they cannot establish that the MIND diet directly caused the slower brain changes.

The researchers also note that food frequency questionnaires rely on participants accurately remembering what they ate, which can introduce recall bias.

They were also unable to rule out mild cognitive impairment at the time of the first MRI scan, changes in diet over time, or the influence of genetic risk factors.

Because the participants were predominantly White, the findings may not apply equally to people from other ethnic backgrounds.

Still, the researchers conclude: "These findings reinforce the potential of the MIND diet as a brain-healthy dietary pattern and support its role in strategies aimed at slowing neurodegeneration in aging populations."

#9474. How to Stay Informed But Not Overwhelmed by Election News

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

You pick up your phone to check one thing—perhaps the weather, a text message, or the score of a game. A few minutes later, you have read three election headlines, watched a clip from a debate, skimmed dozens of comments, and somehow learned that democracy, the economy, your health care, and the future of the planet may all be in danger before breakfast.

If this sounds familiar, you are not alone.

Election season can make the news feel unusually personal. The issues on the ballot can affect our finances, health, schools, communities, and rights. At the same time, the way we now encounter political information—constantly, emotionally, and often in fragments—can leave us feeling overloaded rather than informed.

There is even a name for this experience: election stress. The Mayo Clinic describes it as the overwhelming anxiety some people feel during an election cycle. And surveys from the American Psychological Association suggest that elections have become a significant source of stress for many Americans. In the lead-up to the 2024 presidential election, for example, 72% of adults said they were worried that the results could lead to violence, and 56% said they feared the election could mark the end of democracy in the United States.

It is understandable to feel unsettled when an election seems to carry serious consequences. But anxiety is not always a problem to get rid of; in small doses, it can direct our attention toward what matters. It may motivate us to learn, vote, volunteer, have difficult conversations, or support people affected by political decisions.

The problem begins when information meant to help us engage instead keeps our nervous systems in a constant state of alarm.

Part of election stress comes from the uncertainty it elicits. We do not know who will win, what policies will change, or how the people around us will respond. Research suggests that uncertainty itself can be stressful because people naturally want to understand and predict the environment around them. When we feel unable to do that, we may feel less safe and less in control.

News can intensify that uncertainty. Negative news is often more attention-grabbing than positive news, and conflict, danger, and outrage make especially compelling headlines. That does not mean journalists are intentionally trying to harm us. Reporting on threats and problems is an essential part of journalism. But a steady diet of alarming information can shape how we feel about the world, especially when it leaves little room for context, solutions, or signs of human cooperation.

This can create a difficult cycle. When people feel anxious, they often seek out more information in an effort to regain a sense of control. Yet the more election news they encounter—particularly news marked by uncertainty, conflict, and emotional intensity—the more anxious they may feel. Then they check again.

In other words, we may turn to the news to calm ourselves down, only to leave feeling more activated than before.

Political stress is not new. But the way we receive political information has changed dramatically.

When John F. Kennedy and Richard Nixon debated on television in 1960, viewers watched in a far more contained media environment. There was no endless stream of clips, reactions, memes, push notifications, and commentary arriving at every hour of the day. People could discuss the debate afterward, but they were not also carrying the debate around in their pockets.

Today, election news can follow us almost everywhere: to the grocery store line, the waiting room, the car, the dinner table, and bed. Social media makes it easier for people to participate politically and amplify voices that were once excluded from public conversation. Those are meaningful benefits. But the same technology can make political information feel impossible to put down.

It also encourages us to consume news in small, emotionally potent pieces. A headline while brushing our teeth. A video clip while waiting for coffee. A dramatic post at a stoplight. These snippets can provoke strong feelings without giving us enough context to understand the story fully.

That matters because headlines often tell us what to feel before they tell us what happened. Pew research found that five out of eight Americans (63%) said they only read news headlines rather than full news articles, specifically when scrolling through social media. When people repeatedly take in emotionally charged fragments of news, they may feel a growing sense of threat while having less detailed information to guide their judgments.

Faced with this constant emotional demand, some people keep checking the news compulsively. Others decide they have had enough and stop paying attention altogether.

News avoidance can offer temporary relief. If every update makes you tense, angry, or helpless, closing the app may feel like self-protection. In fact, a report from the American Press Institute found that a third of Americans want to disengage from news because it feels stressful and overwhelming.

Tips for managing election stress while building a better democracy

But avoiding news altogether comes with costs, especially during an election year. It can make it harder to participate in democratic life, understand issues that affect our communities, or distinguish reliable reporting from misinformation passed along by friends, influencers, or highly partisan accounts.

The goal, then, is not to consume more news or no news. It is to develop a healthier relationship with news: one that helps us stay informed without asking our nervous systems to be on call all day.

1. Choose a news source that includes solutions, not only problems. During stressful times, it can help to seek out reporting that does more than identify what is going wrong. Constructive journalism still covers serious problems, but it also provides context, examines solutions, and asks what people and communities can do next. This approach is not about pretending everything is fine. It is about giving readers a more complete picture: What is the problem? Who is affected? What is being tried? What can citizens realistically do? Solution-oriented reporting may be especially helpful during elections because it can replace helplessness with a more grounded sense of agency and hope for the future.

When you choose a news source, consider asking: Does this reporting leave me better informed? Does it help me understand the issue, or does it only make me feel alarmed? Does it explain possible solutions as well as the threat?

2. Balance distressing news with inspiring media. We do not need to force ourselves to be positive about difficult realities. But we can balance the emotional weight of election coverage with media that remind us of human goodness, beauty, courage, and connection.

Research suggests that stories of kindness, moral courage, and collective care can evoke feelings such as elevation, gratitude, and hope. These emotions can broaden our view of what is possible and help us feel more connected to other people. And new research from the University of Santa Barbara suggests that these emotions can even reduce stress.

This might mean watching a short video about neighbors helping one another after a disaster, reading a profile of local organizers working across differences, listening to music that helps you settle, or returning to a film or show that leaves you feeling more hopeful about people, or nostalgic about the past.

Think of this as building a more balanced media diet. Election news can be an important part of that diet, but it should not be the only thing we feed our minds. Just as eating one healthy meal a week does not transform our physical health, one inspiring story will not undo chronic stress. Over time, though, regularly choosing media that restore us, physically and mentally, can help cultivate resilience, hope, and perspective.

3. Create boundaries around when you check the news. Finally, consider treating news less like a snack and more like a meal.

Snacking on news all day can mean consuming a lot without ever feeling nourished. You absorb a headline here, an alert there, and a few comments in between—but never get enough context to make sense of what you are seeing. The result can be a lot of emotional calories and very little understanding.

Instead, choose one or two intentional times to engage with the news. You might read a full article over breakfast, listen to a trusted news program on your commute, or set aside 15 minutes at lunch to review the day’s major stories. If you are prone to checking headlines compulsively, digital wellness strategies such as app limits or notification settings can make those boundaries easier to keep.

It may also help to avoid making late-night news “snacking” part of your bedtime routine. By the end of the day, our emotional and cognitive resources are often already depleted. A stream of alarming headlines can quickly turn into doomscrolling: the repeated consumption of negative online content that leaves us more agitated and less able to sleep.

Giving news its own place in the day does not mean becoming indifferent. It means making room to take in information carefully, in context, and with enough emotional space to respond thoughtfully.

Election stress is real because elections matter. Feeling concerned about the future does not mean that something is wrong with you; it may mean you are paying attention.

But paying attention does not require constant exposure to distress. We can choose reporting that informs and empowers us, balance difficult coverage with media that reminds us of human possibility, and set boundaries that give our minds a chance to rest.

The aim is not emotional numbness. It is becoming the kind of informed citizen who can face difficult news, stay connected to what matters, and still have enough calm and hope left to act.

Sophie H. Janicke, Ph.D., is a positive media psychologist working as an associate professor at Chapman University, who investigates the role that new and traditional media play in promoting and affecting character development, self-transcendent emotions (such as elevation, gratitude, and awe), prosocial behavior, and happiness.

#9473. Art Toronto reflects Canadian art community’s focus on sustaining domestic ecosystem

Lynn Donoghue's Untitled (Watching) (1996) at Art Toronto Photo: Jenna Marie Wakani

There is something strangely comforting about this year’s edition of Art Toronto (until 1 November), Canada’s biggest art fair. In spite of the vast 20,000 sq. ft of space it inhabits at the Metro Toronto Convention Centre, there is a sense of warmth and grounding in Canadian landscapes made manifest in the installation that welcomes visitors to the art fair’s 27th iteration: Untitled (Watching) (1996) by the late Lynn Donoghue and the first of her Caribou Tarp series to be shown in public, installed here on top of a pile of dirt.

Inspired by the artist’s time in Alberta in the mid 1990s, when she encountered discarded caribou antlers scattered across the tundra, the work speaks to one of the overarching themes at the fair this year, of a return to natural roots. But this Art Toronto is also about uniting the often-scattered Canadian art landscape and, as per the title of one series of talks at the fair, “Building a Stronger Arts Ecosystem”.

These are trying times for Canadian artists and galleries, hammered by a trade war with the US and larger macro-economic forces such as inflation, war and related fuel costs. Happily, though the fair’s new director Emily Jean Alexander tells The Art Newspaper that this year’s Art Toronto is “only down in capacity by 5%”, while some other international art fairs have pared back their exhibitor numbers more drastically. She says there are far fewer US galleries this year than in past editions, while 80% of the 105 exhibitors are Canadian. A commercial gallery from New Brunswick is participating for the first time, alongside dozens from British Columbia, Québec and Ontario. There is a pervasive tariffs-be-damned, “elbows up” sense of artistic solidarity afoot and, Alexander says, a renewed commitment to creating a sustainable art market in Canada.

Rich Loen's Databells (2025) at Art Toronto, presented in partnership with Artist Project Photo: Jenna Marie Wakani

There is a nostalgic, McLuhanesque installation on the convention centre’s ground floor (presented with Art Toronto’s sister fair, Artist Project) by the Ottawa-based former software engineer Rich Loen. Titled Databells (2025), it connects a collection of bells with statistics ranging from the whimsical (the number of female orgasms per minute) to the digital (the number of TikTok videos played globally per minute) to the serious (amount of carbon dioxide removed from the earth’s atmosphere). The installation’s church and door bells chime at numerically precise intervals, creating a balm for our information-overloaded minds and sparking a meditative state akin to a Balinese temple. It is the perfect hybrid analogue-digital cleanse before the throng of Art Toronto’s main floor.

As visitors ascend into the fair, they can contemplate Kathy Slade’s monumental tapestry Sinking in the West (2023), presented by Mónica Reyes Gallery, which considers recurrence, time and landscape. Turning the corner, visitors will find the McMichael Canadian Art Collection stand; the Kleinburg, Ontario-based museum is currently closed for an expansion and renovation. At the fair it is showing off a recent acquisition, My First Medicine Teacher, a large-scale painting by the Métis artist Christi Belcourt.

A view of Art Toronto including, at centre, the McMichael Canadian Art Collection's stand with My First Medicine Teacher by Christi Belcour Photo: Jenna Marie Wakani

Nearby, the Toronto-based Nicholas Metivier Gallery has two stands: one featuring a selection of works by gallery artists, the other showcasing four decades of work by the Canadian photographer Edward Burtynsky. The solo stand includes two new photographs from the artist’s forthcoming project, Mining: For the Future. Burtynsky tells The Art Newspaper that he got his start in aerial photography in Western Australia two decades ago and he returned there last year to revisit a subject he has explored since the mid 1980s. The textural, painterly images in vibrant colours reveal both the brutality and beauty of mining materials such as lithium, copper and cobalt that are needed for components in the technologies that will enable a more sustainable future.

Another highlight of the fair, on the stand of Montreal’s Galerie Nicolas Robert, is Ascension (for Bakers) by the artist Sameer Farooq. An extension of his ongoing Flatbread Library, a long-term research project centred on the political and social significance of the tandoor, the new work connects the forms of collected bakeware with the Buddhist stupa reliquary. The appetising installation features a gathering of vessels, bread forms and tools that honour bakers as sculptors, tracing how ideas, objects and food move across cultures.

Next to it is the Vancouver-based gallery Wil Aballe, whose stand includes a work that has been attracting curatorial interest: Karin Jones’s The Bond (dress) (2023) is a mixed-media take on Queen Victoria’s wedding gown re-imagined with blonde hair extensions as a brilliant expression of the politics of adornment and beauty within contemporary material culture.

Additional eye-catching installations at the fair include Douglas Scholes’s (This is) What happens when a thing is maintained (?) (2024), a large-scale sculpture made from beeswax (presented by Galerie Robertson Arès), and the Montréal-based artist Karine Giboulo’s whimsical environment Joy is a Resistant Bacteria (The Living Room) (2026), presented by Art Mûr. Taken together, they convey a sense of the power of the organic overcoming the antiseptic aesthetics of the digital.

Douglas Scholes's (This is) What happens when a thing is maintained (?) (2024) at Art Toronto, presented by Galerie Robertson Arès Photo: Jenna Marie Wakani

The booth of Toronto’s Nia Centre for the Arts, Canada’s first professional Black arts centre, features the wonderful painting Califia by the Congolese Canadian artist Heritier Bilaka, paying homage to the warrior Queen Nzinga. (Concurrently with Art Toronto, Nia is hosting A Black Art Fair at its headquarters on Oakwood Avenue.)

The Vancouver-based gallery Ceremonial Art is showing works by five artists on its booth, including a remarkable woodblock print by the Tofino-based artist Marika Swan. Titled Embraced in Interdependence, it is both a rare example of West Coast Indigenous art in Toronto and a neat metaphor for the current socio-political climate in Canada and at the art fair.

A nearby stand is devoted to Portfolio, a nonprofit run by a collective of Vancouver artists and dedicated to helping emerging artists via scholarships funded from a percentage of their sales. Among others, the organisation is showing new paintings by Angela Grossman and new works from the Predator series by Lawrence Paul Yuxweluptun—who will open a solo exhibition at the Art Gallery of Ontario in February 2027.

A few booths away, Vancouver’s Equinox Gallery is showing early paintings by the late artist Gathie Falk, mid-century prints from the Fred Herzog archive and a work by Sonny Assu that playfully subverts the colonial landscapes of Emily Carr by overlaying them with Kwakwaka'wakw formline designs.

During the fair’s gala preview on Thursday (29 October), benefiting the McMichael Canadian Art Collection, it was revealed that the federal and provincial governments would provide C$50m ($35.7m) each in funding for the renovation of the existing building and construction of a new wing, all designed by Hariri Pontarini Architects. In a video marking the occasion, Canada’s first lady, Diana Fox Carney, proclaimed: “The world needs more Canada.” At this year’s Art Toronto, there is plenty to go around.

The country’s biggest art fair, with more than 100 exhibitors, is both a centre of commercial activity and a sprawling diorama of a national aesthetic

The fair’s Presents section for younger galleries, often among its most vibrant sectors, features bold stands organised by ambitious dealers who understand the costs of doing business

Collectors came out in force, but much of the art on show was not as exciting as that seen at Venice or offered by the auction houses

From instant cognitive boosts to lasting emotional resilience, cycling offers powerful, science-backed brain benefits.

Cycling is widely celebrated for its cardiovascular and physical health benefits, but its effects on the mind may be just as remarkable.

These mental shifts do not follow a single timeline: while some cognitive and emotional benefits appear almost instantly after a few minutes in the saddle, others unfold gradually over weeks or months of regular riding.

One of the hardest realizations in life, and one of the most liberating, is that our mothers are neither saints nor saviors — they are just people who, however messy or painful our childhood may have been, and however complicated the adult relationship, have loved us the best way they knew how, with the cards they were dealt and the tools they had.

It is a whole life’s work to accept this elemental fact, and a life’s triumph to accept it not with bitterness but with love.

How to make that liberating shift of perspective is what the playwright, suffragist, and psychologist Florida Scott-Maxwell (September 14, 1883–March 6, 1979) considers in a passage from her 1968 autobiography The Measure of My Days (public library).

A mother’s love for her children, even her inability to let them be, is because she is under a painful law that the life that passed through her must be brought to fruition. Even when she swallows it whole she is only acting like any frightened mother cat eating its young to keep it safe.

In a sentiment that calls to mind Kahlil Gibran’s insight into the delicate balance of intimacy and independence essential for romantic love — which is always an echo of our formative attachments — she adds:

It is not easy to give closeness and freedom, safety plus danger.

With a wary eye to the brunt of parental expectation under which all children live, well into adulthood, she writes:

No matter how old a mother is she watches her middle-aged children for signs of improvement. It could not be otherwise for she is impelled to know that the seeds of value sown in her have been winnowed. She never outgrows the burden of love, and to the end she carries the weight of hope for those she bore. Oddly, very oddly, she is forever surprised and even faintly wronged that her sons and daughters are just people, for many mothers hope and half expect that their newborn child will make the world better, will somehow be a redeemer. Perhaps they are right, and they can believe that the rare quality they glimpsed in the child is active in the burdened adult.

Perhaps that glimpse is what Maurice Sendak meant when he observed that life is largely a matter of “having your child self intact and alive and something to be proud of.”

Complement with Kahlil Gibran’s advice on children, the pioneering psychologist Donald Winnicott on the mother’s contribution to society, and Alison Bechdel’s superb Winnicott-inspired Are You My Mother?, then savor My Mother’s Eyes — a soulful animated short film about loss and the unbreakable bonds of love — and Mary Gaitskill’s poignant advice on how to move through life when your parents are dying.

#9470. Does Fluoride In Drinking Water Affect Intelligence? What The Evidence Reveals

Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

Fluoride in community drinking water is not linked to lower adolescent IQ or poorer thinking skills later in life, a long-running US study finds.

Researchers followed a generation of Wisconsin school-leavers, examining cognitive performance from adolescence into their eighties.

Those exposed to fluoridated water did not show a consistent disadvantage compared with people whose communities had no fluoridation.

The findings address concerns that adding fluoride to drinking water to prevent tooth decay could undermine intellectual development.

Professor John Robert Warren, the study’s first author, said:

“Utah, Florida and many municipalities have chosen to remove fluoride from drinking water based on flawed studies that considered the IQ effects of exposure to massive doses of fluoride.

Because levels of fluoride added to municipal drinking water in the U.S. are so much lower, almost all prior evidence from those international studies is not relevant to U.S. public policy debates.”

The research draws on the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study, which began with over 10,000 people who graduated from high school in 1957.

Researchers combined school IQ records with historical information about community water fluoridation and naturally occurring fluoride levels.

Following participants into old age allowed researchers to examine whether childhood exposure was associated with lasting differences in cognitive performance.

Comparing communities requires care because their residents can differ in ways that also relate to cognitive performance.

Once those background differences were taken into account, there was no consistent evidence that exposure was associated with either better or worse performance.

The same broad pattern appeared when researchers focused on people who had lived in the same county since early childhood, increasing confidence in their estimates of exposure.

Overall, the findings suggest that growing up with fluoridated community water is not associated with poorer cognitive performance in old age.

The study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (Warren et al., 2026).

#9469. Vagus Nerve Stimulation Could Help New Skills Stick

Why do some new skills seem to click almost instantly while others remain frustratingly difficult even after repeated practice? The difference may involve more than talent or effort. It may also depend on whether the brain is in the right condition to turn practice into lasting learning.

Learning does not happen independently of the rest of the body. Internal organs constantly send information to the brain through the vagus nerve, one of the nervous system's major communication pathways. Researchers at Tohoku University who study super network brain physiology have now shown in mice that stimulating this nerve after training can strengthen long term motor learning. Their findings point to a previously overlooked role for communication from the body to the brain in helping new skills persist.

The findings were published in iScience on August 25, 2026.

The vagus nerve serves as a major information highway between the brain and the body. It carries signals from internal organs to the brain while also transmitting instructions from the brain back to those organs. Scientists can influence this pathway using vagus nerve stimulation (VNS), which is already clinically approved for treating several disorders.

Earlier research has mainly explored VNS as a form of neuromodulation that changes activity in neurotransmitter systems. The new study suggests there may be another important mechanism involved: rhythmic changes in blood vessels inside the brain.

To investigate this possibility, the researchers created a small cuff electrode designed to stay attached to the left cervical vagus nerve in mice. They then tested VNS during horizontal optokinetic response (HOKR) learning, a cerebellum dependent eye movement task that teaches mice to improve their ability to follow moving visual stripes. The response is similar to the automatic eye movements a person makes while standing on a platform and watching a train move past.

The Biggest Effect Appeared After Practice

The researchers applied VNS after each training session rather than during the learning task itself. The stimulation did not immediately improve performance while the mice were training. Instead, the benefits became apparent later.

On following days, mice that received VNS showed stronger long-term learning. This pattern suggests that the stimulation may influence processes that happen after training, when the brain is consolidating what it has learned into more durable memory.

"The key point is that VNS was delivered only after training," says Professor Ko Matsui. "Our findings suggest that VNS may open a hidden window of opportunity for enhanced learning by making the brain environment more receptive to long-lasting change."

The team next looked for changes inside the brain that might accompany the improved learning. They measured blood volume activity near the cerebellar flocculus, an area involved in HOKR learning.

Using fiber photometry, the researchers found that a single round of VNS produced a two phase vascular response. Local blood volume briefly decreased before rising after a delay. When VNS was repeated, it created rhythmic oscillations in blood volume.

Those vascular rhythms also appeared to be related to learning. Mice with larger blood volume oscillations generally showed better learning by Day 5, suggesting that changes in the brain's vascular environment could be connected to the longer lasting effects of the stimulation.

"Our brains may be more strongly influenced by the body than we imagine," says lead author Junyu Chen. "By tuning the brain's metabolic environment, including rhythmic vascular movements, we may eventually unlock capacities that would otherwise remain latent."

Future research will focus on refining stimulation protocols and determining more precisely how communication between the brain and body supports long term plasticity.

By studying this two way communication pathway in greater detail, scientists hope to better understand how learning becomes lasting and how that process might eventually be enhanced.

Materials provided by Tohoku University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

For courage, says Bulgarian folk wisdom instructs, keep a horse chestnut in your pocket.

Even as a child, I was mistrustful of superstition. But every autumn, I would pick up dozens of them from the sidewalks of Sofia and fill my pockets — not as a spell against fear but as an ode to joy. Conkers, as the English call them, spun me up in delight — shiny as mahogany, smooth as river stones, tiny planets from some other universe, the wonder-smitten eyes of some prehistoric creature.

I didn’t know then that they are emblems of life’s irrepressible insistence on itself — miniature monuments to the stubborn creativity of survival.

Three million years ago, as the Ice Age was beginning to sink its cool blue fangs into the warm body of Earth, the widespread horse chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum) began dying off, until only a small population remained, most of it sheltered in the gorges of Bulgaria’s mountains. There, in their sanctum of stone, the trees found themselves unable to attract pollinators during the slender three-week window of their flowering.

This is the story of life — innovate or die: The horse chestnut evolved enormous white flower spikes with pink tips and a chemical hack to block the oxidation of polyphenols in the petal, which turns each flower brown and sheds it after pollination. For three whole weeks, the horse chestnut remains a bride in a gown of amazement, its crown an aria of perfect white blossoms that no bee can resist, all because there was a safe place in which to experiment with the possible.

That place, I learn from my poet friend Hannah Fries’s absolutely wonderful book A Forest Language, is called refugium. Hannah writes:

When glaciers last crept down from the Arctic, 20,000 years ago, there were places where the icy fingers didn’t reach — mountaintops, hot springs, lowlands beyond the ice. There were pockets of green where things crawled and slithered and ate and mated, protected places where life went on, and from which life set forth again as the ice receded. Refugia.

The gift of a refugium is time. It holds in its small cup of safety a promise for a new world to come. And it lends out to the living all the years, centuries, millennia it might take to finally find that world.

Even in easier times, it is wise to tend the refuge. What is Earth, after all, but a momentary refugium in the inhospitable blackness of space? From a vantage point far beyond our grasping glows the blue-green dot, a brief and luminous memory in the mind of the universe.

It is the memory of a place where a simple cell had the ambition to harness the energy of a star, and from it, the green wonder of leaves, the trunks rising up, bursting and blooming into the sky — all of life in the sweet, cool shade below.

We too need them, these refugia that shelter us, that save us in the ice ages of life. Whatever your refugium may be — a place, a person, a practice, a poem — it is worth tending to with all the might and all the means you have.

#9466. What’s Important to Us When Making Political Decisions?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

A core assumption in any democracy is that citizens with access to information will make reasoned decisions on political candidates and policy issues. But a new study by UC Berkeley social scientists finds that Americans usually don’t consider the full scope of difficult issues, instead basing their opinions on mental shortcuts that sidestep complexity.

The paper offers striking insight into the differences in cognitive reasoning patterns among Americans. While some people in the study did closely analyze a range of issues before coming to an opinion, others did a quick back-of-the-napkin tally of plusses and minuses, or even more commonly based their opinions on just one factor, the authors found.

“When people make complicated choices with many considerations—which political candidate to support, which immigrant they would rather admit to the country, which climate policy they prefer—we tend to assume they’re weighing all the factors,” said Berkeley political scientist Kirk Bansak. But, he added, “we find that most of them aren’t. Most commonly, people rely on a mental shortcut, effectively deciding based on the single factor they care about most and largely ignoring the rest.”

For example, when asked to choose between two fictional U.S. Senate candidates based on age, gender, race, education, military experience, and political experience, many of the study participants would make their decision based on just one of those factors.

That doesn’t mean that people are irrational, said coauthor Nidhi Banavar, a Berkeley cognitive scientist. “The kind of rationality that we define in the paper is quite different from what many humans actually do in real life,” she explained. “We have these amazing brains, but they’re not the infinite computational machines that would be necessary in order to do the kind of ‘rational’ we imagine in our paper.”

Still, the findings have clear implications for politics and political communication. For example, Banavar said, if a leader knows that public opinion on climate change is dominated by pocketbook concerns to the exclusion of other issues, then that single factor might weigh heavily in political advertising. Complex science issues, meanwhile, might be downplayed.

The paper, “Classifying Strategy Use in Multi-Attribute Subjective Choice: Application to Conjoint Experiments in Political Science,” was published recently in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Bansak is an associate professor of political science at UC Berkeley; Banavar is a postdoctoral researcher in political science at UC Berkeley.

The foundational ideals of American democracy grew from the Enlightenment era some three centuries ago. Central to that framework was a belief that humans, being rational, are capable of governing themselves—and justified in demanding political power. A core concept has been the marketplace of ideas, a constant competition between political and policy goals, plans, and analysis that would inform citizens and help them to govern themselves.

While many eras in U.S. history feature episodes in which reason faltered, modern social scientists have detailed the ways in which cognitive bias, rational ignorance, and other behaviors short-circuit reasoning. Still, the hopeful assumption about human reasoning persists.

Social scientists have long studied human decision making at the aggregate level. Banavar and Bansak set out to build a new kind of cognitive model, a complex tool that can enable researchers to see an individual’s decision making mid-process, in detail.

The model doesn’t give them a view into the minds of their research subjects, but the researchers can study hundreds or thousands of decisions by an individual; from these patterns, they can perceive the values and reasoning processes that shape their decisions.

In all, nearly 3,800 people were involved in the study. Each participant sat at a computer screen, and the computer generated a random set of choices in three areas: which migrants they would rather admit to the United States, which Senate primary candidate they would rather vote for, and which climate policy package they would prefer the United States to adopt.

Consider the basic question comparing two hypothetical migrants to the U.S. Their profiles appeared side by side, each described by six factors: region of origin, education level, gender, age, English proficiency, and whether they were seeking economic opportunity or asylum. The research subject would have to choose which of the migrants they preferred to admit to the U.S.

The computer randomly presented 30 different sets of hypothetical migrants. If a participant consistently chose the younger migrant or the migrant with greater English skills, for example, the researchers could conclude that that was the most important factor for that participant.

The same decision framework was presented for comparing potential climate change policies and fictional U.S. Senate candidates.

The research did yield some insights about basic priorities: Participants preferred younger political candidates. They preferred climate change policy that minimized economic impact on their household. They preferred immigrants who were seeking asylum as opposed to seeking economic opportunity, and those who were below retirement age.

But that wasn’t the primary purpose of the study. Banavar and Bansak were less interested in what participants decided, and more interested in how they decided.

The results were striking: In 68% of the cases, study participants used shortcuts and did not deeply assess all six factors when choosing between hypothetical Senate candidates, migrants, or climate policies.

Nearly 54% showed a pattern of making choices dominated by one of the six factors. Another 14% took a different shortcut: Given six factors for each candidate or policy, they counted the total number of factors that they preferred for each, then chose the one containing the greater number.

How many used a comprehensive evaluation of all six factors—a rational assessment, without any shortcuts? Just under 30%.

Interestingly, Banavar said, a majority of participants did not consistently stay with the same strategy. Some might rely on just one factor in choosing a climate policy, while more fully weighing all the factors in deciding which migrant to admit.

“You can’t put people into buckets to say, ‘OK, this is someone who’s actually only going to care about only one thing,’” she said. “People are actually relating differently to each of these different domains and choosing to use different levels of effort, for want of a better term.”

To understand why people shift strategies will require further research, she said.

The study comes with some important caveats: If a participant favored female candidates, for example, or migrants who were seeking political asylum, and if both choices had those attributes, the participants had to consider other factors. That reduced, but did not eliminate, the pattern of making a choice based on one factor.

But when the researchers asked the participants to rate each profile before choosing one of them, the participants were more inclined to consider all factors in making their choices.

Further, the researchers allowed for only two attributes in their comparisons—male or female, for example, white or Black, or aged in their 50s or 70s. That’s not ideal, Banavar said, but to include multiple races, for example, is too complex for the cognitive model, and would dilute the patterns in the data. In the choice of Senate candidates, the study did not include the fictional candidates’ political parties. That question could provoke such strong, reflexive reactions that it would cloud the findings, she said.

The authors say their research has important implications not just for cognitive research, but for real-world, on-the-ground U.S. political processes.

Often, Bansak said, our understanding of public opinion is based on surveys that ask people to choose between complex options defined by many factors. The new research shows analysts that individuals often base their opinions on a single factor, and that can create a clearer picture of what people want in public policy, and why they want it.

“This bears directly on how we interpret the kind of public-opinion and preference data that routinely informs policy debates and news coverage,” he said.

And that understanding, Banavar said, can shape the policy process—and political communication. If leaders present issues in layers of complexity, “how much are people going to read or listen to that?” she asked. “What is the thing that’s really important to them, given a particular issue? That’s completely lost when you don’t think about the decision-making process.”

This article was originally published on Berkeley News. Read the original article.

Edward Lempinen is a writer and media relations specialist with the UC Berkeley Office of Communications and Public Affairs. He has extensive experience in science and science policy communication, including support for global high-level science diplomacy initiatives. He served as producer of the documentary film Science in Exile (2017), which focused on researchers from Syria, Yemen, and Iraq who have been displaced by recent wars and conflicts.

#9465. What happens in the brain when cannabis makes you anxious?

Northwestern scientists have identified, for the first time, a specific group of neurons -- cells in the brain -- that appear to contribute to anxiety caused by cannabinoid drugs, particularly when those drugs are combined with stressful conditions. Cannabinoids are a category of substances that includes THC, the main psychoactive ingredient in cannabis.

To investigate how cannabinoids influence fear and anxiety, researchers exposed mice to a threatening smell derived from fox urine. Before encountering the odor, the animals were given either a placebo or a synthetic cannabinoid drug.

Mice that received the cannabinoid froze more frequently and spent less time exploring the predator scent. Researchers traced these anxiety related behaviors to increased activity in a small population of brain cells known as somatostatin neurons. These neurons are located in the central amygdala, an area of the brain involved in processing fear and stress.

When the researchers genetically silenced the somatostatin neurons, the mice that received the cannabinoid became less likely to avoid the predator odor. The result suggested that these cells play an important role in producing the anxious response.

"The results of this study could explain why a good trip can turn bad pretty quickly if people consume too much cannabis or the situation they are in turns stressful or scary," said study senior author Dr. Sachin Patel, chair of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.

The study was published on Oct. 2 in Nature Communications.

Patel and his colleagues gave mice several different doses of the synthetic cannabinoid and measured their reactions to the predator odor. The researchers recorded how much time the animals spent near the scent and whether they responded by freezing or fleeing.

At the same time, the team monitored activity inside the brain by implanting a small microscope into the mice's brain.

Researchers also studied brain tissue to determine how cannabinoids changed communication between neurons. Their experiments showed that the drug weakened a natural brain mechanism that normally acts as a "brake" on somatostatin neurons. With that restraint reduced, the neurons became more active.

"Higher doses of cannabinoids and environmental stress worked together to synergistically release the 'brake' on the central amygdala, which in turn drove excessive anxiety," Patel explained.

Cannabis use in the U.S. has steadily increased in recent years. At the same time, emergency department visits involving adverse effects from the drug have also risen.

Previous studies have found an association between cannabis use and a higher long term risk of anxiety. Anxiety and mood disorders are also on the rise globally.

"Understanding how cannabis affects brain function to generate its psychoactive effects could ultimately reveal new ways to counteract negative consequences should they arise in some people," Patel said.

The researchers believe the findings may also have relevance beyond cannabis related side effects. Patel said the same neurons could potentially represent a broader target for understanding or reducing anxiety.

"Suppressing the activity of somatostatin neurons in the central amygdala could represent a final pathway for reducing anxiety symptoms, not just in the context of cannabis side effects," he explained.

Other Northwestern co-authors are Farhana Yasmin, Saptarnab Naskar, Danyal Zaidi, Isaac Kandil, Michelle Kwon and Dr. Luis Rosas-Vidal.

The study is titled, "Cannabinoid Modulation of Central Amygdala Population Dynamics During Threat Investigation." It was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grants MH100785 and K08 MH126166) and the Brain & Behavior Research Foundation's Young Investigator Awards.

Materials provided by Northwestern University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
